text:
Good morning, everyone. I declare open this meeting of the Senate Foreign Affairs, Defence and Trade Legislation Committee. I want to begin by acknowledging the traditional custodians of the land on which we are meeting today and pay my respects to elders past and present. The Senate has referred to the committee the particulars of the proposed expenditure for the year 2026-27 and other related documents for the Foreign Affairs and Trade portfolio and the Defence portfolio. The committee has set 5 November this year as the deadline for senators to submit questions on notice. The committee has also set 17 December this year as the date for the return of answers to questions taken on notice.

Under standing order 26, the committee must take all evidence in public session, and this includes answers to questions on notice. I remind all witnesses that, in giving evidence to the committee, they are protected by parliamentary privilege. It is unlawful for anyone to threaten or disadvantage a witness on account of evidence given to a committee, and such action may be treated by the Senate as a contempt. It is also a contempt to give false or misleading evidence to a committee. The Senate has endorsed the following test of relevance of questions at estimates hearings: any questions going to the operations or financial positions of the departments and agencies which are seeking funds in the estimates are relevant questions for the purposes for the purpose of estimates hearings. I remind officers that the Senate has resolved that there are no areas in connection with the expenditure of public funds where any person has the discretion to withhold details or explanations from the parliament or its committees unless the parliament has expressly provided otherwise.

The Senate has resolved that an officer of a department of the Commonwealth shall not be asked to give opinions on matters of policy and shall be given reasonable opportunity to refer questions asked to a superior officer or to a minister. This resolution prohibits only questions asking for opinions on matters of policy and does not preclude questions asking for explanations of policies or factual questions about when and how policies were adopted. I draw the attention of witnesses to an order of the Senate of 13 May 2009 specifying the process by which a claim of public interest immunity should be raised, which I now incorporate into the Hansard.

The extract read as follows—

Public interest immunity claims

That the Senate—

(a) notes that ministers and officers have continued to refuse to provide information to Senate committees without properly raising claims of public interest immunity as required by past resolutions of the Senate;

(b) reaffirms the principles of past resolutions of the Senate by this order, to provide ministers and officers with guidance as to the proper process for raising public interest immunity claims and to consolidate those past resolutions of the Senate;

(c) orders that the following operate as an order of continuing effect:

(1) If:

(a) a Senate committee, or a senator in the course of proceedings of a committee, requests information or a document from a Commonwealth department or agency; and

(b) an officer of the department or agency to whom the request is directed believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the officer shall state to the committee the ground on which the officer believes that it may not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, and specify the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(2) If, after receiving the officer's statement under paragraph (1), the committee or the senator requests the officer to refer the question of the disclosure of the information or document to a responsible minister, the officer shall refer that question to the minister.

(3) If a minister, on a reference by an officer under paragraph (2), concludes that it would not be in the public interest to disclose the information or document to the committee, the minister shall provide to the committee a statement of the ground for that conclusion, specifying the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document.

(4) A minister, in a statement under paragraph (3), shall indicate whether the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee could result only from the publication of the information or document by the committee, or could result, equally or in part, from the disclosure of the information or document to the committee as in camera evidence.

(5) If, after considering a statement by a minister provided under paragraph (3), the committee concludes that the statement does not sufficiently justify the withholding of the information or document from the committee, the committee shall report the matter to the Senate.

(6) A decision by a committee not to report a matter to the Senate under paragraph (5) does not prevent a senator from raising the matter in the Senate in accordance with other procedures of the Senate.

(7) A statement that information or a document is not published, or is confidential, or consists of advice to, or internal deliberations of, government, in the absence of specification of the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or document, is not a statement that meets the requirements of paragraph (1) or (4).

(8) If a minister concludes that a statement under paragraph (3) should more appropriately be made by the head of an agency, by reason of the independence of that agency from ministerial direction or control, the minister shall inform the committee of that conclusion and the reason for that conclusion, and shall refer the matter to the head of the agency, who shall then be required to provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (3).

(d) requires the Procedure Committee to review the operation of this order and report to the Senate by 20 August 2009.

(13 May 2009 J.1941)

(Extract, Senate Standing Orders)

Witnesses are specifically reminded that a statement claiming that information or a document is confidential or consists of advice to government is not a statement that meets the requirements of this 2009 order. Instead, witnesses are required to articulate the harm to the public interest that could result from the disclosure of the information or the document.

I remind senators of their obligations under the Behaviour Code for Australian Parliamentarians to treat witnesses with dignity, courtesy, fairness and respect. I ask members of the media to follow the established media guidelines and the instructions of the committee secretariat. I remind everyone in the gallery that they are not permitted to speak or interfere with the proceedings or with any witness at any point during the hearing. Witnesses and senators who are seeking to table documents during the committee hearing are requested to provide an electronic copy of those documents to the secretariat so we can easily circulate them to members of the committee.

I welcome Senator the Hon. Murray Watt, who is representing the Minister for Defence—just in case anyone is wondering why the senator is here. He is representing the Minister for Defence and the Minister for Veterans' Affairs. Good morning, Minister.
Morning, Senator, and I can confirm I am not in the wrong room!

Thank you; it's good to see you. Before we begin, I did want to acknowledge the service and the sacrifice of Corporal Brendan Hannam, who tragically, as we know, died during a training exercise in Darwin on 5 October. I understand that officials at the table will also make further statements, but I did want to place on the record that he was a much-respected soldier who was deeply valued not just by his unit, his mates and his commanders but also by his friends and family. On behalf of the committee, I'd like to extend our deepest condolences to the corporal's partner, children, family, friends and colleagues and to the wider defence community. Given that a number of us in the committee have dealt with many brave men and women who put on that uniform every day to protect our great country, it was really sad to learn the news of what unfolded. But we honour his service to Australia, and may he rest in eternal peace.
Hear, hear. Well said, Chair.
I'd like to now ask if the minister or any of the officials at the table would like to make an opening statement. Minister?
Not from me, Chair.
Secretary?

Yes, I would. The Department of Defence continues to deliver the government's priorities, with a particular focus on reform, capability building and our people. I wish to acknowledge the tragic death of Corporal Brendan Hannam during a training activity at Mount Bundey earlier this month and pay my respects to his family and friends. We are also thinking of the five soldiers who were injured and wish them a full and speedy recovery. This is a reminder that the men and women who serve in the Australian Defence Force may undertake dangerous activities in order to defend Australia. Their service is occurring against a backdrop of increasing global uncertainty, heightened strategic competition in the Indo-Pacific and conflicts in the Middle East and Europe. This global context has direct implications for Australia's security and national interests. It reinforces the relevance of the 2026 National defence strategy and the urgency of delivering on its priorities. Importantly, international partnerships remain central to strengthening collective deterrence, regional security and capability building.

I will now take the opportunity to highlight a few activities from Defence since we last were before this committee. On 1 September 2026, we marked the 75th anniversary of the ANZUS treaty—the foundation of our enduring cooperation with the United States and New Zealand. We have strengthened our partnership with Papua New Guinea under the Pukpuk Treaty, with PNG citizens now able to apply to join the ADF. The first round of applications will open on 16 November. The Australia-Fiji partnership has been strengthened with the signing of the Vuvale union treaty and the Ocean of Peace Alliance. We established the Defence Delivery Group on 1 July and have made significant progress towards establishing the new delivery agency, which will begin on 1 July 2027. We've consolidated capability development functions for the five war-fighting domains within the Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group, and we've redesigned our defence capability system to support clear accountability across capability development, delivery and operation.

The Defence portfolio board has been established. This board provides strategic oversight of the entire portfolio, which strengthens coordination across Defence, the delivery agency—or the delivery group at the moment and the delivery agency once it starts—the Australian Submarine Agency and the Australian Signals Directorate, amongst other entities in the portfolio. The Defence estate divestments process has progressed, with 11 sites transferred to the Department of Finance and the remaining transitions being carefully managed to support our people, preserve capability and meet operational effectiveness. This week the government introduced legislation to modernise aspects of our administration to support capability development, security, enhanced oversight and powers to respond to threats posed by drones and other uncrewed systems.

In July, we released the updated Defence Industry Development Strategy. In August, we released the updated Defence Innovation, Science and Technology Strategy. We continue to translate priorities into practical outcomes, such as advanced autonomous maritime systems, including Ghost Shark, Speartooth and the Australian developed Bluebottle. We have advanced the Henderson Defence Precinct in Western Australia as a centre for continuous naval shipbuilding and sustainment, with the selection of the site and boundary announced in August. The government signed an arrangement with Canada for Australia's largest ever defence export, an over-the-horizon radar system, drawing on technology developed through our Jindalee Operational Radar Network.

We continue to work diligently to support the government's response to the recommendations of the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide. We released our Respect@Work policy, which requires senior leaders to proactively address the risks of sexual violence and unacceptable behaviour. Our updated corporate plan provides a framework to measure progress and hold ourselves accountable. Our people remain our greatest priority. The progress we are making reflects their dedication, professionalism and commitment. I thank them for the work that they do every day in service of Australia's security and national interests.

I note the discussions in various supplementary budget estimates hearings this week regarding the Secretaries Board submission to the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Parliamentary Standards inquiry into the operation and effectiveness of behavioural codes and standards in the Commonwealth Public Service working place. I and other staff in the department were consulted and contributed to the preparation of that submission. As such, I support the views expressed in the submission. Given the terms of reference of the inquiry, the intent of the submission was to provide a perspective from official witnesses who appear before parliamentary committees. The submission is clear that the board strongly supports parliamentary accountability, transparency and robust scrutiny. The board's concern is not robust questioning itself. The concern arises where conduct experienced by staff may conflict with the secretary's duty as an employer to ensure, as far as reasonably practicable, the health and safety of public servants while at work. As noted by the Secretary of the Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, the secretaries have welcomed the resolution agreed by the Senate on 9 September 2026 regarding the broadcast and publication of proceedings. I will now hand over to the Chief of the Defence Force.
Alright, Admiral, you have the call.

I'm going to start out by setting the context within which our sailors, soldiers and aviators are serving, before heading onto a few other pertinent points. For context, we are increasingly serving in a complex and uncertain strategic environment. The rules based order that we have known for over 80 years is under pressure from those who seek to challenge it and change it for their own benefit. More actors are using coercion and force. In 2025, we saw the highest number of state based conflicts since 1946, with 65 conflicts recorded in 35 countries.

The continued deterioration of the global economic environment also has implications for stability and security around the globe, particularly for our region. Conflict in the Middle East has continued to drive up the cost of fuel and other essential commodities, placing additional pressure on economies and communities. Domestically, the counterterrorism threat in Australia remains set at 'probable'. The espionage threat level is at 'extreme'. Social cohesion is under increasing pressure. At the same time, the forecasted intensity of this year's El Nino system is likely to be very strong, increasing the risk of natural disasters across Australia and throughout the South Pacific.

Collectively, these factors mean there is an increased demand for ADF capabilities, increased demand for ready standby forces to support our allies and partners and increased demand to support potential stability and security contingencies and, inevitably, to support disaster relief operations.

Against this backdrop, we have been very busy since the June Senate estimates. Our sailors, soldiers and aviators have conducted numerous activities at home and across the globe. In Eastern Europe, we continue to train personnel from the armed forces of Ukraine as part of the Norwegian led Operation Legio in Poland. Several ADF members are also embedded in the NATO security assistance and training for the Ukraine headquarters.

In the Middle East, we continue to support the collective self-defence of our partners in the Gulf nations via the deployment of Royal Australian Air Force E-7 Wedgetail aircraft. In the Indo-Pacific, we've conducted operations alongside our allies and partners, including operations Render Safe, Gateway and Solania, and regional presence deployments to support regional security and stability. We've increased interoperability and deepened partnerships with our allies and partners through exercises such as Southern Jackaroo, Rim of the Pacific, Pitch Black and Keris Woomera. Notably, HMA Ships Supply and Stalwart have recently conducted Indo-Pacific deployments, delivering critical replenishment sustainment support to ADF operations and our partners and demonstrating the growing maturity of the Australian auxiliary oiler replenishment capability.

Of note, a fault in the propulsion systems of our two landing helicopter dock ships has been identified. That is being remediated. Adelaide is currently undergoing repairs, and, once completed, Canberra will then have that defect remediated. During this period, HMAS Choules continues to provide coverage for amphibious and domestic support requirements, ensuring Defence retains an appropriate level of contingency response capability.

And earlier this month we commemorated the 25th anniversary of the commencement of Australian operations in Afghanistan, our nation's longest military campaign.

Our people undertake far more activities than I can cover in this opening statement. These examples, however, covering the period from June until now, demonstrate the breadth, scale and impact of the ADF's work. The ADF remains focused on the three strategic objectives we've been directed to achieve in the 2026 National Defence Strategy: to shape, to deter and to respond. To guide how we will deliver on this direction, the senior leadership team and I have developed my commander's intent, which sets out the shared vision, priorities and values for the ADF, following a meeting on my first day in this role with the three-stars in this room. It calls for us to optimise the use of our resources, to be lean where we can so we can invest where we must, and to create a force which is as large and lethal as we can make it with the available resources. We are doubling down on diplomacy, deterrence and partnership, and we will continue to leverage the force-multiplying impact of our allies and partners. Importantly, we are strengthening the resilience and wellbeing of our people and their families to ensure they are supported, respected and protected throughout their service and beyond. A key part of this effort is the continued implementation of the recommendations of the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide, with work well progressed on the 76 recommendations for which Defence has full or joint accountability.

October, though, has been a difficult month for the ADF. We experienced the tragic loss of one of our soldiers when Corporal Brendan Hannan was killed during a training exercise and five of his mates were injured. An investigation into this accident is ongoing, but the accident highlights the risks our people confront every day. Training as we intend to fight is essential to our ability to fulfil our mission to defend Australia and its national interests. This demands realistic training and conditions mirroring those our sailors, soldiers and aviators would likely face in conflict. Realistic training requires us to approach risk professionally and deliberately, identifying, understanding, assessing and appropriately treating it in the context in which we operate. This approach enables us to train how we intend to fight and then come home safely. As such, I have directed the Inspector-General of the Australian Defence Force to conduct a review to determine if there are common causal factors that may have contributed to fatal training accidents over the last few years. My commitment to both the nation and our people is that I will be transparent about the findings of the review and any changes that follow.

Ultimately, our profession is one where our members must be able to rely on and trust one another in the most challenging circumstances. In this context, the act of betrayal involving a recording device in a bathroom on HMAS Leeuwin was an appalling violation of that trust, and the person responsible will be held to account. While I am unable to comment on the ongoing investigation, I will state that my top priority is ensuring that those affected by this incident receive the support they need. A complete fleet audit has been completed. No additional devices have been identified, and HMAS Leeuwin is now at sea on operations.

I'd like to finish by acknowledging all of our people—Australian Defence Force, APS and contractors as well as our Defence families—for their efforts and service; in particular, the roughly 2,800 men and women currently deployed around the world. As an all-volunteer force, every member of the ADF has chosen to serve our nation and, in doing so, willingly accepts the demands, risks and sacrifices that accompany that commitment. Australian sons and daughters, brothers and sisters, mums and dads, friends and communities—every one of us—stand ready to do the nation's toughest work, under the most challenging conditions imaginable, wherever and whenever directed. These people are our greatest capability. Our success depends on their readiness, their commitment, their professionalism and the support of their families and Australians writ large.

Finally, they are represented here today not just by the senior officers and veterans in this room but also by our nation's most senior sailors, soldiers and aviators from the services, seated behind me in the gallery today. I'd like particularly to pay my respects to those individuals for their decades of service and leadership as our senior non-commissioned officers.
Thank you, Admiral. We echo that. Welcome to Senate estimates, folks in the gallery. Senator Paterson will kick off with questions.

At the outset, I associate the opposition with your opening remarks about Corporal Brendan Hannam and express our sincere condolences to his family and teammates. Secretary and CDF, thank you for your opening statements. I'd like to table a letter I wrote to you earlier this week outlining the areas of questioning that I will be pursuing today to give you all an opportunity to be prepared to answer questions in response. I want to start with the cuts to the Integrated Investment Program. In doing so, I note that a large number of answers to questions on notice arrived at 9.40 last night and another large number arrived at 9.07 this morning. These were very overdue and have arrived at a time that makes it very difficult for senators to get across the material in order to ask informed questions today and make the best use of our time on behalf of taxpayers to scrutinise the decisions of the government in this space. Do you know why those answers were returned so late and so close to this hearing?

Before Ms Quinn answers, of course we reject your suggestion that there have been cuts to the IIP. I realise that you'll make that political point over the course of the day, but I want to be very clear that the government does not accept that there have been cuts to the IIP. As you well know, there have been significant increases in funding under this government. But Ms Quinn can obviously answer your question.

Senator, thank you for your letter foreshadowing areas of interest for this committee. It does help witnesses to prepare their answers, and they will come prepared to answer to the fullest extent that they can. On the questions on notice, I wish to apologise to the committee. There were some logistical issues with miscommunication in parts of the organisation. That was one of the contributing factors. The second was to be able to provide you with as much information as we could. Apologies for the elements that were miscommunication within the department.
Could you explain what those logistical issues or miscommunications within the department were?

As you know, the department drafts elements of the answers on notice, consulting across the different areas as required to provide the answers. They then go back and forward with ministers to ensure that they're aware of the questions and they are comfortable, as we're answering on their behalf. There were some issues with that communication back and forward on our behalf.
Back and forward between the minister's office and the department?
Yes.
When were the draft answers first submitted to the minister's office?
In late June.
We're now in late October.
Correct.
That's an enormous amount of time that has elapsed. These were due in early September. What happened? How did that—

Given the large volume of questions on notice, there's a lot of back and forward between the department and officers, and some got lost in the process. Upon receipt of your letter, we did a sweep through everything. I agree the questions you raised were very important and we wish to provide the information, and unfortunately there were delays in providing that information.
Is it just a coincidence that they're in the most politically sensitive area in the portfolio?
As far as I'm aware, yes.

The minister demonstrated by the statement he made on behalf of the minister this morning how anxious the government is to deal with criticism about cuts, and we can have a debate about that if we need to. It just so happens that questions about cuts to the IIP are the ones returned at the last minute. It doesn't seem like a great coincidence to me.
I have nothing to add. I'm not aware of any specific issues.

I understand also that the defence minister's office provided a statement and information on background to the media this morning which related to these issues, just before the committee was due to meet. Are you familiar with that statement that was provided to the media this morning?
No, I'm not.
The department wasn't consulted on any material to go into that statement to the media?
I'm sure elements of the department would have been. We have a very active media area that provides briefing back and forwards.
Is there anyone in the room who has that knowledge? If you do have that knowledge, please come forward.
I can just check. I don't think there's anyone here right now, but we will follow up.
It appears that answers to questions taken in Senate estimates, and taken on notice by the department, were effectively provided to the media before they were provided to the Senate.
I have no visibility of that.

You would understand the obligations that the department has to the Senate and, through us, to Australians and taxpayers; if a question is asked and taken on notice, it has to be returned in a timely way. If the information is available to the minister's office to provide to the media, then it should have been available to provide to the Senate. It's not a great look that it was given to the media before it was provided to the Senate.
We understand our obligations to the Senate.
It doesn't seem to me that the obligations have been fulfilled in this instance.
I accept that. I have apologised for the late delivery of the questions on notice.

Let's get into the substance of the issues. There was a media report by Andrew Greene in the Nightly on Tuesday, I think—or maybe Wednesday—about a budget review that has commenced inside the department. Is that accurate?
No.
There is no review happening in the department?

Not in the sense of anything beyond what we would normally do at this time of year. As part of the PGPA responsibilities and the budget rules, we do a review of our budget on a regular basis. We review it at our defence committee every month, and there are various other mechanisms. We are following our usual process in relation to looking at our budget and managing to meet the budget rules and my PGPA responsibilities as accountable officer. There is nothing unusual in our processes this year. We are working through the mechanisms for the mid-year economic and fiscal update. We have various mechanisms through the course of the year, in the lead-up to the budget and the finalisation of our financial accounts.
Is it true that, as part of this process, nothing is off the table?

We have a process. Our project managers and our program managers review their activities. They provide information into our systems, including our Defence Finance Group. We always review everything at all points in time.
Right. So everything is on the table?
As it is every year.
You won't rule out any further cuts to the Hunter class program?

We go through where programs are up to and projects are up to. We have a series of different processes. We've talked to this committee before about projects of concern and projects of interest. There's detailed project management that occurs through the course of a year. We also do detailed work with our industry partners to see where they're up to in terms of milestones and deliveries. That process occurs on a regular basis. There are sometimes shifts and movements in program deliverables because of either industry concerns or other supply chain constraints and the like, so it's impossible to rule out any change in timing and schedule because there are plenty of things that intervene along the way.
You can't rule out further cuts to the Hunter program?
I can't rule out changes to any of the programs in the department.
Infantry fighting vehicles?
It'll be the same answer if you go through a list of the many hundreds of programs and projects.
AUKUS?
We are working very hard to make sure that we don't have shifts in deliverables and milestones, but we do not control all elements that affect the delivery of projects.
What about the LHDs? Will their retirement be brought forward?

It's the same answer. We go through all the projects. We look at how they're tracking. We look at what the deliverables are and how industry partners are managing. We assess what's happening, and then we respond to the circumstances that we face.
I may need the VCDF for the following questions, which are in relation to what I think you call reprioritisations—what I call cuts—in the IIP.

I will ask the vice chief to come forward to discuss the Integrated Investment Program. I would note that the article you refer to doesn't even get my rank right. It is not the only error. It is speculative. I fully support the secretary's comments. As you know, this is MYEFO time of year here. Of course we are reviewing our budget and finalising budget submissions at this time of year.

I think the journalist gave the government opportunity to comment, and I'm not sure that they took that opportunity to deny it, but anyway. VCDF, when you last testified, you told me that, in the 2026 IIP, there were 22 projects which we'd either cut, descoped or delayed. Of those, you said there were four that had been cut. We talked about one of those, which is the Spartan, while 18 had been descoped or delayed. Can you now tell me what those four programs are.
I don't think I used the term cut. We did use the term divestment—
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: It's my terminology. Use whatever terminology you prefer.

Of the $5 billion that we were talking about over the forward estimates that we were seeking to free up through adjustments in our programmed activity, the vast majority of those were delays and rescoping of projects, reprofiling of their budget, so that we could bring that money forward to higher priority investments. That was the intention of those adjustments. Of that $5 billion, about $500 million was realised through projects where we sought to divest those capabilities. Some examples of this, which we have provided on notice—acknowledging that that did come to you late—was that we had a couple of projects related to deployable infrastructure that we needed to support expeditionary air operations. One of those was a deployable hangar, which in fact we're not even in contract for. We had not even spoken to industry. It was an activity that we had programmed beyond the forward estimates, and, as we look at the priorities and the things that we seek to invest in the nature of the way in which we operate from northern Australia, we have come to conclusion not that it's not necessary and not that it's not a capability that would bring value but that it's a capability that is a lower priority than other things that we seek to invest in. We made similar judgments around some deployable air traffic control facilities.

The other discussion we had to an extent at our last hearing was around the C-27J Spartans. This is not a cutting capability. This is a transition from a platform that, in our experience, has not been value for money, despite the fact that we have achieved extraordinary outcomes with that capability. The team, our 35 squadron at Northrop Grumman that our sustaining that capability, are achieving wonderful things with that aeroplane, but it is an expensive airframe to operate for the outcomes that we get from it, and we are seeking to transition that to a more cost-effective outcome.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: I've got Spartans, hangars and deployable air traffic control. I do have specific questions about each of those, but that's only three. What is the fourth?

The fourth is related to another capability that, at this stage, we do not wish to disclose the adjustments which have been made of. That would compromise our national security in the sense that we would be providing information into the public domain that would be available to our adversaries that we think would be a disadvantage to our national security.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: I'm happy to accept that that is true. I do not think that you would deliberately withhold information like that unless it were genuinely sensitive to national security. I take you at your word. Why hasn't the government offered a classified briefing on that in advance of Senate estimates?
That's not a question I can answer.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: It is utterly routine when there are genuinely sensitive national security issues for a briefing to be offered. If there are questions that can't or shouldn't be asked in this forum, I take that very seriously. We now have a defence committee which can take and receives classified briefings and already has. To my knowledge, that capability change has never been disclosed to that committee, certainly not any meetings that I've attended. I'm in this invidious position where I can't ask reasonable questions about a change that's been made into how taxpayers' money is spent on Defence capability, and I'm none the wiser as to why. This is not a reasonable approach to parliamentary scrutiny of significant expenditure of public money in the national interest.

There are a range of other matters, Senator, that you have sufficient information to inquire. Of course, if you would like to seek a briefing about a particular matter that is not able to be disclosed here today, that request would obviously be considered.
I didn't know that I needed to seek one, because I didn't know that it couldn't be disclosed.

It is not unusual at Senate estimates committees, whether it be this one or other committees, for it to become clear on the day that certain matters can't be discussed, and what happens in that situation is a private briefing, where it's appropriate, can be arranged afterwards.

Minister, I asked questions about this at the last Senate estimates. I sent a letter to the department and the CDF advising that I would have further questions at this estimates. When it comes to issues of national security, we have a very bipartisan approach to this. I have a very good working relationship with the minister and his office. They provide briefings on a routine basis on things that are sensitive. They are always respected, and I don't pursue them if they are genuinely dangerous to national security. But I am in this position where I just have to take you at your word. No information has been provided proactively so we can manage this.

As I say, there are means available to obtain those briefings. The officials have said to you what it is possible to discuss here in an open forum, and, of course, we welcome any other questions you have about those matters. They've made clear that they're not in a position to answer certain other questions, and I'm sure, should you request a private briefing on something like that, the minister's office would consider that.

But, Minister, I now have this problem. There's a secret cut that has not been disclosed that may be to some critical capability. I've got no idea. It may be something inconsequential. I've got no idea.

Again, I reject the assertion that it's a secret cut. There is a process that you can undertake following this hearing to obtain the information that you're seeking, and I'm sure that, once you received that briefing, you would make decisions about what use you want to make of that information.

But I flagged in advance of this hearing, at the last Senate estimates, my interest in these issues. I then wrote in advance. I've been very transparent about what I'm asking about here today. This is not 'gotcha'. This is information that the public has a right to know. I've given you advance warning. You can prepare your talking points—your defensive arguments that you need to justify the government's decisions. This is not some game. These are reasonable questions to ask in the public interest.

I understand that, and I've just had another look back at the letter that you sent. What it has asked is about certain projects. What you've been told today is that there are some of those that can be discussed in an open forum. To me, it sounds like there's one category that can't be discussed in an open forum. There are ways that that can be examined outside of this open forum.

Yes, and if the question on notice had been answered when it was required, by September, we would have had plenty of opportunity to request this briefing. If this letter had been replied to prior to estimates instead—
To be fair, this letter arrived on—what was it—Monday?
Yes. That's more notice than you normally get. Normally, there's no notice at all. I just turn up and ask the questions, but I'm giving you advance notice of my questions. That shows intent.
But you asking in a letter for information to be provided in an open hearing doesn't automatically mean that the officials can provide that information in an open hearing.
Exactly, Minister.
There are other ways to provide that information—
Indeed.
and I'd encourage you to use those other ways.

It hasn't been—that's my point. Look, it is not productive to continue this discussion in perpetuity, but I think this is a very poor approach to parliamentary scrutiny. These are reasonable questions. I would handle it sensitively, given the opportunity to do so, but you've put me in a difficult position. Let's briefly explore those new capabilities. We've talked about Spartan a little bit, and we may get back to that if we have time today, but I'm particularly interested in these new capabilities that are now not proceeding—the deployable hangars and the deployable air traffic control. VCDF, isn't it the case that many of the bases to which these capabilities would be deployed are our bare bases in the north and north-west of Australia that don't have either hangars or air traffic control?

The deployable hangar was more focused on lessons that we had learnt from our deployments over many years in the Middle East, where we had maintainers operating on tarmacs with temperatures exceeding 70 degrees. Therefore, our ability to sustain our aircraft in that environment was not very productive. It meant that we had to have particular PPE. Coolant vests can only work for limited periods. We had to do maintenance activities at night-time. The motivation behind a deployable hangar was more to make sure that, when we're operating in those extreme heat environments, we're able to sustain our aircraft productively.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: Do bases like Learmonth and Curtin and Scherger have hangars?
They certainly do have carport facilities, yes.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: And they're adequate if we had to deploy a large number of airframes there?
Yes.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: What about the air traffic systems?
We currently do have deployable air traffic control systems in the infantry today. This was a decision not to further those investments.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: So we will continue to have deployable air traffic systems.
That's correct.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: Why are we going to buy new ones then?

Our judgement is not that we don't need new capabilities; our judgement is that these capabilities that we had planned to acquire in the 2024 Integrated Investment Program are no longer a priority in comparison to all the other things that we're seeking. We're not saying that they're not useful. We're not saying that there's not a need for them. We're saying that they're now, in our judgement, a lower priority to get after the specific tasks that government has set for us through the National Defence Strategy.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: So is it your evidence that we will have an ongoing deployable air traffic control capability?
Yes.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: What was the advantage about the new air traffic deployable capability that we now will not have?
I don't have that specific detail with me. I'll have to come back to you.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: You just gave me evidence that you were confident that this was not going to be a problem, because we have this other capability, but you can't actually tell me what the difference between the two of them is?
I can tell you that, through our assessments, our judgement is that these additional investments were not a high enough priority to be funded.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: I understand that, but I was starting to be reassured that this was not going to be a meaningful problem, because we have this other capability. But you're now telling me you don't know what the difference between them is.
What I'm telling you is that we assess that we have sufficient capability to be able to operate our aircraft from a deployed facility—to operate them from austere environments.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: A decision was obviously made at some point that we needed to upgrade, extend or expand the deployable air traffic control capability. Obviously, it had some virtues; otherwise it wouldn't have been put in the IP in the first place. But you don't know what they are and you don't know what the deficiencies might be now that we have to continue with the old system.
I can come back to you on notice on the specific elements and advantages of the discrete capabilities that we have chosen not to invest in.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: Thank you. Is it also the case that changes have been made to acquiring minehunters?

There has been a decision taken. We are currently assessing whether we can bring forward the decommissioning of our minehunter coastals and accelerate the introduction of robotic systems to conduct that mission. We do believe that there would be savings achieved if we were able to do that.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

We estimated at the time of the IIP that that would be up to $100 million, but we made the point at the time that that is subject to negotiations with industry around those arrangements.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

We haven't yet come to that conclusion.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

We would seek to bring them forward as soon as possible. That could be even in this financial year.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force
