text: When would the replacement be available?

We are already operating systems within our Navy that are autonomous remote systems and capable of doing a de-mining mission, and they are very similar to systems that are deployed by our like-minded allies and partners currently in operational theatres, including the Strait of Hormuz.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: I was going to ask about that. I know the Chair is looking to rotate the call, so I'll end on this point: hasn't the Strait of Hormuz demonstrated that demining capability is more important than we might previously have thought?

It's a really important point and it's the same point that we have made with the C-27J. We are not divesting of a capability; we are divesting of a platform that achieves that capability and looking for a more cost-effective alternative.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: We might come back to that.

I'd just like to make the broader point that just in the last two years there has been so much change in our operating environment that we do need to continually assess the prioritisation with the Integrated Investment Program to release funds for enhanced cyberdefence capability, UAS and counter-UAS capabilities et cetera. That's the process of racking and stacking relative priorities in the context of the day as opposed to the context of a few years ago. On the mine detection and clearance capability, Sydney Harbour was cleared ahead of the anchorages requirements for our 125th anniversary fleet review earlier this year using entirely autonomous systems. Similarly, we have exercised the capability in Western Australia as part of the Exercise Dugong to clear the anchorages off Fremantle and the approaches down through Success and Parmelia channels to Fleet Base West. So we already do have a capability. The question at play is the value-for-money assessment of continuing to operate crewed systems where we can achieve effects with high-end autonomous systems, and that's what we're working through.
Senator Shoebridge.

Thanks all for your attendance. Admiral Hammond, have you reviewed the executive summary of the IGADF's inquiry into the cultural context in which command over special operations task groups or special forces personnel was exercised in Afghanistan?
Yes, I have.
Has any disciplinary action been taken against anyone in a leadership position as a result of the findings of this inquiry?

Those findings and recommendations were actioned by my predecessors. All departmental actions relevant to that inquiry have been completed and referrals made, where necessary, to government. I've no additional testimony to add to my predecessors'.

Previously, we didn't have this inquiry. We didn't have this report. It was only posted this week by the IGADF. Are you saying you're unable to advise whether anyone in a leadership position within either Special Operations Command or in Defence headquarters has been disciplined, demoted or in other ways brought to account as a result of the findings in this inquiry and the matters contained in them.

There's been previous testimony on accountability for commanders and previous statements made in committee by my predecessors. What I can say is that some actions were referred to the Australian government by former CDFs and I wasn't part of that process. As I understand it, all actions relevant to implementing the recommendations of that report were completed by my predecessors.

That's all well and good, but I'm going to read you out a number of the findings here and I'm going to ask if any action was taken. One of the parts of the summaries of issues from the IGF is:

There was also a significant failure of good leadership and effective command within the Special Air Service Regiment, the Special Operations Task Group and Special Operations Command in the period in question. This was particularly evident in failures to address discipline and compliance, before and during the Afghanistan deployment. Ultimately, these matters contributed to an environment that enabled those who chose to engage in the serious misconduct identified by the IGADF Afghanistan Inquiry.

To be clear, the serious misconduct included allegations of unlawful killings at significant scale. Do you agree with that finding that there was a significant failure of good leadership and effective command?

I have nothing to contest the findings or recommendations of the Inspector-General IDF report, which, again, has been actioned by my predecessors. I remember General Campbell providing testimony on this, including making recommendations to government regarding honours and awards. I understand that previous actions have included accountability for personnel in leadership positions in those operations. The report also highlights that deliberate attempts were made to obscure the facts from high command, and the IGADF therefore came to a conclusion that there was a limit to which personnel could be held accountable.

Well, you must be reading a different report to the one I'm reading. What about this:

Signs of broader decline appear to have been evident to some in higher headquarters. That there was no effective intervention and that this decline was allowed to continue, suggests an absence of effective leadership at various levels.

Do you deny that finding.
No.

I just heard Admiral Hammond say words to the effect that he accepted what was in that report, so I don't know that there's any point asking him whether he disagrees with particular findings. He's accepted that.

Admiral Hammond, you said words to the effect that this report found that there was no basis upon which to hold leadership to account and therefore leadership had not been held—I assume that's one of the reasons you have not held leadership to account. Did I misunderstand your answer?

Again, we're dealing with a historical issue that predates my tenure here. The Deputy Prime Minister advised parliament on 12 September 2024 that he had written to relevant commanders about his decision in relation to medals awarded to them as part of their service during periods proximate to the incidents which are at the heart of the Brereton report. General Campbell provided multiple statements to various committee hearings about taking action with respect to commanders involved in the timeframe you're talking about. We're talking, in many instances, about more than 15 years ago.

General Campbell never once identified a single commissioned officer who had been held to account, disciplined or had any adverse action taken against them. There has not been a single instance of a commissioned officer—anyone in a leadership position—being held to account. How could that possibly be, given what we read in this report?
You'd have to refer that to General Campbell.
No. I'm referring it to the current Chief of the Defence Force. That's you.
If you want me to look into historical actions against individuals, that, of course, is a different question. What's your question?

I would like to know whether or not anyone in a leadership position was held to account because of what they knew. I'll give you another report:

There was tangible data available for higher headquarters through trends in growing numbers of Enemy Killed in Action. This included growth and spikes in these statistics over time, as well as features such as a lack of wounded insurgents (only deaths) and the lack of ADF casualties. By historical standards, elements of this data presented as most unusual. Some commanders were alert to this data and rumours that accompanied it while others were not, which may suggest an abandonment of curiosity.

Was this data about the number of deaths, the absence of wounded and the absence of ADF casualties available to higher headquarters, and why wasn't any action taken?

I'll have to take that on notice. What I can talk to is what has been done since the inquiry report with respect to improving command accountability across the service in the Australian Defence Force, the introduction of an appointment to command certificate to provide greater accountability of commanders. Just in the last three months I've replaced the ADF chiefs of service committee system with the ADF command board system, and in our very first day in job, the respective service chiefs and I had a very long conversation at the defence academy about command accountability. But your questions go to historical issues. I'm happy to take them on notice and come back to you.

My primary question isn't just being asked by me; it's being asked by current serving members of the ADF and by retired members of the ADF and the veterans community. They are saying, 'Well, if headquarters was aware of the deaths and was aware of these reports, and if commissioned officers and the headquarters of the special operations team was aware of this, why is it that only non-commissioned officers are being held to account and prosecuted, and why is it that nobody in a commissioned officer position is being held to account?' That's the question that's being asked, and it's eroding confidence in the ADF.

There are two parts to your statement. One is about being prosecuted, and that is different to being held to account. I acknowledge there is some overlap. It is true to say that there are no commissioned officers being prosecuted. What I can state is that the Brereton report and the subsequent investigations have focused on evidence availability that's led to charges and will be dealt with in accordance with the Australian legal system. When it comes to command accountability, your assertion that no commissioned officer has had consequences amounting to being held accountable is something that I can't speak to, because I haven't been involved in that process. I'm quite happy to take that question on notice. Have senior officers or commissioned officers, as I understand it, had consequences amounting to accountability? Is that your question, Senator?
Yes. That is one of my questions. If so, can you identify them by name and rank—if not by name, then by rank—and the consequences that were put in place?
I'll take that on notice.
One of the most disturbing features in this report is the practice of throwdowns. Do you know what the practice of throwdowns is?
Yes. I've read the report.

This is where people in Afghanistan were killed by the special operations group and then, after they were killed, weapons were placed on their bodies and photographs taken to seek to justify the unlawful killing of people in Afghanistan. We're of one mind about what throwdowns are?
Yes. My answer to your question is still yes.

This comes from the IGADF report:

The unwillingness to challenge non-commissioned officers was particularly apparent from the breakdown of military discipline through a lack of proper supervision. The failure to address the widely known use of throwdowns is an example of this for which substantial comment is provided in the report. This was also a manifestation of a broader breakdown of military discipline within the Special Air Service Regiment. The tolerance of officers of overt non-compliance sent a powerful signal.

The thought that officers who either were deployed on the operations or were in the Special Operations Task Group headquarters were aware of this practice and did nothing is incredibly disturbing. Being aware of that unlawful practice, which was disguising unlawful murder, would be a matter that I would have thought would see you, if it was proven, exiting the Defence Force at a minimum. Has anyone had that consequence attached to them? They were aware of this unlawful practice; they did nothing. Has anyone exited the Defence Force because of this?

Firstly, I agree with your response to the allegations. It is extremely unprofessional. That behaviour is absolutely not in concert with our values, our professional standards of behaviour that we expect of our personnel. So I absolutely agree with your reaction to that allegation. I cannot speak to the second part, though, which is your question as to whether or not people have been exited from the service. I'm happy to take that on notice.

It's not just about the unlawful murders and the throwdowns that were happening in the field. It's also about the practices in the barracks, which I understand to have also included the mocking of dead people from Afghanistan, including drinking out of a prosthetic limb. That happened in plain sight of officers repeatedly, it's my understanding—repeatedly—on base. Has anyone been held to account for allowing that practice to continue, and, if so, what happened?

Again, I agree—completely unacceptable behaviour. An 'inversion of authority' is what the IGADF referred to—a breakdown in culture, a normalisation of unacceptable practices. All of that is contained and utterly unaligned with the expectations we have of our personnel. It also talks to relatively junior officers, the people who were on the ground, and makes a whole bunch of recommendations about how we should do things differently in the future, which have been taken into account. Again, with respect to consequences, I'm not in a position to speak to that. Many of these issues have been dealt with over a period exceeding 10 years. I'm happy to take it on notice.

I'm happy you're taking that on notice, but your answer again mischaracterised this report as being only related to junior officers on the ground. There are repeated references to headquarters having data that should have alerted them to the fact that something very bad was happening in Afghanistan. One of the elements of that was, for example, the reference to the higher rate of kinetic operations, and it's this:

With each successive deployment the number of Afghanistan deaths and collateral damage increased. Whether through enhanced insurgent activity, an unhealthy familiarity with the operating environment, or the presence of hubris, the inference could be drawn that appetites for kinetic operations grew at the expense of the winning over of the local population.

Now, that data was available to headquarters—the fact that more and more Afghan deaths were happening in the course of each deployment, and you kept sending the same people back for tour after tour after tour. And the deaths were rising. Headquarters was aware of that. Headquarters made the decision to continue to send the same people into Afghanistan, and nobody in headquarters has been held accountable for that. How is that the case? Yes, people who have potentially engaged in war crimes are being prosecuted; that's what should happen. But headquarters made the decision to keep sending the same people into deeply traumatising situations. The data's coming out about what happens, and everybody in headquarters just walks away with retirement packages and promotions and no accountability—nothing. That's what makes people so angry about this. Why is nobody in headquarters held to account?

You're talking about historical issues which predate my tenure. I can state that I agree with the findings of the IGADF. I reject the fact that people should be able to behave that way and get away with it. I'm absolutely in agreement; there are serious failures here that need to be addressed. Ultimately, those recommendations have been made to my predecessors. They've been actioned. The recommendations have been made to the Australian government.

Your predecessor was in the exact same chain of command. He was, for a significant part of his career, out in that operation space, and he was in the chain of command. That's why people are saying, 'How can we have faith in the response?' We now know that there are all these concerns about what headquarters knew or should have known—and you keep pointing back to your predecessor, who was in the chain of command at the time.

To the last point you made—'at the time'—the period that this report is looking at is in some contexts longitudinal. It talks to a greater period of time. The period that the war crimes are looking at is a much more discrete point of time. I acknowledge that we had many commanders circulate through the Afghanistan conflict in different locations during different times, and, absolutely, the majority of operations and personnel who served in Afghanistan did so with complete professionalism and acquitted themselves to meet the highest expectations of the Australian people and the Australian Defence Force. These particular issues have been completely investigated. Some of them remain under active consideration by the Office of the Special Investigator. I've offered to take on notice questions as to what accountability actions have been executed by the department before. I'm in no position to take action against my predecessor.

I took issue with your statement earlier about junior officers. We've had the exchange about headquarters; we're clearly not of one mind about that. But another key part in this finding that goes well beyond your positioning of it being about junior officers on the ground is finding 21:

Some legal officers and intelligence officers may have facilitated the concealment of misconduct through production of reporting and adjustment of intelligence. It is not clear to us as to whether this was inadvertent or not.

Has any action been taken in relation to legal officers and intelligence officers as a result of this finding?
Many of those officers would have been Australian Public Service members who were also serving in the field. I'm happy to take that question on notice.

I'd ask you both to take this on notice, because I understand some legal officers were uniformed, some intelligence officers were uniformed and some were in the department. Paragraph 39 of the summary talks about the relationships and the preceding bits—the relationships between the special operations task groups and the intelligence and legal officers who were meant to be providing some independent review about it:

It is not suggested that legal or intelligence officers consciously facilitated misconduct, however; it seems clear that some obstructed the proper investigatory mechanisms, including by the Provost Marshal—ADF, within the governance system that may have allowed misconduct to have been detected sooner.

I know you accept these findings, Admiral Hammond. Do you accept the findings too, Secretary?

I do. The findings go to operational training and support and oversight mechanisms. We will incorporate all that into reviews and consideration of how things are structured now. We take the IGADF report seriously. It's an excellent mechanism to provide oversight of activities in the department and in the defence forces. Of course we take it seriously, and we will take into account as we review all the mechanisms and supports we put—when we put people in harm's way, we need to make sure the systems are supporting them.

One of the key reasons the IGADF didn't delve further into these individual instances of misconduct was that the IGADF didn't want to prejudice potential or current criminal proceedings underway. But the department has an obligation to investigate this. The department has an obligation to see whether or not any legal or intelligence officers employed by the department obstructed the proper investigative mechanisms, including by the Provost Marshal. Has the department done that?
I'm happy to take that on notice.
Admiral Hammond, to the extent that these individuals were uniformed, the same obligation lies upon you and the three services. Has the ADF undertaken that?

I agree that the behaviour you're describing is completely unacceptable. I'm quite happy to take the question on notice. I would like to speak to the current expectations on command accountability. I am absolutely of the view that commanders should be inquisitive; you get what you inspect, not what you expect. Over the last three years in my previous role, eight people in command positions have been removed from those positions for failure to meet those expectations and requirements. This is something we agree on. I absolutely agree with you that there should be the highest standards of expectation with respect to our behaviour and the performance of our senior leaders, and we should be inquisitive. I'm happy to take on notice those questions on the historical matters you were talking about.

If there have been effective and real consequences taken against more senior officers, if there has been any effective action taken against people in headquarters, both in the Special Operations Task Group and here in Defence headquarters, there's an obligation to tell not just the public at large but the ADF community, because the thing that is eroding faith and trust in what's happening at the moment is this seeming accountability gap between what happens if you don't have a gold braid on your shoulders, where the book gets thrown at you—and I'm not in any way criticising accountability for potential war crimes; that absolutely should happen. But it's the accountability gap. Between the people on the ground and the people who are in leadership positions who were either aware of it or had the data that should have triggered that and had not taken action—it's that accountability gap that is eroding trust. If you have evidence of any accountability being taken against senior officers, that would go some way to assisting that accountability gap. In the absence of that, it will continue to grow.
On that note, we will go to Senator Dowling.

I've got some questions about the Defence budget. With some of the recent speculation about cuts and what it all means, I think it's good to get a few points of clarification. First, can you clarify that, through both the 2024 National defence strategy and the 2026 National defence strategy, government measures add up to $117 billion additional over the next decade of funding.
That is correct.

On the topic of overprogramming—I've heard that term a lot—can you explain what overprogramming is. I understand a big focus of the government has been making the Defence budget more sustainable. The committee has already heard evidence about this at previous estimates. I understand overprogramming is something that you use to manage the IIP, but perhaps you can refresh everyone's memory with an explanation of what overprogramming is and how it's used.

Overprogramming is a situation where you guard against the budget underperforming, in terms of not being able to spend all the money you've been allocated by government within a certain particular year. It's a method used in various different portfolios; it's not just confined to Defence. It happens where you've got complex projects over multiple years where there might be shifts in milestones and schedules. When you've got multiple projects of such a nature, you want to make sure you're maximising the capability delivery in any particular year. So it can be the case that individual projects are financed and then you add in more projects than the total budget will ultimately support within year, with the intention that, if there are shifts in schedule, you can continue to fund other ones that are ahead of schedule. It happens in infrastructure projects. It happens in capability development. It also happens in sustainment activities within Defence. It's a process that's used in the private sector and across government. It's something that I used as the Secretary of the Department of Industry, Science and Resources relating to, particularly, capital projects. It's also the case for the infrastructure program that there is a level of overprogramming. It is a natural way to ensure that we don't have a surplus at the end of the year and that we're delivering within year to meet government's priorities.
So it's effectively like a budgeting tool?
It is absolutely a standard budgeting tool.
In the 2026 national defence strategy, what was the planned overprogramming level in both the NDS and the Integrated Investment Program?

I'll just call my colleague to the table. Within the Defence budget, the Integrated Investment Program is the largest acquisition budget, and it has a level of overprogramming. Historically, it's been very high. Over time, we've sought as a department—and the government has supported this—to bring that down to lower levels, partly because the nature of the processes and programs we're now looking at suggests we should move from the low 40s down to a number around 20. The level of overprogramming you want to put into a program is going to depend on the precise activities that are being supported. The uncertainty related to timing and slippage of different activities is greater at the start of a significant program than it is at the end, so the timing and sequence of projects mean that the precise level of overprogramming that is prudent will shift over time. I'll pass to the vice chief, who was looking at the Integrated Investment Program overprogramming levels.
The overprogramming targets that we set for ourselves in the 2026 Integrated Investment Program were, over the forward estimates, 21 per cent, 19 per cent, 17 per cent and 16 per cent respectively.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: Is that significantly lower than what was in the 2024 national defence strategy?
Yes, it was. In 2024, we were working to caps that were at 28, 24, 22 and 22 per cent.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: Okay.

As I mentioned, as we move further into a delivery cycle, it makes sense for us to think about the overprogramming levels. We review what's appropriate every year and provide advice as part of the usual budget processes, so the overprogramming level does shift, as I said, depending on how we're working with industry partners to deliver. You can understand that a project that's an innovative technological project and that's in spiral development, where there's an iteration, may have a different certainty on its milestones compared with a straightforward infrastructure project that has well-established capability within industry and well-understood timelines and project management. There were some issues around managing the budget through the post-COVID period, where supply chains were interrupted. It's also an issue that, when there's been a change in the relative priority stack within the Integrated Investment Program, you also get some changes to the timing of delivery of projects. So it's a very focused effort from the department to think about what overprogramming level makes sense.

Within any one year, if you start the financial year with a level of overprogramming, the requirement of accountable authorities and all the delegated authorities within the department is to work within year to reduce that level of overprogramming so that the overall budget comes in as required by the budget rules. Every year, there's a mechanism of reducing overprogramming such that we end up on balance. In the last few years, the Defence budget has been slightly over budget, but by less than one per cent of the target. In previous years, there was an underspend. So the other aspect is making sure that we're thinking about the maturity of our capability system and other aspects of the department to make sure that we meet the budget requirements.

It sounds like quite a different shift. In the 2024 NDS, I think it was on target to get as high as 40 per cent or something like that. Now you're saying that, across the forward estimates, it might come down to 16 as the target?

That's right. There has been a shift as we've worked with industry and as we've been clearer on their capability to deliver and our capability to manage the requirements. It is a focus of the reform within the department on improving our capability system for us to work on the cost capability, the schedule, timing and scope to make sure that we can reduce the level of overprogramming. It would be better for everyone if we could be more targeted, but, in a very complex acquisition and sustainment with $40 billion any one year, it is always going to be the case that we will have elements of overprogramming.

It was in the 2024 IIP that the overprogramming was set at caps of 28, 24, 22 and 22. The number that you're referring to, where overprogramming peaked as high as 42 per cent, was actually back in 2022.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: It sounds like things are improving, though, in terms of how you're looking to manage the IIP. Have you put in place new procedures or processes in how you actually make sure you're better targeted around achieving those overprogramming—

As I mentioned, we are looking at improving our ability to manage the acquisition sustainment budget and projects, so there's a whole sequence of reforms that we're working through. I mentioned some of them in my opening statement. One aspect is the redesign of the capability of the entire system so that we've got a greater focus on making sure that, at the front end, we've got commercial realities, industry input and cost efficiency, including using market intelligence and other data tools that are available to us now. The intention there is that, once projects are provided to the delivery agency, they are scoped and targeted in a way that allows for us to understand their milestones appropriately. That's one aspect. The second aspect is just the improvement in the professionalisation of our project managers to be able to manage those projects and for them to have the skills and capability. The third aspect is working with industry so industry is upskilled and the cooperation between the department, the services and industry is close and well managed so that we've got a good understanding of where there are issues and how we can manage those quickly and effectively. The fourth aspect is the creation of the delivery agency, which will be singularly focused on delivering against the IIP and supporting on sustainment projects. The intention over time is to continue that professionalisation that's already happening, but it'll have a singular focus on managing the projects. That will all go together to allow us to think about overprogramming, but, as I said, we don't control all aspects of a project. There are reasons beyond our capability, to do with industry supply partners and supply chains. We've seen some impact, for example, on cost and schedule as a result of the Middle East, flow-on consequences for the higher oil prices et cetera. We are always going to have movements in such a complex program, so there will always be some level of overprogramming.
Thank you.
Senator Pocock, I know you've got to get to another committee, so I'll come to you.
Thanks for your time this morning. I've got some questions about Defence's contract with Bupa.
Bupa, the health provider?
Yes.
I'll just get a witness that may be able to answer.
Who's the official coming up to the table?
We'll have Chief of Personnel Lieutenant General Fox and the Surgeon General of the Australian Defence Force.
That's a very thick folder. I understand that defence has awarded, following an open tender process, the next ADF health services contract beyond 27 June to existing provider Bupa. Is that correct?
We are currently in an open tender process and are currently in negotiations with a preferred provider, so it's not yet been awarded. The operative date for that contract will be end of June 2027.
On the current contract, has Defence now recovered the full $7.12 million in incorrectly paid performance bonuses to Bupa?
I will defer to my colleague.

I can confirm that there are a range of recovery payments under the contract that have occurred over the last few years. The $7.9 million was one. There are still also a couple of outstanding recovery payments underway, so I could take that on notice and confirm for you what has been recovered and what has not yet.
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: That would be good. So you think there still could be payments that need to be recovered?

A small amount. The vast majority of payments for recovery have occurred over the last 12 to 24 months—to an amount that is beyond the $7.9 million. From memory, I'm thinking approximately $40 million.
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: In going through this tender process, what weighting is being given to the performance of the incumbent, Bupa, as part of the tender evaluation?
Because we are still in negotiations and we do not yet have confirmed outcomes of those negotiations—they're actually currently underway as I speak—I could take that on notice.
Okay. More generally, do you take performance into account when you're going through a contracting process, things like ADF member satisfaction, outcomes, complaints—all those sorts of things?
Yes, we take into account past performance of contractors in relation to a raft of measures to assess suitability for future contracts.
Do you look at the broader corporate and regulatory record of companies, or is that beyond the scope of what Defence looks at?

We look at those measures in terms of the relevant company and their performance and their financial viability, as examples. I could bring the relevant commercial expert to the table, who assists us in those negotiations and what we look at.
Senator, we do operate under the Commonwealth Procurement Rules, which do require us to look at—
Very loosely.

We do comply with the procurement rules. We are audited on that as part of ANAO's audit program and take seriously our obligations under the frameworks that the government provides through the Department of Finance. In those procurement framework rules, there is a requirement for us to look at the fit-and-proper activities, the governance, the legal veracity, anything to do with regulatory procedures et cetera. That is taken into account in all our contract and procurement processes.
In terms of the Commonwealth Procurement Rules, what is Defence's definition of an Australian company?

We comply with the updated definition of an Australian company. The procurement rules were changed—I can't remember the exact timing; it was certainly in the last 12 months—to provide a definition for an Australian company, to expand it beyond just a business number location. We comply with that change in the procurement rules—from the time at which it was included.

Why is it, then, that at previous estimates, when asking about procurement, I've been told by Defence that a sovereign Australian company is any company that sells anything to any of our allies? That's very different to the CPRs.

I'd have to look at the specific question that you put previously. There has been a change in the procurement arrangements for us, in terms of procurement within Australia and the Australian change. That was largely so that the government could track, across government spending, what's going to Australian companies, because an ABN is one aspect but it's not the full captured aspect of it.
So Defence does comply with the Commonwealth Procurement Rules?
Yes. We're required to under the PGPA Act obligations, and that is the expectation of all officers undertaking procurement.

I've been told that under the current contract with Bupa there are a high percentage of units not medically fit. For example, one battalion in the NT had 35 per cent of ADF on some form of medical restriction. Perhaps on notice you could provide a summary of how many serving personnel are medically unfit or on some form of medical restriction that would impact deployment.

I can answer that now. In fact, over 75 per cent of the ADF are actually in a deployable military employment classification. We have some that are temporarily downgraded, and those that are temporarily downgraded in a military employment classification might be for an injury that has an ongoing rehabilitation requirement, but it's only a temporary downgrade. So over 75 per cent are in military employable capability or classifications.
What's the breakdown of the other 25 per cent?

There's just over 13 per cent temporarily in a military employment classification, which is classification 3, and then in classification 4, there's just over four per cent. We have a number of people who are on a transition pathway, and that's just over one per cent.

I have some questions to follow up on from last estimates about the Defence Home Ownership Assistance Scheme. I was concerned that I couldn't find any announcement of the successful tenderers for the new Defence Home Ownership Assistance Scheme lender panel. The tender closed a year ago, and it was due to commence on 1 July this year. Why the delay, and when will the new panel be announced?

As we discussed at the last hearing, we undertook an open tender process for the new panel. We have largely concluded that work now. We are in the final stages of negotiating the deeds of agreement to establish the panel. We extended the existing panel until December of this year to enable us to continue work with the successful tenderers, and we are working with the relevant minister, the Minister for Defence Personnel, to finalise those arrangements and anticipate an announcement by the end of this year.
Why is it running so far over time?

It's not unusual in complex tender evaluations and negotiations against a number of providers for that to take a little longer. The existing panel did have the capacity for us to undertake an extension, which we've done, and I would say that, as we're settling these arrangements, we have been concerned with the new panel arrangements to really negotiate through the measures of effectiveness and the elements that we want to see to make sure we've got a good opportunity across the new panel to keep delivering great outcomes for members.
It strikes me that this is certainly not the most complex procurement Defence does. That aside, how many additional providers on top of the current ones will be included?
Until we've settled those negotiations and agreed, there are a couple of regulatory elements that the relevant minister needs to make. I'm not in a position to talk to the final arrangements.
Thank you, Ms Perkins. So those negotiations haven't concluded; you haven't locked in any additional lenders?
We're in the final negotiations on the deed of agreements with the preferred tenderers.
Are there any changes to the scheme design being contemplated to deliver a better deal for ADF personnel? As we covered last time, it's a bit of a raw deal.

As we discussed last time, the Defence Home Ownership Assistance Scheme, which is now supporting over 30,000 eligible and current members, is legislated. The essential arrangements through the panel will be largely consistent with what those 30,000 members are currently experiencing. But, as I said, part of the work we've been doing to settle the deeds of agreement has been to strengthen the capacity for ourselves and the Department of Veterans' Affairs in the administration of the scheme to implement some of the policy changes that were worked through over the last year or so to expand eligibility. But also we're really keen to—we already do very regular testing of the competitiveness of the scheme—increase the transparency around that and increase our ability to share back to those 30,000 members good information about the scheme and how to use it well and how to work with their home loan providers.
Has Defence assessed how many eligible members and veterans forgo the subsidy because they can get a better deal elsewhere?

It would be very difficult for us to assess the individual financial choices of members and veterans. What I can say is that, over the last number of years, we've tracked a year-by-year increase in people accessing DHOAS. As I mentioned, we're about 30,471 members now. That's up over 3,000 members from 2024-25. And, as I said, we're keen in the new panel to really work hard on how we engage members using the scheme and veterans and those who might seek to use the scheme to understand its benefits and how to work with their home loan providers.

It struck me, if you actually want to ensure that it is a better deal, that you would find a way to track whether people think it's a better deal or whether they are just going to another bank. Under the new lender panel, with the arrangements that you're negotiating, will you require participating banks to make their products available through accredited mortgage brokers? Currently, I think only one of the three providers permits mortgage brokers.

The design of the panel arrangements, as I've noted, in many ways is prescribed through the relevant legislation. I might take on notice the specifics of that question, because, as I said, we're still in those final negotiations on the new deeds of agreement.

Sure. I don't think anything in the legislation precludes them allowing the use of mortgage brokers. I assume this has been raised with you as an issue through consultation. Surely you could actually require them to allow mortgage brokers so that people can get a better deal.

Let me just make sure that I work with the team settling the agreement so that we get the right answer for you. The legislation doesn't allow mortgage brokers to be part of the panel. You're right, though—how those home loan providers operate. I just don't have the specific details of where we've landed on that.
Okay, thank you.
I'll come to Senator Lambie now and then Senator Paterson after that.
I'll need Lieutenant General Fox.
Perhaps we'll just clarify the topic of the questions that you have so that we can ensure that we've got the appropriate witnesses up.
Sorry, it is abuse in Defence.
It may go to a policy question et cetera, so we're happy for you to ask the question, and we'll make sure the right person is at the table.

On 2 December 2025, Minister Keogh stated that sexual misconduct in the Defence Force is unacceptable wherever it occurs. Do you accept that Australian Defence Force members should be protected from sexual discrimination and sexual harassment under Australian law, regardless of where they are serving?
I can answer that—yes.

The law firm JGA Saddler has started a class action in the Federal Court of Australia on behalf of current and ex-serving ADF members, females who have experienced sexual assault or discrimination while serving in the ADF. I do understand, though, the case is before the courts and technically falls under a different portfolio. However, Defence still has a responsibility to explain its policies to serving members. Has the Australian Defence Force bothered to inform their members that the legal protection against assault, discrimination or abuse may not apply to conduct that occurs on overseas bases or ships on international waters?

I might just put this into context and then the specifics on the ADF side. Right across both the Public Service and the ADF, we have a requirement under the respect-at-work act to provide the protections that you're talking about. We have implemented our internal policy on that, which requires every commanding officer and every public servant within the Public Service as well to understand their obligations, to look at a risk assessment and to take action against that risk assessment to ensure a safe workplace for their staff, particularly related to sexual violence. That policy has been implemented. It has been communicated and will be actioned with a high priority across the Public Service and the ADF. There's been a great deal of work with experts on how to do this and the support mechanisms, and we've put a lot of effort into making sure that senior officers understand their obligations and have the capability and tools to be able to undertake it. We have been very clear, both I and the CDF, that there is no place in either the Public Service or the defence forces for abuse against other staff, including relating to sexual violence. There is a unified view amongst our leadership about the importance and focus on this issue, and we take it very seriously.
You are talking about when it happens on overseas bases or ships on international waters?
We have accountability for our staff wherever they are.
I know you've got accountability, but when did that change in law? I'm sorry; I haven't seen a law change with that up here yet.
The respect-at-work act requires accountable officers to ensure a safe workplace for their staff wherever they are.
Okay, so that will now cover what has been missing. Is that what you're telling me?
It requires us to ensure a safe workplace for wherever our staff are.

Yes, I know. That's not what I'm asking you though, okay? I haven't seen a law change on that. That's the first place. You might have said a 'workplace', but it hasn't been changed in law. That is one of the reasons that JGA Saddler has been fighting in court—because they didn't have that. Can you tell me if that's been changed in law?
I'll pass to our legal colleague.

In terms of your question, which relates to the extraterritoriality of the Sex Discrimination Act, the law has not been changed, but, in the context of the matter, this issue will be considered as part of the proceedings.
How long do you think that law change will take?
I couldn't talk to the law change. That's obviously a different policy authority, as the Attorney-General's Department actually own—
Who in Defence is dealing with the Attorney-General's Department on this issue?

There are a range of engagements going. It's a policy authority of the Attorney-General's Department under their human rights legislation policy, so that engagement continues on an ongoing basis across a number of agencies.

So we've got no timeline on this or anything. Even though there's an abuse problem in our defence forces which has come out quite clearly, which I haven't finished with yet, we've still no timeline on this to have this changed for these women.
Certainly this issue on the Sex Discrimination Act is a different issue to our Defence Force Discipline Act, which of course does apply extraterritorially.
All of us are very aware of the illegal camera incident that occurred recently on HMAS Leeuwin. Has the audit of all bathroom facilities across the naval fleet been completed?

Can I just start by personally acknowledging your service in uniform and thank you for it and your advocacy for our people and, particularly noteworthy, shining a light on women's health issues. It has made an impact, so thank you. With respect to the HMAS Leeuwin incident, I note you were not in the room when I made my opening statement this morning, where I briefed the chair and the senators here that the audit of the entire fleet has been completed and no other devices have been found. The investigation remains ongoing. The member has been stood aside, and the ship is at sea on operations.

I did miss that, sorry. It must have been while I was coming up. I was watching some of that. Do you know whether that's gone across the other forces as well? Has Air Force done the same? Has Army done the same?
That has been directed. To be honest, the service chiefs had pre-empted the order. Our reflex is to take action as a leadership team. I have not yet had a closure report on the other two services.
When do you expect that closure report from the other two services? Do you have any idea?
I'll follow up during the break. I'll get back to you.

Thank you. This might be an IGADF thing. Do you know how many investigations relating to an alleged act of military sexual violence against a member of the Navy are currently being conducted by the Joint Military Police Unit? Do we have numbers of that across the board?
Can I take that on notice? Let me come back to you. We'll discuss it during the break.
We do track investigations—numbers—against all those categories, on both the APS side and the ADF side. We will have those numbers somewhere, and we can definitely take it on notice.
Okay. Can I have the numbers on whether those issues have been resolved? I don't need to know the case names or anything.
We track incidents as reported incidents as they go through processes and then the different resolution mechanisms.

If I may, my preference would be to take it on notice, so I can give you a fulsome answer. There's a difference between allegations and outcomes. I'd like to give you the full appreciation of the number of investigations and those that have been closed.
Okay. That'd be good. Can you tell me how it runs when there is sexual violence against a member, whether that's Navy or—I'm not sure if it should be any of you answering those questions.
It's service wide.

I'm happy for you to answer them, Admiral, but how does it work? How long does it take to get to the top? How long does it take to get to you? Tell me what the procedure is. When something happens, how long does it take from the point that it's happened, when they find out—whether it's ship, land, Air Force or whatever—to when it gets to the top?

It's minutes or hours. I have a critical commander's information requirement that requires the service chiefs to report to me in a timely manner any allegations relating to sexual violence. In relation to the Leeuwin incident, I was flying overseas on Monday, and you can imagine my reaction to the report, particularly noting my previous role. And, yes, I was advised in a very timely manner, and I would like to commend Admiral Buckley for his leadership in responding to this incident, particularly the support to our personnel who were affected at HMAS Leeuwin. I'd also like to acknowledge the professionalism and teamwork displayed by the crew of HMAS Leeuwin in resolving this incident, bringing it to our attention in a timely manner and allowing us to deal with it.
Can you tell me whether, as soon as these cameras were found—
It was one camera, for the record.

Sorry—one camera. As soon as this camera was found, how many days did it actually take to remove those women off the ship? What was the lag time? Did that happen after I came out and spoke? What happened in those three or four days?
I'll ask Admiral Buckley to come to the table to speak to the specifics that he can, whilst recognising the sensitivity of the ongoing investigation.
Thank you.
What I would note is that the investigation was underway before you drew national attention to it.
I understand that.
And my preference, if you would indulge me, would be, where you become aware of an active investigation, perhaps bring it to my attention first.
Yes, I'm going to do so after this, because I need to see you—because I do not want to speak about some of the other things I've heard in the last week. I do want to speak to you about that.
We'll have a conversation.

I think one is enough. Nobody wins out of it. But I want this fixed, because my thought would be that I'm working very hard on that bill that I have produced, and I'm listening to amendments. We've been through it. Maybe it's time to take this out of Defence's hands. It's not what we train you for.
You'll find an ally in me.
Keep working on that.

I have one of my children—in fact, 80 per cent of the three-stars in this room have partners or children—serving in the Australian Defence Force. I assure you we are absolutely committed to eradicating sexual violence in the Australian Defence Force.

Senator, I'm just mindful of time. I'm happy to come back to you. I'm assuming you've got other questions on this matter or matters relating to your line of questioning. I'll have to come back to you, if that's alright.
Okay.
Senator Paterson.

We'll have some further questions on the IIP. I just want to follow up Senator Dowling's questions about overprogramming, because I had some similar questions, in particular because I caught a podcast that the VCDF did recently, where he mentioned one of the ways Defence is engaging with risk is through overprogramming. Secretary, if I understand your evidence correctly, overprogramming is quite a legitimate tool to make sure that we don't have underspends in Defence. Is that a fair summary?

That's correct. In Defence and elsewhere, with quite a number of complex programs and projects, we want to make sure that we get best value for money in any particular year. It is a mechanism to track to ensure that we come in close to our budget. We've had slight overspends and slight underspends, and we manage that through active management of projects but also active manage of the whole portfolio of projects.
And if there wasn't over programming, just due to the nature of Defence procurement, there would be underspends on a routine basis, wouldn't there?

Possibly. It depends a little bit on whether you've got the ability to bring things forward. If you got halfway through the year and realised there were some projects running late for some extraneous reason, if you had the ability to bring things forward, you may not need as much overprogramming. But, given the time and complexity of some of the projects and the need to work with industry partners to upskill or add additional facilities, it has been a legitimate exercise in big infrastructure projects and big capability projects to think about overprogramming as a legitimate tool.
On the overprogramming that is in the 2026 IIP, would you say that those projects are unfunded, or would you say it's just part of the management of the Defence budget?

The individual projects have been allocated funding that meets the requirements put forward through the capability process. Individual projects are funded, and then the question is how to make sure that the whole program comes in on budget.
Yes. So they're not unfunded, right?
No. Individual projects are allocated funding.
Right. Why does the Deputy Prime Minister describe overprogramming under the previous government, which is the same as under this government, as unfunded projects?

You would have to put that to him. There is a requirement—while individual projects have got allocations of funding, it's important that we think about the overall balance of projects to make sure that we can deliver the capability over time. I'd have to see the specifics of the information you're talking to, to be able to provide that additional view.

I think the key point the Deputy Prime Minister has made, is the scale of overprogramming that existed under the former government. My recollection is it was in the order of 40 per cent, which is a lot higher than it has traditionally been and certainly a lot higher than what this government has allowed for.

In one financial year, when Defence spending was increasing. But, anyway, let's have that debate another time. I want to return to this mine hunter issue in the IIP reprioritisations, to use your language. Just for absolute clarity, CDF, you were talking about how this is deployed in Sydney Harbour and I think also off the coast of WA. What are these autonomous platforms deployed from? How are they delivered to the area of operations?

ask the Chief of Navy, Admiral Buckley, to come to speak to the contemporary specifics, but many of them can be deployed from any vessel. There are the REMUS uncrewed underwater systems. There are tethered systems. Where we find a item of interest, we can interrogate it with underwater cameras, or we can send our marine clearance divers down to inspect or to finish with a suspect package. So there's an array of systems at play.

In regards to the specifics of the program, we are currently in the test-and-trial phase of some autonomous systems. They are systems that are used by a number of our partners around the world. They are military off-the-shelf rather than a developmental set of systems. The deployment model for those is quite wide and varied. The concept, as I would describe it, is not about putting crewed ships into a minefield situation but, rather, having distant ways of deploying those particular autonomous systems into the minefield. The kinds of capabilities are: you could deploy them, you could put them into the back of an aircraft—for example, a military aircraft like a C-17 or a C-130—or you could send them to a port. You could deploy those capabilities from the wharf. You could deploy them from relatively small vessels—tugs, harbour-support vessels—or you could deploy them from larger ships such as landing helicopter docks, landing offshore patrol vessels and so on. The concept is that you can deploy them from a wide range of either ships or shore based, and for the majority they'll be air transportable as well.

If we needed to deploy them to a maritime choke point—Malacca, Sunda, Lombok, any of those—which would be obviously critical to our national interest in keeping the sea lines communication open, you could do that. You could do that from a ship or even from air?

The concept is to be able to deploy them from multiple means, including in different ranges of conflict and crisis scenarios, bearing in mind that, from a clearance point of view, the first and most important thing is that we can clear our own harbours and approaches. If you think about it, that's a defensive posture. There are a large range of options available to us there, including, like I said, even commercial options where you could deploy them from harbour-support vessels and the like.
How much should I read into the fact that you're describing this as a concept? How close to being able to be deployed in those contexts is it? Or are we still testing this?

We have been through the test phase for a bit over 12 months. We're in the process of finalising some detailed advice to government about how we move this forward. I would describe our closeness in the maturity of that program as, once we've had some final decisions made in regard to that capability, we should be able to field it over the next 12 to 18 months on a larger scale than what we've done under a test phase. It's a relatively mature capability. It's not an experimental capability, so it can be fielded today. As Chief of the Defence Force said, we've proven it as recently as a couple of weeks ago in Exercise Dugong. If we needed to field it quickly, we could field it very rapidly.

If it is 12 to 18 months and if we are contemplating retiring our existing minehunters this financial year—that is within six months or so; let's call it eight months—there seems like there could be a potential gap in capability there.

What the VCDF said was that the opportunity existed to sequence and decommission some of those existing minehunters as early as this financial year. My job is to ensure that we have a graduated transition of capability. If I could put it to you this way, we will need to liberate some of the people, some of the expertise, from part of the mine-hunting force into the autonomous force, and we will build that capability over time. I would not anticipate that there will be a gap in our ability to clear mines, but there will be a deliberate transition phase as we move from the last two crewed minehunters into this autonomous system.
Can you tell me how many of these autonomous systems we have currently, and can you say what their names are?

At the moment we have a small number of those systems. The REMUS 300 is one example of those particular systems. I'd certainly be happy to be able to provide you a more detailed brief of that in a classified environment. Clearly, some of these are military off-the-shelf technologies. They're not commercial technologies, but they are already in operation with some of our partners.

I will revisit that in another forum then. Moving back to the IIP—I may need the VCDF for this. This might be in my inbox in the form of a QON, but I haven't had time to review it, so apologies if so. Have we confirmed that $5 billion figure that we discussed in the last Senate estimates of reprioritisations, to use your language, within the forwards?
Sorry, Senator, I missed the question.

witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

My recollection of our discussion at the last hearing was that we were in agreement on the $5 billion. I was confused about the $10 billion.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group

That's correct.

text: Yes; $10 billion over the decade is what I believe the QON says.

Why weren't you familiar with that figure when we discussed it last time? You seemed quite surprised when I asked about it, and we had a long back and forth about whether this came from the minister or the industry minister and was briefed to journalists or not.

It was simply that my focus, as we were preparing the IIP, had been more on the forward estimates than over the decade period, and I had not considered the tail of the decisions taken over the forward estimates and their impact over the decade.

text: We went through those three, now public reprioritisations, and we've noted that the fourth is classified. For the record, I put a request into the minister's office today and asked that I be briefed today, ideally in the lunch break, so that if there are any questions arising out of it that can be asked in a forum like this, I can do that this afternoon after we return. We're waiting for a response from them on that. But are all of the 18 other descopes, delays et cetera now public?
No. We have not made all of those public.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

The issues that we have discussed publicly are the C-27J's transition to a new capability and the Integrated Air and Missile Defence program. Those are the two that have been made public.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: So, once I get on top of my QONs, I will only know two of the 18 projects descoped, delayed et cetera.

We have given a little bit more insight into the nature of those 18 projects. There were some—$2.5 billion of the $4.5 billion—that were saved through reprofiling. It was done with facilities, infrastructure and logistics projects. Again, that reflects the priorities in the National Defence Strategy. There's a balance of investments and savings that were made there that go to capability outcomes that we have not been able to disclose due to the nature of their classification.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: Does that mean we know three of the areas of savings, and there are 15 that are unknown.
There are multiple projects that involve facilities, infrastructure and logistics support.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: Help me. I'm just trying to establish, of the 18 that you've said are in there, how many are public and how many are not.
I think it would be in the order of eight that we can openly disclose. But, again, there are about 10 that are related to capabilities that we're less capable of talking about in this environment.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: I'll give the minister a heads-up. I know he'll object to this, but we've got 10 secret cuts.
Thank you for the heads up.
You're welcome.
Of course, I reject that categorisation. Funding has not been cut from the Defence budget. Funding has been substantially increased in the Defence budget.
We're talking about individual capabilities, Minister.

Yes, and, if I can complete my sentence, the Chief of the ADF was only this morning pointing out that we need to be flexible and respond to changing conditions. So, quite rightly, decisions are made to use that increasing bucket of funding to prioritise particular things that become more important than others.

Yes, and this committee is in no position to assess whether the right decisions have been made because 10 of those reprioritisations, delays, descopes or whatever language you want to put around it—10 of those capabilities are not being disclosed. Our job, on behalf of the people of Australia, in this committee is to assess the decisions of government and to contest them if necessary or agree with them where they're reasonable. We cannot do that if they're secret.
Well, sorry. We had a discussion earlier about the opportunity for classified briefings where that's more appropriate.

Yes, but as we also discussed earlier, Minister, I had no idea that I needed to request a classified briefing, because when I asked in previous estimates months ago or in questions on notice since you didn't tell me that there are these undisclosed reprioritisations, descopes or delays that you can't tell me about in this forum.
But you've now requested a classified briefing.
It turns out that I needed to request 11 classified briefings, not one.
I don't know that anyone's saying you need to request a separate briefing for every particular item.
I didn't know there were other items. I thought there was one!
The officials have provided you with the information they can, and there are opportunities and avenues to request classified briefings.

The IIP was released in April. We had a budget in May. We had budget estimates after that at which I asked questions about this. It has always been the case in the Integrated Investment Program that there are elements of that program that are at a higher classification than can be discussed in an estimates forum. These are decisions that are taken through corroboration across the department and with our ministers to make sure that we've got our assessments accurate of what can be discussed publicly. Then we have tried to make as much information as possible available to you in response to your questions. There are still some capability issues, where there are issues around national security, which we do not feel comfortable talking about in an open forum, but we have tried to the maximum extent possible to respond to your questions.

under the LOTE project, but we're $680 million in the hole. This is defence all over, isn't it?

text: Alright. I might move onto another point, about a disturbing series of events that seem to have happened at ADF bases. We understand that the US Naval Criminal Investigative Service, the NCIS, sent undercover agents into Australian Defence Force bases, including HMAS Stirling in Western Australia and HMAS Kuttabul in Sydney. Was the ADF advised in advance that these US undercover agents would be infiltrating Australian bases?
Can I say one thing before the officials answer. We do not accept the characterisation that's been given in those reports. But the officials can provide you with more detail.

Was the ADF or the department given advance notice before the Naval Criminal Investigative Service from the US deployed undercover agents who then entered HMAS Stirling in Western Australia and HMAS Kuttabul in Sydney?

I'll respond to that in the first instance. That report is wrong. It is factually incorrect. What does occur around the world where US naval assets visit foreign ports is a collaborative arrangement between NCIS, US embassies and host defence organisations to assess and agree security protocols for visiting programs, and that has always been the case. We've been supporting those ship visit security protocols collaboratively with US authorities for decades.

How was this report incorrect? Did US undercover agents from the Naval Criminal Investigative Service enter HMAS Stirling and/or HMAS Kuttabul to 'test existing physical security measures'? Did they enter either of those bases?

We're aware of the reporting in the Daily Telegraph that purports to draw on whistleblower statements and statements from former serving members with no contemporary knowledge of the work that we do. I would reinforce both the CDF's comments just now and the comments that the Deputy Prime Minister has made to the media in reference to these claims. We don't accept the suggestion that any assessments happen without the knowledge of the Australian government. We have longstanding arrangements, including treaty-level, security and information-sharing arrangements, that guide the routine work that we do with many partners, including NCIS, and the security and force protection procedures that we share and are developing together, particularly in support of the AUKUS program, are robust and regular—and we reject any suggestion that activities are undertaken without the knowledge of the Australian government.
Well, you spoke about transparency, Admiral Hammond, barely five minutes ago. Do you remember that?
Yes.

So I'm now asking you to live up to that commitment. There's reporting here that the US deployed undercover agents to key Australian Defence Force bases, including HMAS Stirling in Western Australia and HMAS Kuttabul in Sydney. I get a generic response that that's not correct. How is it not correct?
The inference in the article is that it was done without the concurrence and knowledge of Australian authorities.
So you're not contesting that the undercover agents went into HMAS Stirling and HMAS Kuttabul? You're not contesting that part of it?

The NCIS agents work with us—and I have personal experience in my previous job—in preparing an understanding of security arrangements for US warships visiting Australia. That is a well-established practice. We do it in concert. We do it in partnership, and it's not just Defence; it's a whole-of-government activity. So that's the characterisation that is accurate. The inference that this was done as some undercover activity without the knowledge of the Australian authorities is just categorically wrong.

Well, on a national security basis, one of my primary concerns is that, even if it was with consent, we have foreign agents who are—I'll quote from the article—'reportedly able to move through restricted areas without being challenged and photograph areas subject to security controls'. These are not US bases; these are Australian bases. If you consented to foreign security officers infiltrating our bases and photographing security areas—
That's not my testimony.
that is extraordinary.
You should not misrepresent what Admiral Hammond has said.
That is an extraordinary breach of our national security.
It would reflect much better on you if you did not misrepresent what Admiral Hammond has said.
I'm reading from the article.
Which he has already said is factually incorrect.
Well, no.
It is, in various respects.

I understood that what you were contesting was that you didn't have consent. That's how you contested the article. The inference that it did not come with our consent was what you were contesting with the article. We now know that in fact there were undercover US agents in HMAS Stirling and HMAS Kuttabul.
No, he said exactly the opposite. You need to stop misrepresenting what Admiral Hammond said.
Well, I'm happy to go back and read over the transcript, Admiral Hammond. Do you now say that that's not true?

I have said consistently that the report is factually incorrect and any inference that there was an infiltration of Australian bases by foreign US agents is factually incorrect. I have stated that we work in partnership with US authorities so they can understand the security apparatus in place for their visiting ships.

So is it your evidence that there have never been, to the extent of your knowledge, undercover agents from the US Naval Criminal Investigative Service entering, in a covert way, HMAS Stirling in WA or HMAS Kuttabul in Sydney? Is that your evidence?

The evidence is that the Australian government has various arrangements with security partners. All work is done with our full knowledge and concurrence, and, in relation to the type of activity you've just referred to, it is done jointly with Australian authorities.

Were US agents undercover inside Australian Defence bases, moving through restricted areas without being challenged and photographing areas subject to security controls? Did that happen, Admiral Hammond?
With Australians, doing joint operations.
Are you saying that, at each point, the undercover US agents were walking together with Australian personnel? Is that your evidence?

The activities are undertaken jointly between Australian and US officials. The exercise that you're talking about was a joint activity, done with the full knowledge and concurrence of Australian authorities. In terms of the specifics of particular buildings and locations, I can't go to that level of detail, but I can assure the Australian public that we take our security seriously. We do have detailed arrangements and oversight with our security partners through a whole layer of treaty obligations and memoranda of understanding. We undertake this work jointly with other partners within the Australian system, including our ASIO and AFP partners. I can assure the Australian public that we protect Australian bases. That is a core sovereignty requirement, and we work very closely with our partners to make sure that occurs. We completely reject the characterisation that it was done out of line of sight or done independently. It was always joint and it was done with full knowledge and concurrence.
On how many occasions since the signing of the AUKUS agreement have undercover agents from the Naval Criminal Investigative Service of the United States entered Australian bases?
I'm happy to take that detail on notice. I just note that it would've occurred prior to the AUKUS agreement as well. We have—
By all means give me the last 10 years, if you would like to do that.
We have had these arrangements in place since the 1960s.

By all means give me the last 10 years. I'm more than happy to extend the request for data to 10 years, but I'm separating them. My first request is: on how many occasions since the signing of AUKUS? Then, by all means, if you think it's useful, you can give any data before that.
I'm happy to take it on notice.

In terms of when they can be delivered?
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group

text: Yes.

We're in that process at the moment. Our ambition is to deliver medium-range air defence as quickly as possible. Part of our discussions with industry is to understand how quickly that can occur, but we haven't yet got to the point of concluding when they might be able to deliver.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

We will be establishing milestones such as initial operational capability and final operational capability, and we'll be putting those to government as part of their second-pass considerations. But we haven't established those milestones yet.

witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

We have an operational concept document. We haven't prepared tender documentation at this stage.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group

Only to the extent that we are delivering medium-range air defence as quickly as possible.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

Our ambition is to field a medium-range air defence capability in the early 2030s.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: Right, so there are dates in this document?
Only to that vague extent, not to any detail and certainly not to a contracted level that you would expect at a gate 2 submission for initial operational and final operational capability.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: Is that a document that can be provided? Is it a public document that can be provided to the committee?

We would not normally release capability development documentation. We would normally have a security classification that protects the nature of the capabilities and the vulnerabilities that we're seeking to avoid.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: I've been provided with a document that doesn't have any classifications on it. It is entitled 'Land 6504 medium ground based air defence industry engagement'. Would that be a classified document, or is that a public document?
No, that is not a classified document. It was discussed at Land Forces as part of the industry engagement to start this process of understanding what is actually achievable.
So that document could be provided to the committee?
Yes.
That is not an operational concept document; that is a document that seeks industry solicitation so that they can provide options to us.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: I asked you to nominate what documents are available that specify this, and you told me about that version of it. If there are other documents that specify timelines or capabilities, that was the question that I asked.
We will provide to the committee the information that was provided as part of the industry engagement activity.
In this document, are there any timelines specified?
To the vice-chief's testimony, it says 2030s is what they're aiming for, but I'll have to confirm that.
In this document, are there any particular capabilities identified?

We're soliciting that information from the market. We're not, for example, going to go to the market and say, 'We want X, Y, and Z.' We're going to the market to say, 'We want this type of capability,' and invite them to come back and tell us how they might fulfil that requirement.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: Do you want to clarify that answer at all?
That document also included the work that we're doing with the US government on the foreign military sales process and the pricing availability information that we're going out for.
My understand is that there are three foreign military sales identified in this document—three specific capabilities that are named in this document. Is that correct?
Yes.
I'm getting contrary evidence here, and I'm having difficulties reconciling it.

To be clear, the information that we're seeking is not part of a tendered process. What we're doing is trying to shape and understand what's available in the market. The testimony that the vice-chief gave is absolutely correct. We're in a stage of looking at what's available. We have explored with the US government what those existing systems are to be fair to industry so that they understand what we're doing, both from a direct commercial sales potential outcome and through a foreign military sales lens. We advise what systems we are looking at because we know they exist.
I appreciate that clarification.

Some of this is obviously subject to current government consideration, so it may not be possible to provide quite the level of detail you're seeking. I'm sure the officials will do what they can, but we may not be able to provide everything you're after.
