The questions I asked were open ended. They weren't specific about any particular document. I asked if there were any capabilities identified; I was told no. I asked if there were any timelines specified; I was told no. It turns out that there is a document, it does specify particular capabilities, and there are timelines in it.

Can I clarify—maybe there's a different interpretation of identified here—as the witnesses have discussed, they were in the pre-tender process of going to market, testing things, talking to industry and talking to other partners. Of course, military-to-military discussions around what other forces are using et cetera has identification of options. That is different from formal identification within a particular program where there's been a decision on what we're doing. Just to be clear, the difference between interpretations of that single word would explain the answers that witnesses are giving to you.
When does identification not mean identification?

We are not at the stage of identification within the program and within the specificity that the government has decided X, Y, Z, as the witness has said. The process of broad identification of what's in the market is going on and so are others asking for information.
I didn't specify that it had to be that level of—

I am just proposing that the interpretation of what you were asking might not have been what you were asking, so I've just explained the confusion here. There is no intent to prevent information from being provided to the committee.
Ben Packham in the Australian reported today that this project is not anticipated to be fully operational until the mid-2030s. Is that fair?

That is not the intention. We're aiming to do it as soon as possible. My expectation, given the technological advances that are occurring within this area of capability, is that we will have different capability at different stages through time. It is a rapidly developing area. We can see what's happening in Ukraine and the Middle East, where we're seeing significant innovation as a result of live action, so we have been instructed to put together a program of work to have activity in the early thirties. That is what we're aiming for, but this is not going to be a set-and-forget; this is going to be an ongoing iterative process as we respond to the capabilities that are available to us in the marketplace.
Sure. But I've asked for timelines and I've been provided with the 2030s, and the reporting says the 2030s—
There's a difference between early thirties and mid-thirties, and we are aiming to do it as quickly as possible.
I've heard mid-2030s. For argument's sake, let's now say it's early 2030s. Let's say that's what we're aiming towards.

The way I would characterise it—and Ms Kuczma might have a be able to strengthen this argument—is that we have put framing questions to industry and we are soliciting information from them. What we haven't yet done is take that information that we've got back from industry and build a deliberate program around that. As the secretary has said, it is a very dynamic environment, and the fact that there is such high expenditure on these type of weapons and that they're in such demand around the globe at the moment does mean that we need to understand what the market looks like today.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: Surely, when we're asking for industry to provide information, we should be as ambitious as possible and ask for capability for it to be provided it as soon as possible. I think it was the DSU in 2020 which first said that the 10-year warning time for conflict was gone. If we're hoping to field a critical capability like integrated air and missile defence by the early to mid-2030s—almost a decade away, or half a decade away if we do better—it doesn't feel like we're living up to those warnings that we've had in all of our strategic documents for years now.

No. But that would be to suggest that there is no integrated air and missile defence capability in Australia today, which is not the case. This is part of a layered system. It is a ground-based medium-range system that we are seeking to prioritise. The discussion that we had at the last hearing and the decisions that were taken by government with the last IIP were to change the priorities in the way we were delivering integrated air and missile defence. You'll recall that previously we had focused on command and control systems. The decision that was taken to accelerate medium-range air defence was one that descoped the more advanced elements of command and control systems and focused on delivering the medium-range effectors. So this is a change in emphasis. It absolutely responds to our circumstances. Would I like these capabilities today? Yes. But we have changed our priorities, and the government has made a decision to increase its expenditure focus to deliver as quickly as we can.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: Sure, but this is not the first time the government has changed its priorities. You're right; in the NDS 2026 there were changes to IMD. There were also changes to IMD in the 2024 NDS, weren't there?
That's the purpose of a biennial cycle—it's to look at our environment, to look at technology that's evolving, to respond to disruptions in our delivery program and to prioritise our investments.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: Why was AIR6502 cancelled in the 2024 NDS?

AIR6502 was not cancelled in the 2024 NDS; the scope of 6500 was broadened to incorporate 6502. There was never an intent under 6500 in the 2024 National defence strategy to not deliver medium-range air defence. That was to be delivered under a future phase of 6500. What we have done is reprioritise within 6500, and rather than deliver it under 6500, we have stood up a new project under Army, LAND6504, to deliver medium-range air defence.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: What were the timelines for AIR6502 before it was changed?
I'd have to take that on notice.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: Was it to deliver medium-range capability earlier than it will now be delivered?
No. Absolutely not. The intent in 2026 was to accelerate the delivery of medium-range air defence.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: In the reporting, it says that among the FMS capabilities we're considering is a technology that is now in the United States but is based on Israeli technology, part of Iron Dome. I think the OEM is Rafael. Is that correct?
We are looking at the United Arab Emirates system, which is a Raytheon version that works with some of the technologies that are coming from Rafael.
Would Rafael be involved in delivering this capability if we went down that road?
It will be delivered under an FMS system, so the P&A is to the US government. As to how the industrial base cooperates in that, we are a very long way away from that, so we don't have visibility.
But the US capability is a joint venture, isn't it?
I think it is, yes. That's a US based system, but, to my knowledge, it is a joint venture.

So, if Rafael and Raytheon are delivering a JV to deliver this capability to the US, and we are looking at that capability for us, is it possible or likely that Rafael will be involved in delivering it to us as well?
I just note that that's a hypothetical. We're not at that stage yet. We are going through the process of market development. All of those considerations will be part of government deliberations.

The reporting by Mr Packham in the Australian today suggests that there's a risk of political interference because of the Israeli origins of this technology. Can you reassure me that, if the best capability happens to be derived from Israeli technology, that won't be a barrier to deploying it for the ADF?

We can't give you any absolutes around government decision-making, as you understand. We provide the best advice. We provide all the information, and then it's a matter for government decision-making.

Sure, but the reassurance I'm seeking is that, if it is the best capability, it won't be discriminated against or banned just because it's of Israeli origin and that the government and Defence will choose the best capability that we can get the soonest for the ADF.
We work under the direction of the government. We provide the best available information based on the parameters that we're asked to provide that advice on.
That's not instilling me with confidence.
I cannot give you an absolute about a hypothetical in the future.

Sure, but I would have thought it was relatively easy—maybe it's more appropriate for the minister rather than the secretary to do this—to say: 'Of course we will not choose an inferior capability because of sensitivity about the nationality, source or origin of the technology. Of course we will always give the best capability to the men and women of the ADF.'
I just want to be clear that we do place restrictions, for a whole bunch of national security reasons, on some capabilities because of the security implications et cetera.

Yes, and I'm the first to encourage you to do that, but that's an operational consideration, not a political consideration, and that's what I'm trying to get to the heart of. I'm not advocating for buying Chinese integrated air and missile defence, obviously. There are very good operational reasons why we shouldn't do that. But what I'm seeking—given that the defence industry holds this belief that there is a shadow ban on Israeli technology and that the ADF will not buy it and Defence will not recommend it, because of the political sensitivities around Israel and the bilateral relationship—is your reassurance—I'm not reassured so far—that the political sensitivities of the origin of the technology would not be a consideration and we would focus on what is the best capability that we can get the soonest.
As a general proposition, what I can say is that the government will always seek to deliver the most suitable military technology.
Regardless of the country of origin and any political—
I've given you the general proposition. We will always seek to deliver the most suitable technology available.
So, if it happens to be of Israeli origin, it won't be excluded for that reason?
If there's anything I can add to what I've said, I'll add that.
I'm not sure that will instil confidence in people bidding this process. Chair, I'm conscious you may need to share the call before I move on to other topics.
I'll do that, and I'll come back to you. I think Senator Payman's been waiting there. I'll come to you, Senator Payman. Then, depending on others, I might come back to you, Senator Paterson.

My question is around shipment of firearms with regard to question 74 of BE 2026-27, which related to a shipment of firearms for Defence that was blocked as a consequence of the changes to firearms import permits that were rushed through parliament in January. What type or types of firearms were purchased in this order, and how many of each type were purchased?
I'll ask the relevant officials to come to the table.
Can you repeat what document it is you're reading from?
I'm reading from budget estimates 2026-27. It's question 74, dated 9 June 2026.
Can you repeat the question please?

I would like to know, for the shipment of firearms that was blocked as a consequence of the changes to firearm import permits, what type or types of firearms were purchased in the order and how many of each type were purchased?
I'll see if my colleague has the detail. I do recall the response, but I don't have the detail.
I can read out the response if you'd like.
Does that not clarify the answer?

No. You've said: 'Defence experienced a 42-day delay to one order of firearms due to import permit changes, which required permit applications to be resubmitted under the new process. The complete order was received in May 2026 without impacting Defence capability.' I'd like to know what type or types of firearms were purchased in this order and how many of each type were purchased.
I'll just see if we have the answer. If not, we will take it on notice.
I'm aware of the issue. I don't think I've got the detail here, and I might have to take on notice what the weapon itself was that was delayed.
Do you know what the value of the order was?
Again, I'd have to take that on notice.
Was Defence made aware that it would have to update its import processes following the January amendments?

That would have occurred. We monitor changes to arrangements both domestically and internationally. Then, we have a process of making sure that our procurement areas and—we also have a regulator. When there's a change in law, we go through and update our systems and procedures and manuals.
What action did Defence take to update its import processes? It clearly wasn't enough to prevent this shipment from being blocked.
I'm happy to take the details on notice in terms of what the procedures were.
What changes has Defence made to ensure it is up to date with regulatory changes in the future so that things like this don't happen again?

I've taken on notice the procedures that we undertook at the time. It's not clear to me how speedy and fulsome that was. Generally, we have an area that looks at the legislative changes in Australia. In terms of overseas changes, we've got a network of overseas attaches and overseas posted staff, and one of their responsibilities is to monitor changes in international arrangements. That is compiled and goes through the system to make sure that our procurement officers and our project delivery officers understand the changes in the legislative regimes. It's a system that's been in place for a significant amount of time.
But we don't know what process took place around this?

That's why I've taken this particular item on notice. But, in general, it would have been someone being notified of a change in legislation, identifying who in Defence needs to know about that and then information being provided in different mechanisms, either in an updated manual or a direct instruction.

I look forward to receiving the answers for that. Why did Defence fail to comply with FOI request 329/26/27 within the statutory timeframe, which relates to this issue, despite the 30-day extension being granted?
I'd have to see whether we've got information on that particular case. Sometimes it's a matter of processing. Sometimes it's a matter of internal mechanisms.
I'm just pulling up 329. My technology is failing me, Senator. I'll be able to get back to you before the hearing is out. I'll pull up the record for that number.
Yes, please, because it seems like Defence is preventing scrutiny on this matter. I'm wondering why it hasn't complied. We'll move on to—

I want to be clear. We comply with the legislative obligations. They're legislative obligations on officials. We train our FOI officers. We have our legal framework. People are fully aware of their legal obligations. There are parts of the framework that allow for us extensions. Some of it is about negotiating with applicants. We take seriously our obligations to meet, and we operate under the—

Thank you, Secretary. I've got a list of other questions, and the chair is going to pull me up on time. I've got questions on the Abrams M1A2 SEPv3 main battle tanks. I note that Defence purchased 16 simulators to train ADF personnel to use the Abrams M1A2 at a cost of $60 million. Extrapolating this to the 75 main battle tanks that were purchased, 75 simulators would cost approximately $281 million. What was the cost of the 75 main battle tanks?
You're just after the cost—
For the 75 main battle tanks.
The total spend for the program, which is 907, is $1.8 billion, but that includes 75 main battle tanks and assault-breaching capabilities as well.
But do we know the cost of just the 75 main battle tanks?
I don't have the breakdown.
Are you able to get that for us on notice?
Yes, sure.
Where are these main battle tanks located, by state and territory?
These tanks are located in Townsville and in Puckapunyal.

How does Defence justify the difference in cost between buying these tanks and buying simulators, given its previous evidence, in BE26-27 question 72, that these tanks have only been used for training purposes and the fact that Australia has not deployed a tank in combat since the Vietnam War?

What I can tell you is that we have a range of capabilities in the Australian Defence Force which are prudent for our ability to fight and win Australia's wars. Through government direction and decision, tanks are a part of that capability. They are an important part of our capability of the Australian Army in order for us to be able to fight and win the land combat battle. They are an incredibly potent capability, and they also form a part of our deterrence.
$1.8 billion is a lot of money.
It's a lot of armour.
What wars are we hoping to win?

The predominant strategy, as set out in the National defence strategy is one of strategic denial and deterrence. We are hoping and posturing and working with partners to not have to fight a war, but one of the most potent methods of having deterrence is to have capability so your adversaries think twice before they engage in armed combat.
So was the purchase of these tanks solely based on a need to increase defence spending as a proportion of the GDP?

That is not correct. We go through a very detailed process. There's been in recent years—every two years, approximately—an update to the National Defence Strategy through the Defence Strategic Review. There was a strategy update in 2024 and 2026. We have cascade down from the National Defence Strategy. We have an Integrated Investment Program that talks about the acquisitions to be able to deliver that strategy. That's combined then with our workforce plan and our sustainment plan in order to have an integrated force that will defend Australia and deliver the main purpose of the National Defence Strategy, which I've highlighted is one of deterrence.
So we bought these tanks to win wars, but we haven't used a tank in a war in 50 years?
Just to be clear, we do not buy equipment in the hopes of using it. We invest—
But we spent $1.8 billion, which is a lot of money.
That's over a long period of time. We invest in capability to defend Australia and to protect our national interests, which is intended to not have a war.
Senator, we'll just clarify the dollar figure.
The 75 main battle tanks is $1.2 billion.
That's still a lot of money. Thanks.
Senator Paterson.
I have questions about SRF-West, if relevant officials are available.
I'll just note that we've got the Australian Submarine Agency coming on after us. So they might take questions of more detail.
I think this will be a Defence matter, but let's see how we go. When is the rotational presence of US and UK submarines coming to an end at SRF-W?

Currently we have a strategic arrangement which sets out the plans between now and into the 2030s. Getting towards the end of that, there will be a discussion with our partners about the next phase of that. So we don't have an end over the process. We have the current arrangement that's in place, which ends, I believe, in 2032. Then the expectation is we would have conversations with our strategic partners about our needs under the National Defence Strategy at the time leading up to the end of the current agreement.
So it won't come to an end in 2032?

That will be a matter for the government at the time. The expectation, though, of the National Defence Strategy going out further is that we will work with alliance partners in the defence of the nation. So the expectation is that there would be continued arrangements between us and our allies, but the exact nature of those would be subject to government-of-the-day decision-making.
Would you describe it as 'time limited', or would you describe it as 'enduring'?

I would characterise it as ongoing review points to make sure that it meets the purposes of the National Defence Strategy of the day. We have set timelines. We have arrangements. We negotiate, discuss and agree. It's a quite complicated process depending on whether it's a treaty, levy or MOU or more strategic operational planning. There's a whole layer of discussions. Those come to an end. We have ongoing discussions, and they shift over time depending on the nature of the context in which we're operating.
Right. Thank you.
The only thing I'd add is this. You would be aware of the Deputy Prime Minister's reference to this being an enduring arrangement.
Yes. That's why I asked the question. So it is an enduring arrangement?
That's what he said.
Right. So it's not time limited?
Not that I'm aware of, no.
It's not coming to an end?
Obviously if any official at the table knows differently—because they are much more across this than me—
I've got lots of shaking of the heads. Admiral Hammond was shaking his head. It's not coming to an end?
Individual agreements will come to an end because they're time limited. But individual negotiated arrangements can be time limited within an enduring relationship.
But the presence, particularly US presence, is either enduring or it is time limited. It cannot be both.
I may be able to help in this instance.
Please.

What will help clarify this is that the reference to 2032 is under the optimal pathway, working with the United States to ensure that Australia is sovereign ready to operate nuclear powered submarines. That's dated 2032, and that's when SRF-West is designed to be able to meet that date. As Minister Watt said, the Deputy Prime Minister said earlier that SRF-West is intended to be an enduring feature of our cooperation with the United State and with other partners. Obviously, the facility at SRF-West is designed to be able to sustain not only our submarines but also those of our partners, and so it's obvious that we would seek to ensure that that capability is enduring, but it would occur under our arrangements that exist outside the Optimal Pathway. As you know, all US military activity in Australia occurs under the US force posture agreement, which is a treaty the two countries signed in 2014. That agreement determines the terms under which US forces deploy to Australia, and so any enduring US presence would occur under that treaty.
It's in our national interest, is it not, to have that enduring presence at HMAS Stirling beyond 2032. We wouldn't want our partners to step up and go in 2032 would we?
That National Defence Strategy is clear about the need for us to work with allies, yes.

I visited HMAS Stirling recently. I must say I was very impressed by the work that is happening there and the scale and the pace of the build out here. It would look to me like a very excessive build out if our partners were leaving in 2032 and only Australian submarines were being hosted there. It's clearly being built to have that in an enduring way—partners there for a long period of time beyond 2032, isn't it?
It's being built against the arrangements of the Optimal Pathway, and that includes partners with the US and the UK.
We're only going to get, hopefully, our first Virginia class submarine in 2032. It would be a very lonely submarine and a very big berth if it were the only one there, wouldn't it?
We have US and UK submarines using that facility in the current plans.

If it is enduring, if it is not time limited, if it is not coming to an end in 2032, why did the defence industry minister say in an interview on the 7.30 report on 29 July on four separate occasions that it was coming to and end, that it was time limited, that it would expire in 2032 and that US submarines would be gone beyond that date.
I think, to be fair, you would be aware that Minister Conroy clarified those comments subsequently and has also made that point about the enduring nature of this arrangement.
So his original comments were not correct?
I'll let you describe them however you wish.
I don't wish to. I'm asking you to.
I think you are trying to describe them in a certain way. I—
You can describe them any way you like. It's up to you.
I've done that. Minister Conroy clarified those remarks.
You would only have to clarify something if it were wrong, right?
Again, you can describe it however you wish.

In that interview with Sarah Ferguson on 7.30, this concept of the US submarines departing from 2032 was used as an answer to a question about Australia's nuclear non-proliferation obligations. Minister Conroy was explaining to Sarah Ferguson and her viewers that we need not worry about Virginia class submarines potentially being equipped with nuclear weapons in the future, because they were not going to get those weapons until 2032, and they would be gone by 2032. If their departure in 2032 is not the reason why we don't need to worry about that, what is the government's policy on US or any other partner having nuclear equipped platforms at our bases?

The Australian government continues to invest in and use our diplomatic and strategic weight to support international strategic arms control, including nuclear non-proliferation and disarmament. It's a key part of Australian foreign policy and statecraft. As you know, Australia has a number of treaties and agreements which preclude the stationing of nuclear weapons on Australian soil, and the Australian government has said repeatedly that it does not seek and will not seek to develop an independent nuclear capability of its own. However, that arrangement does not preclude the visits by nuclear-capable American assets, and we regard those visits as consistent with our obligations under the South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone Treaty, also known as the treaty of Rarotonga. We, of course, respect the United States policy of neither confirming nor denying the presence of nuclear weapons on particular platforms, and visits by US strategic assets support credible strategic deterrence in the Indo-Pacific to benefit Australia's security and our own regional stability in the Indo-Pacific.

I understand this is a sensitive, important issue. I'm not going to press you into a difficult position on this. To be transparent about my motivations, I want a clearly articulated government policy on the record to point to because this is a question that is of interest to the community and they have legitimate questions about it. So, to be very clear, can you just explain how it is consistent with both the US policy of neither confirming nor denying, which is understandable and reasonable, and our obligations under the treaty of Rarotonga?

The treaty of Rarotonga requires us not to station nuclear weapons in Australia. But, as I said, the government has no intent to acquire nuclear weapons or to station nuclear weapons in Australia. I would note, of course, that the United States does not station nuclear weapons in the territory of its Indo-Pacific allies. It has not done so for over 35 years. It only stations its nuclear weapons in continental United States and United States territories, not in its Indo-Pacific allies. That said, we are part of extended nuclear deterrence arrangements with the United States. As you know, famously, US president Kennedy said in the 1960s that his concern was that, at the dawn of the nuclear age, there would be in 30 years 25 nuclear weapon states. That did not turn out to be the case, and one of the key reasons is that US allies agreed to fall in underneath a US nuclear umbrella, and that has been a critical and, I would say, undersung asset in global non-proliferation efforts in relation to nuclear weapons.

Part of those arrangements is that it's in our interests to support the visits of nuclear-capable American assets from time to time. As you know, those visits have been occurring for many years, and it is US policy as part of those arrangements to neither confirm nor deny. Obviously, you would appreciate that this is the most sensitive operational feature of American force presence globally, and they do not declare whether those assets are nuclear armed or not. It's the longstanding practice of Australian governments to respect that position. But, of course, the United States also respects Australia's international and domestic legal obligations and conducts its visits in a manner accordingly.

I think that's important to have on the record. I'm grateful for that, Mr Jeffery, and I'm happy to move on to another topic. I have questions about counter uncrewed autonomous systems. While any relevant officials are coming forward, I want to note and welcome the government's introduction of new legislation to deal with this issue of drone incursions on Australian bases. Subject to an appropriate parliamentary inquiry, the opposition is strongly supportive of bringing this legislation forward in a timely way. It's critical that our men and women on our bases have both the capability and the legal authority to safely bring down any drones that are coming over our bases. As you know, there have been a number of media reports about these incursions. One public report says there have been 147 incidents of drones flying onto or over active bases over the past year. In particular, RAAF Base Williamtown has attracted significant media interest. Starting with RAAF Base Williamtown, what can Defence say in this forum about the reported drone incursions between 11 and 13 July at RAAF Base Williamtown?

There were a number of drone incursions over that period at RAAF Base Williamtown. If I could broadly characterise them, they were detected visually, not often on sensors. We have sensors at each of our air bases that detect most drones. Again, it depends on the technology being used. But there were a number of drones over that date period. They were monitored and tracked by our personnel at RAAF Base Williamtown. They were reported, and appropriate measures were taken by the personnel on the base, given the authorities we had at the time.
witness_position: DSC, CSC, Chief of Air Force

text: Can you explain why it would be the case that it wouldn't be detected by the current equipment on bases and had to be visually identified.
'It depends' is the short answer to that question.
witness_position: DSC, CSC, Chief of Air Force

text: You can give a longer one if you like.

I'll give some characterisation. It depends on a number of factors: it depends on how it's being operated; it depends on the OEM, the original manufacturer of the equipment; it depends on the technology being used to control it; it depends on our sensors and the technologies they're using to detect it; and it depends also on the database libraries in those sensors to characterise them correctly and therefore maybe display them on the detection system. So it could be that there was a mismatch in the technologies on those particular days. It could have been that they were being operated in a way that the sensors were unlikely to have detected and it was just going to be a visual pick-up.
witness_position: DSC, CSC, Chief of Air Force

text: Can you confirm in this particular incident how many drones were visually detected.

I don't have those numbers on those dates with me. I can look to try and get those back to you over the course of today. But there were occasions when we had a single drone detected and monitored by our personnel or the sensors or both, and there were one or two occasions when there was more than one UAS system operating over Williamtown of a night.
witness_position: DSC, CSC, Chief of Air Force

text: And New South Wales police are investigating these incidents, are they not?
We are in close contact with the rest of our defence stakeholders, not least security and estate group, and the New South Wales police on these matters and other appropriate agencies.
witness_position: DSC, CSC, Chief of Air Force

text: What can you say about the progress of that investigation?

The New South Wales police investigation would be a matter for New South Wales police. What I can say is we continue to work very closely with New South Wales police and the rest of the defence and other agency stakeholders on either investigating drone incursions or looking to work together to detect and respond to, deter or find the individuals who might be operating these drones and have the police take appropriate actions.
witness_position: DSC, CSC, Chief of Air Force

text: To your knowledge, has the person or people responsible for this been identified by police?
For those dates, no, I am not aware. That would be a matter for New South Wales police.
witness_position: DSC, CSC, Chief of Air Force

text: If it's the case that they haven't been identified, and my understanding is the drones were not able to be taken down for reasons we'll discuss in a minute, their motivation is unknown at this stage as well?
We do not know. No-one has apprehended said individuals on those dates, so we would not know their motivations.
witness_position: DSC, CSC, Chief of Air Force

text: In simple words, we don't know if this is a silly teenager or something much more nefarious.

No, we don't know that. We do know that the incidents of uncrewed aerial systems around defence bases, as elsewhere, have increased as technology has gone up. We have seen a significant increase over the recent years in identified uncrewed aerial systems across the whole estate. That is one reason why we've moved to update regulations and the government's moved with the legislation.
It's an offence though, isn't it, to fly a drone above a military base?

There are a number of different pieces of legislation that apply here. One of them is the Civil Aviation Act. So there are a number of offences that might be applied or might be related to flying drones over defence bases, defence air bases or other airfields around Australia. The bottom line is the information for drone operators in Australia, if I may, is very simple to come across. You can literally Google or otherwise search Know Your Drone with CASA, and it's very, very clear what the obligations are on the individual operators of UAS systems around any airfield, let alone defence airfields.
witness_position: DSC, CSC, Chief of Air Force

text: I'm not sure if it's the case for RAAF Williamtown, but certainly there are facilities where there are quite large signs that say, 'You should not fly a drone in this area.'
Those are correct, and I'm sure one of my colleagues could expand on that signage and the additions that have been put in place over the months.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: As we've been, as the secretary said, noticing a significant increase in drone activity, we have been very concerned to not just work on the capability uplift but understand the nature of this as a global challenge and an Australian challenge. We work very closely with our partners in police forces—the AFP and state police force—and the intelligence community to understand the problem and the capabilities to respond around what we are seeing and what might be driving activity. What we know is that there is a really high prevalence of ownership in the general community, and one of the important pieces of work we've done closely with CASA over the last year is not just signage—as you mentioned, particularly around our air bases—that make it clear to plane spotters and enthusiasts that it's not okay but letterbox drops in those areas around our air bases. We want to stay really engaged with the community to understand that it is harmful, disruptive and potentially dangerous. We're very concerned to understand the difference between silly teenagers and a higher end threat.
Is it true, as the Daily Telegraph reported, that in this instance of these incursions that personnel were told to close the blinds in response to the drone incursions?

I saw that news reporting, and I think there's a much more important and broader point to make there. We have a national system of emergency response procedures and security procedures that we practice annually. It's really important for all our people all around the country on a site that when an event occurs we have a standardised way to respond. We've modelled those over many years on the Australia-New Zealand Counter-Terrorism Coordination Committee models for emergency responses, lockdown procedures, escape hotel procedures, which you may be familiar with. It is a standard response when we alert an incident on a base.

You'll appreciate—you've visited many of them—that our bases are often largely geographically dispersed in many buildings. The alarm will sound. Individuals won't necessarily know what the event is, but these standard protocols that we use are designed to keep people safe no matter what the incidence is. Closing curtains is great because you'll appreciate we started these emergency procedures and we've embedded them on the ANZCTC model really in a counterterrorism paradigm. If you were, for instance, facing an active shooter, that would feel quite different to many other events that might occur. It's standard protocols that are easy to repeat, understood by all our people and rehearsed on an annual cycle onsite so we get a good, consistent response.
Sure, and the point about an active shooter is self-evident. I recognise that, but this wasn't an active shooter. It was a drone.
The point is that the siren goes off and the same procedures are activated. Individuals don't necessarily know what the incident is.
No, but presumably the person who's conveying the instruction knows. You can tell me. Maybe it wasn't the case. Was a specific instruction given to close the blinds?
There would have been an instruction that there was a security incident, and people would have followed protocols.
So they were not told to close the blinds. That was not a specific instruction that was given.
Closing the blinds is a standard part of the—
That's not my question. Was there a specific instruction given?
I couldn't speak to what happened at Williamtown, but it is standard. I was recently at RAAF Darwin during—
I'm not interested in the generality; I'm interested in this specific incident. I want to understand. Was that instruction specifically given in this instance?

We can take the sequence on notice, but if the normal procedures were followed, which I would presume is the case, there would have been a notification to those on base that there was a security incident and they would have followed the normal procedures. There is usually not additional information provided at that time. People just follow the usual procedures. We can take this specific on notice, but the idea that people would close the blinds is standard procedure. We can take on notice if there was any variation from the communication, but it would be unlikely. We are happy to check it.

It may well be that someone was reminding a colleague to follow the normal protocols. As the Chief of Air Force, I'm very comfortable and pleased that our members, whether they're aviators, APS or indeed soldiers and sailors, might be on RAAF Base Williamtown on that particular day, they would both comply with the standard protocols, would remind each other if a protocol had not been followed in some case. Also, from a safety and security point of view, drone wise, that the protocol would be followed for very good safety and security reasons with drones over the base.
witness_position: DSC, CSC, Chief of Air Force

text: Sure, but we obviously need a much more robust way of protecting our people, and the things they're working on, than closing the blinds.
And that is in train.
witness_position: DSC, CSC, Chief of Air Force

text: Indeed. Chair, I'm just seeking your indication on timing. I've got further questions in this area if that's okay.
Yes.
It's been publicly reported that there've been 147 incidents like this, Australia-wide on our bases. Is that number accurate, or do you have a different number?

Senator, I can speak to security incident reporting. In the 2025-26 financial year, we had 204 incident reports of UAS security incidents. In 2024-25, it was 141, so that's the step up we're seeing. This financial year to date, we've had 42 incident reports.
As you say, that is quite a step up. Are you able to break those numbers down by Defence base or facility?
We can take that on notice.
Yes, but you collected it in that form and—
Yes.
Thank you.
We'll extract that from the security reporting.
Can you go back any further than 2024-25?
I can.
Please.
In 2023-24, we had 56 incident reports, and in 2022-23 we had 19.

So obviously we're on quite a steep curve, but this has been happening for some time. Why is it that it is not until now, this month, that legislation has been introduced to give our ADF members the legal authority to take it down, if this has been happening for five or six years?
We've had a series of responses, including regulation that was put in place at the end of last year that provided an additional sort of framework and powers, and we've also—
But not sufficient, as I understand it.

They have some gaps in them because the regulation can't override certain aspects of legislation. It was clear at the time, when the regulations were being worked through, that it would provide some cover but not full cover because we needed to work through the legislative process. The legislation package that's before parliament has been in gestation for quite some time. It's a complex piece of legislation. It's important that we take the opportunity to get it right, to modernise aspects, not just on the security side but also on the capability development side. We have worked as expeditiously as possible to have that package ready for government, and, as you say, it's been introduced for consideration this week.

We have also been working, separate to that, with other regulatory authorities to increase our capabilities, including with CASA, in particular, for them to be able to delegate some authorities to the Air Force to be able to take some activities. So there have been active considerations. It's not the case that this is recent. The department and government have, under government instructions, been working on this for a matter of months and years.

Sure, but a matter of months; this has been going on for years. My understanding—you can correct me if I'm wrong—is that it is legally unclear whether ADF members had the authority to bring these drones down in these recent incidents, including at RAAF Williamtown, therefore, they were not able to be brought down.

It depends on the modality and method of engaging with drones, and it depends whether they're in the air, over airfields or the ground-based operations. So it is a complicated regulatory architecture that we're operating in because the legislation, across different aspects, were not drafted with the knowledge of uncrewed aerial systems.
But my understanding is that it was not legally clear that the commanding officer of these bases could issue an order to a defence member to bring these drones down. Is that true or not true?
It depends on the method by which they bring them down and the circumstances that they're facing.
That's what I mean by 'not clear'.
Well, there was clarity that it was possible in certain circumstances and not possible in other circumstances.
So in these circumstances, let's take RAAF Williamtown or any other incident, has there been a time when there have been drones over bases where it was not legally permissible to issue that order?
The orders were not issued over the dates you're talking about because we did not feel we had the lawful authorities to respond.
witness_position: DSC, CSC, Chief of Air Force

text: Thank you.
I now have the appropriate delegations from CASA to respond over Defence airfields.
witness_position: DSC, CSC, Chief of Air Force

text: Thank you. That's why I was asking the question. If it's not legally clear, then clearly regulatory or legislative change was necessary. This is not a new issue that's just cropped up this week or this month or this year. It's been going on for some time. So I come back to my question. When these incidents first started escalating in the early 2020s, why wasn't legislation introduced or regulations issued to deal with that problem? Why is it only now, when we're getting into this financial year, that we're contemplating this?

We've been working on this issue, working through the complexities. It is not straightforward because of the overlay of different legislative and regulatory environments. This process has been going on, and we have been working through it.
When did this process start? When did government instruct—
The actual framework for the safety and security zones et cetera certainly started years ago.

The arrangements in relation to what you've seen before parliament this week have been evolving for some years now. We had a number of public consultations from about 2023 onwards. We have been working on this issue, in terms of the interim solution. Obviously, this issue, which is before parliament now, gives us the whole solution. But the interim solution has been worked on for the best part of a year as well.
Remind me when those regs were issued by the assistant minister.
Late last year—I think it was December. I'll check the date.
Thank you. I've got, cumulatively, about 500 incidents over the last couple of years. Does that sound ballpark right, Ms Perkins?
I'll give you 480, yes.

That sounds good. Are any of those suspected, or have any of those been confirmed, to be at the more serious end of the spectrum in terms of motivation, foreign interference, espionage—those kinds of issues?

You'll appreciate that we tend not to speak in detail to what we're analysing when it comes to serious security events. I can say we're working really closely on the motivations. I'll just also add to colleagues' testimony that in this period, as we've been developing the responses, we have, of course, worked very closely with some of our security partners including the AFP and state police forces, who, at certain sites, provide a response capability for us. So the AFP's a really important partner for us here.
Sure.

In terms of the way that we analyse the incident reporting, we haven't identified particular high-end concerns. But we are very concerned that this is a growing challenge, and we're extremely alert to the international experience. And that's why this work is so important.

This will be my last question, because I know the chair wants to rotate the call. Of those 480 known incidents, can you tell me what proportion are of unknown origin, what proportion are known to be a stereotypical teenager doing something silly and what proportion have been identified to be foreign interference, espionage or something more serious.
I will take it on notice. My sense is I will struggle with that level of detail, but let me see what we can analyse in the incident-reporting database.
Thank you.
I'll hand over to Senator Shoebridge before we break for lunch.

In relation to the incident in Williamtown—I think there were a number of incidents in Williamstown in the middle of this year—is it true, as reported, that personnel at Williamtown, when the drones were intruding into the airspace, were instructed to close window blinds to protect sensitive information? Is that true?
We've just had this conversation at length.
Was that true?

It is standard protocol, when there's a security incident at a base, for people to close blinds et cetera. We have taken on notice whether there was any deviation from standard protocols at Williamtown.
Could you just confirm that the drones were left unmolested, but the blinds were pulled down. That's what happened at Williamtown. Is that right?
We have taken on notice whether there was any deviation in standard security protocols, which involve—across bases in response to any incidents—all blinds being closed.
But, to be clear, that was the net result—drones left unmolested and blinds shut down. And everybody stayed inside.
That's what's being checked for the purpose of the question on notice.

Sorry, I missed that previous engagement on the way over here. Could I ask you about comments that were made by the former chairman of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee, US Congressman Michael McCaul, who met, I think, with the Prime Minister, the defence minister and the Foreign minister when he visited here a few months ago. Who would be best placed to answer these questions?
You might need to just go for it and officials can come to the table.

Either just before or just after those meetings, Congressman McCaul, the former chairman of the US house foreign affairs committee, who was here on a congressional delegation, said that it was 'logical to assume' that some US Virginia class submarines rotating through HMAS Stirling in Western Australia from 2032 onwards would be carrying nuclear weapons. Is US Congressman McCaul correct?
You are talking about a foreign official providing an opinion. We have just also had an extensive conversation about the position regarding Australia's obligations under the treaty of Rarotonga.
I'm aware of that.
Also there is the US position of not confirming or denying the presence of nuclear weapons on their platforms. I certainly have nothing further to add to the evidence that we've already provided.

Did the congressman make that clear in his meetings with the defence minister? And I point out this is not just any congressman. He was coming here as part of an official delegation to talk, amongst other things, AUKUS. He's the former chairman of the US house foreign affairs committee. Did he advise the defence minister, in discussions with the defence minister, that it would be logical to assume that some US Virginia class submarines rotating through HMAS Stirling in Western Australia from 2032 onwards would be carrying nuclear weapons? Did he say that to the defence minister?
I'll have to take that on notice. What I would say is that we've been very clear that we won't be allowing nuclear weapons to be stationed in Australia.

But, you see, what you also said to the people of Fremantle and the people of Perth when your government agreed, at the cost of about $8 billion, to build the US nuclear submarine base at HMAS Stirling was, 'Don't you worry because these Virginia class submarines won't be carrying nuclear weapons.' You made it very clear in repeated statements to the public that the Virginia class submarines would not be carrying nuclear weapons. Since your government made those statements, the United States government have made it very clear that they intend to put nuclear weapons on their Virginia class submarines, with nuclear armed, sea launched cruise missiles. Are you going to go and speak honestly now to the people of Fremantle and Perth and correct the situation?
I've learned through bitter experience, Senator Shoebridge, to check assertions that you make, and I will do that on this occasion as well.
Mr Jeffrey?

You're referring to a program that the United States military is engaged in, which is to sea launch a cruise missile that could be conventionally armed or nuclear armed. I'll need to check the details on this. That program, when last I checked, was not operational. So it's not possible at this juncture to equip US—
That's why he said 2032.

I wanted to make the point that's it's not operational now. It's a program that is designed to be developed or delivered into the 2030s. That date, of course, will need to be determined as the program proceeds. Of course, as you know—and we have discussed this before—Australia's treaty obligations mean that we are not permitted to station nuclear weapons in Australia. I have spent some time getting on the record today our position in relation to engagement with or the visits of nuclear capable platforms to Australia.

Foreign minister Wong, in her April 2023 National Press Club address, made it very clear to the public that AUKUS submarines visiting Australia would be conventionally armed. Of course, now the US has changed its policy. It's investing billions of dollars to enable its Virginia class submarines to have nuclear armed, sea-launch capable ballistic missiles. At any point has the government come forward and told the public, 'Actually, what we were saying before about them not being nuclear armed is now wrong because the US has changed its policy and, while we're not going to confirm or deny, there is absolutely a very real possibility'—or, as Representative McCaul says, it's logical to assume—'that now US Virginia class submarines, or at least some of them, will be nuclear armed.' Have you come clean with the Australian public and said this at any point?
You're making a whole series of assumptions in your question to officials—
No, I'm not.

around testimony or discussion of a US official, projecting that to be US official policy. That is an assumption that I cannot verify on the basis of the information you've provided. The Australian government's been very clear and we have obligations under the treaty of Rarotonga. We have also been clear about the nuclear propulsion capability, which is very different from nuclear weapons. I have nothing to add to the official government statements, which have been very clear about government policy.
We need to break for lunch. If you ask one last question, Senator, then we will break.

Previous government statements, including coming from the Foreign minister at the National Press Club address, made it clear that visiting US nuclear submarines would not be nuclear armed. Since then, the United States government has changed its policy, passed legislation and committed to a multibillion dollar program to enable some of its Virginia class submarines to carry nuclear weapons in the form of a sea launched ballistic missile. Given that has changed, can you point to any point, any public statement or any utterance from any official or minister that has explained that change to the Australian public, and particularly the people of Fremantle and Perth, given the change of circumstances?
Unfortunately you missed the testimony of Mr Jeffrey. I draw your attention to where he laid out the government's position.
I've seen the transcript. None of that did that.
Then that's a matter of opinion. We have set out—
It's not a matter of opinion. It's a question—have you done it?
Let the official finish.

And the answer has been set out on the record in terms of the obligations under the treaty of Rarotonga, and it's been very clear—you've heard the minister talk about it—that nuclear weapons won't be stationed in Australia.
We'll come back to this.
Senator Paterson, did you have some more questions you wanted to continue with?

I have an infinite number of questions! We're only limited by time and everyone's patience. I've received some representations from ADF members about meal and incidental allowances being cut, particularly while on overseas deployments. Is that correct?
We might call Justine Greig, Deputy Secretary, Defence People, for a policy perspective, and then Lieutenant General Fox, Chief of Personnel.

As you get settled, I'll ask the question again. I've had representations from ADF members telling me that meal and incidental allowances while undertaking overseas deployments have been reduced. Is that correct?

The meal and incidental allowances have been updated to align Defence with Foreign Affairs and Trade. DFAT do an annual review. Defence had been slightly out of step with that review arrangements, so what we have done is ensure that they're aligned.
Has the alignment increased it? Or has it decreased it?
It has varied across posting locations. In come cases it's decreased and in some cases increased. More have decreased than increased.

I certainly haven't received any complaints about increasing the allowance, but I have received quite a few about it being decreased. Can you give me more detail on how many locations it has been decreased and how many locations it has been increased?

We looked at this very closely. I haven't got it here, but we can absolutely provide what the review process was and the changes to those incidental and meal allowances. It's important to note that they are representative of what is required in country. So they are reviewed against what the cost of living and so forth is within the posting location.

I appreciate that, but, if you're a Defence member serving overseas and had been used to receiving a certain level of meal and incidental allowance and it is cut, whether or not the new rate is aligned with the local cost of living, that is still a cut effectively to the take-home pay of an ADF member serving overseas, isn't it?
We don't consider it as take-home pay; rather, it's to ensure that our ADF and APS members have available to them the meal costs and incidental costs of the country in which they are posted.

Sure. It's not literally their take-home pay, but, in practice, if you're an employee and you're receiving your salary and wages, and you're receiving allowances, that is your total remuneration package. If it is reduced, then your total remuneration is reduced too, isn't it?

The allowances are for a purpose. So, in terms of remuneration, that is a concept. In terms of allowances, that is for a particular purpose—in this case, for meals and incidentals. I do take your point that for a good majority there has been a reduction in a number of locations. So I take your point, but it isn't part of the remuneration package.

I'm not hung up on the terminology. I'm trying to use interchangeable language, so we don't get distracted by that. The total amount of money that ADF personnel receive from government has been reduced in many instances. They've had a hit to their income or their living standards or their remuneration or whatever terminology you want to use. They receive less now than they used to as a result of these changes.

I'll just say it again, because it is important that this is not part of the remuneration salary construct. It is to ensure that members have the meal allowance and the incidental allowance that is benchmarked against the country of the posting. But, again, I reflect that, yes, there has been a reduction in some of those locations, but the purpose is quite clear, and it's really important in terms of a whole-of-government approach that there is that alignment for those people that are working alongside our partners.

Sure. But for ADF members serving overseas, who've constructed their financial arrangements, whatever they may be, expecting a certain level of compensation for their deployment, that compensation is now less than it was before as a result of these changes and that's had a real tangible impact on them, which they have written to me to raise their concerns about.
I have just a couple more comments, if I might. We'd be really keen to get those comments, firstly.
I'm not sure they would give me permission to share their private correspondence to a parliamentarian with their employer.

The reason I'm asking is that the policy is very careful to ensure that there are exemptions or requests that can be put forward for consideration should there be some impact that the member or the APS employee can't manage. So there is that avenue.

Thank you. And if they don't see this, I will draw that to their attention and let them decide whether they want to take it up with you, rather than me breaching their confidence by sharing their correspondence to me. Is it true that in some instances the reductions are as much as 50 per cent or more?

In a few instances, that is right. But I really would like to provide you the whole—for each location, how the index was applied, so you can see that in the context of all locations. But, yes, that is correct.

I would like you to provide that to me as well. But since we don't have it, I have to, in the meantime, persist. I look forward to receiving it on notice as soon as it can be provided. Is it in the majority of locations, or a large number of locations, that we're talking about a 50 per cent or more reduction?
Not the majority, no.
What is the highest proportion of reduction? Is it 60 per cent, 70 per cent? How high are we talking in some locations?
Again, there are so many locations and, in terms of the translation between the currency in the actual country in which people are posted, I'd really prefer to provide the whole table for you.
I look forward to that. How much will Defence save as a result of these changes?

I can't answer that. We would have to do some form of projection on if we had left the amounts as they were. The aim of this was to ensure we had the contemporary standard and that it was aligned with DFAT.

Surely you know, though? Money is tight in the Defence portfolio, we want to make sure it's spent as well as it can be. You should roughly know the quantum of savings. Is it millions of dollars or tens of millions of dollars?
Can you just bear with me for a minute?
Of course.
I don't believe I've got the price difference here, but it was not in the order of what you're describing.

We're happy to take the details you're asking for on notice, but this wasn't a policy that was necessarily driven by a savings exercise. It was, as Ms Greig has said, around consistency. It's not clear to me that an APS officer serving in a particular country in Defence requires different meal allowances or other incidental allowances than a DFAT officer, a DISR officer or an agriculture officer operating at the same post. So this policy was around looking at the consistency across the arrangements for both APS and ADF, and it applies consistently to both sets of employees.
What prompted this? How did it come to the department's attention that there was a lack of alignment that needed to be resolved?

We had been aware of this for some time and that the work needed to be done. Again, I need to come back to you on when exactly that misalignment was recognised. We certainly had discussions within the department on the timing, conscious of giving people sufficient notice. The other aspect I will reinforce again is that if members or APS employees can demonstrate that additional costs were necessary for meals and incidentals then that is absolutely an avenue.
Sure. I appreciate that. You said that you were aware 'for some time'. Have you known of this problem for years or more recently than that?
The last couple of years, yes.
At what level was this decision made? Who decided that this needed to be done?

We took this situation, knowing that we needed to align and that it was overdue, to our enterprise business committee, which all deputy secretaries and service chiefs are part of, and that is chaired by the associate secretary.
How did you first become aware? Was it a jealous DFAT officer saying: 'This is pretty unfair. These guys are getting more than me'? Dave would never have done that back in his day, I know!
We regularly review our ADF and APS employment policy. That was part of a regular review. But I really need to come back to you on the actual timing of that.
Does Defence have visibility of what DFAT pays? Is that how you became aware? Was it brought to your attention?

It was part of our regular review and, indeed, other overseas conditions of service are, by and large, aligned with DFAT. Whether that's your cost-of-living allowance or your location allowance, that is all aligned with DFAT. There was quite a big review of overseas conditions of service done a few years ago, and a number of alignments were made at that time. I think that was 2016, from memory. That has been revisited a number of times. There are still some elements where there are specifics to the unique nature of the ADF, but, by and large, conditions of service are matched to DFAT for non-operational roles and postings.
Was the minister required to sign off on this? Was the minister briefed on this, or any of the ministers?
I'm going to check on that, but this was a departmental decision.
We may well have reported. It's not unusual when we make decisions at the departmental level that we provide information to ministers about the activity that we're doing.
In this instance, could you take on notice whether that happened?
Absolutely.
How was this change communicated to personnel?

The change was communicated through our usual mechanisms. We make sure we're communicating with each service through the chain of command. We have what we call Defgrams—I think you've heard us talk about those before—
Indeed.
which are a very standard way of communicating across the workforce. There were other updates through our internal internet, but we're always conscious that people don't all have access to that.
Each post has a hierarchy within it, so it would've been communicated through the line management areas in the individual posts as well.
Can those Defgrams be provided? They're not classified, I assume.
We can provide those.
And it's your evidence that that's the most appropriate way to communicate a change to people's entitlements?

What we have learnt over time is that the best way to communicate with service members is through the chain of command. In terms of the APS workforce, often we use different mechanisms to communicate. But, as the secretary just noted, communication to post is also a key element of this.
If the chair's happy, I'm going to move on to another topic now.
Yes. I was going to hand the call to Senator Lambie, but keep going with your next topic, and then I'll come to Senator Lambie after that.

These questions are about the Henderson defence precinct. My colleague Senator Blyth might have some follow-up questions later, but I've got a couple I want to ask now. In response to portfolio question on notice 49, the department said:

Establishment of the Henderson Defence Precinct is being undertaken through a phased approach and remains on track to meet capability delivery milestones.

Is that still the case?
I believe so, but I'll get confirmation from the capability delivery manager.
Would you mind repeating the question, please?

Yes. In portfolio question on notice 49, you said:

Establishment of the Henderson Defence Precinct is being undertaken through a phased approach and remains on track to meet capability delivery milestones.

Is that still the case?
Correct.

In your answer, you outlined that 'facilities and infrastructure are being developed for construction of Austal Defence Shipbuilding Australia landing craft heavy and landing craft medium vessels commencing this year, contingency docking capabilities for Australia's future conventionally armed nuclear powered submarine fleet from the early 2030s and depot-level maintenance, including graving docks, by the late 2030s'. In that QON, there was no mention of the Mogami class. Why is that?

It's an oversight. We will be building shipbuilding and ship sustainment facilities for the fleet that will be in being in Western Australia. That will include facilities that will support landing craft heavy, landing craft medium and construction of Mogami.
What is the timeline for Mogami class facilities to be available at Henderson?

The plan is to start construction for the shipbuilding and ship sustainment precinct in time to support landing craft heavy and medium first. That is beginning later this year and early into next year. That will include the facilities to do consolidation of the landing craft heavy. Those were originally planned to be temporary facilities, but now we're going to build permanent facilities. Those facilities will be able to cater for both Mogami and landing craft heavy.
So it doesn't need to be separately developed; it will be the same facilities, and Mogami can be constructed after landing craft heavy and landing craft medium are finished?
It's continuous naval shipbuilding, so the idea is to dovetail one end to the other, correct.
We are on track for Mogami to be constructed at Henderson from which year?
Prototyping will begin in 2029.
When will construction at Henderson begin?
Shortly thereafter.
And that's on track?
Correct.
In that QON, you outlined some pretty high-level milestones. Is there a document that's got more detail about that, a master schedule or similar for Henderson, that sets that out in more specificity?

There is a level 0 schedule, as we call it, which has got the major phasings. On that will be the construction of the key facilities, like the construction hall, by example. On top of that will be when we start construction for landing craft heavy and medium and Mogami.
Can that document be provided?
I'll take it on notice to provide it.
While I've got you, is there more detail that you can provide about the timeline of key deliverables or decision points for Henderson?

You would have seen recently, around August, Minister Marles announce the siting precinct, which is the spatial area where the precinct will be for shipbuilding, ship sustainment and nuclear power sustainment. The task from now through to the end of next year is to do what's called concept design. That will be the 30 per cent design milestone for the area. We're doing that in packages of work based on the priority of work. You can imagine some of the key milestones like the contingency dock for nuclear power sustainment is the first work package we're doing right now. Then we'll do a phased approach to that through to the end of next year, and then we'll have our 30 per cent design.
The 30 per cent design will be available when?
At the end of next year. At that time, we will then start turning soil in earnest for the majority of the facilities that we plan to have on the precinct.
What's the next design milestone after 30 per cent design?

It's really construction milestones from there on. We will refine the design, of course, as we go forward, but we're into construction. We'll do early works starting next year—things like moving breakwaters and dredging where we need to do dredging. That'll be mid-2027 through to 2028. Then we'll start concreting and digging up the sites and reclaiming land where we need to reclaim land. That will proceed in 2028 and 2029. It's more of a construction schedule that takes over from the design schedule, just like any other project.
I look forward to what you can provide on notice on that.
Will do.

On costs, in QON 139, which is one of those ones we received last night, you said:

The project will require tens of billions of dollars of investment in infrastructure and facilities over the next two decades.

'Tens of billions' is a very broad range; it could be anywhere from $20 billion to $99 billion. Could you be a bit more specific?

I think the government are on the record as stating two key numbers. One is $25 billion for the Henderson precinct. That is based on some early planning advice that we had back in 2024. Then $12 billion was the initial funding commitment, which I think is in the QON. It talks about that initial investment to get us through to the end of the decade from today. We are progressing through planning advice. Some of the planning advice informed the siting analysis we did. That is very much a long-term view. It's a very broad brush of where the site will be and what will be inside the siting. As we go forward through detailed planning, we'll get more refinement on the design. My hope is that, by the time we get to the 30 per cent design at the end of next year, we'll have more detail on the total cost both over the decade and through life.
So at this stage you have no more updated estimate than the $25 billion. That's the most recent number, and you don't have any data or insight into where it goes from there.
Correct.
There was media speculation, I think, around the time of that announcement that the total project cost could be in the order of $70 billion or $75 billion. That's not a number you're familiar with.
It's not a number that came from Defence at all.
How many dry docks will there be at Henderson for AUKUS?

My job is to take requirements from Navy and from the Australian Submarine Agency and then deliver against those requirements. The number of docks is actually an ASA question because they drive the requirement for the number and size of the docks.
So you don't know?
At this point, I have a requirement for two docks. If that changes from ASA, I will deliver to that requirement.
Sure, and my colleagues may ask later about whether that's sufficient. I accept it's not your responsibility; that's not your decision. But, currently, you're only constructing two dry docks?
Correct. Can I just clarify: I'm designing for two docks; I'm not constructing anything at the moment—
Of course.
I'm just designing for two docks.
Yes, understood, thank you. I have some related questions. The Captain Cook Graving Dock at Garden Island in Sydney—what's its current state?

It's what we call a product of interest. It has some remediation work that needs to occur to it. It's currently serviceable. You will know that we have a landing helicopter dock sitting in there today, HMAS Adelaide. At an ideal opportunity, we will continue to do remediation work. Thales is the contractor that we use to support us in making sure that the dock stays serviceable.
When is that remediation work scheduled?
We're waiting for the right opportunity to schedule it in based on availability.
Availability in terms of—
In terms of use, because we're not the only—it's Defence use, but it's also other commercial uses.
There's commercial use as well.
Correct.
So, basically, you need a gap in the pipeline of work to be able to do it—
Correct.
because, right now, what is our alternative to Captain Cook if it is not available?
Right. So what we're trying to do is stage the remediation in chunks—
That wasn't rhetorical; that's actually a question. What is our alternative?
Our alternative for Captain Cook Graving Dock?
Yes.
We don't have anything of that size and scale today, so it's very important that we maintain the availability of the Captain Cook Graving Dock.
But, if remediation has to occur, at some point it will be unavailable.

Correct. We work closely with Navy on making sure that, in contingency arrangements, depending on the size of the ship—if it's a smaller-sized ship, clearly that can go elsewhere. But, if it were a large ship, like a landing helicopter dock, then, yes, we would work with Navy on prioritising that work over the remediation.
But, once the remediation starts, it has to be finished, presumably.

Yes, and it's like any other project: we can do it in a staged way that ensures that it's not down for considerable periods of time—matters of years. We can do it in months. We're working through that now with our contractor to work out how we deliver that.

But we can't always anticipate the demand for facilities like these. I don't think the LHDs were expected to be where they are for as long as they have been. So let's say we go into remediation at Captain Cook and then we discover that we do need to do work on one of the larger ships that can't be done elsewhere. What would those contingencies be? What are those backups?
Senator, sorry to interrupt Mr Hanley—
Please.

That's probably straying into my accountabilities. As we plan to sequence the remediation work on that dock—the first thing, as Mr Hanley said, is we will clearly do that at a time when we're not going to be undertaking scheduled dockings. And, to be clear, we're only talking about those larger ships in the fleet—the landing helicopter docks, the auxiliary oilers and so on. For frigates, destroyers and conventional submarines, there are other options available.
What about Supply?

The auxiliary oilers, Supply and Stalwart—of those four larger ships, the LHDs and the AORs, Supply is one example. We would sequence that work in accordance with that. Clearly, as Mr Hanley said, there is no other dock of that size in Australia, so we would make arrangements with partners in the region, just as other partners could make arrangements with us. There are other facilities, with allies and partners, that we would seek to make, in advance of that, such that we could do that. They could also include commercial arrangements. For example, sometimes we dock our ships, even now, in Singapore. Singapore, Japan, the Republic of Korea, the United States—you can think of the sorts of partners that we would have to make arrangements with in the event that we had a contingent dock.

The other thing that is worth noting is we've significantly advanced our capability, with our partners, on doing in-water maintenance. One such example I'm thinking of was about 18 months to two years ago. We had to do some work on one of the auxiliary oilers. That work would have normally been done at a dock, but we used some new technology in cooperation with the United States Navy to be able to do that work in situ, in the water—using some of those technologies. The amounts of times that you have to dock a ship or a submarine are reducing in the context of the sort of work you can do in the water.

Obviously this is a worst-case scenario, but, if there's conflict in the Indo-Pacific over which we have no control, we're not going to be sending our heavy ships to facilities in the region to be maintained. How many options would we have in that instance if Cook is under remediation?

Clearly, in a conflict scenario, that is going to change the shape of optionality, and we need to look at that. There are less options in the Southern Hemisphere than there are in the rest of the world. But, by way of example, it's still early in the development but the New Zealanders are building quite a large dock—I think it's called the Northland dock—which we'd investigate, but there are other ways of doing that. You can actually bring docks to the country as opposed to the other way. Very large floating docks can actually be sailed or towed into locations, so you don't need to necessarily send the ship to the dock.
You're probably not going to be moving a slow-moving target across the Indo-Pacific in a conflict period, though.

Sure.

Senator Shoebridge interjecting—
Yes. Actually, I have one related question there, and then I should cede the call. What's the current state of the docks at Williamstown shipyard in Victoria?
We have been keeping an eye on that as part of maintaining our industrial base, if you like. You are aware that that site was sold.
I don't think it's been sold yet. I think there's interest in it.

We're going through a process, clearly, and, yes, we were asked by the government to monitor and manage that as an option, potentially, for us. It has changed a lot in the decades since we were last doing warships in that dock. It's not just about the infrastructure. It's also about the workforce and the supply chain that needs to exist where you have docks like that. My job is to make sure that we're looking at a national industry base to support all our warships, and, at the point in time that we became alert to the fact that it was being sold by BAE, we did not see that as a viable option for us.
