We already have our two major precincts: one in Adelaide and the one we'll have in Western Australia with Henderson.
Is that primarily because of the state of the infrastructure at Williamstown, or is it workforce, or—
It's all three of them.

On workforce—very quickly, because I know that I'm testing the chair's generosity here—I can't imagine that there's less workforce available in Victoria for a dock like that than there is in Adelaide or Perth, where there are smaller populations in very competitive markets. Surely, in terms of qualified people, in a larger population state with a strong industrial history there would be workers available if you needed them.

Yes, you're absolutely right. In fact, that was the one key positive with Williamstown: Victoria has a very strong workforce that can translate quite quickly to and from shipbuilding, so it wasn't a workforce constraint; it was an infrastructure constraint and a supply chain constraint because those things have moved on.
I'll explore that in more detail another time. Thank you, Chair.
Senator Lambie.
Thank you very much. I want to go to the Henderson floating dry dock, which Leidos Gibbs & Cox was selected to design.
The Australian Submarine Agency is responsible for that program, so this question would be best put to them when they attend estimates later today.
Sorry—what group are we in? I missed that.
It's just that it's—
We're with the department, but the agency might be best placed—
The Australian Submarine Agency is looking after that particular bit of the program.

Yes, Senator. For clarity, ASA are buying the dock. What Defence is providing is where the dock will berth and the shore services for it. Your question, and the particular company that you mentioned, is an ASA question because they are doing that activity.
Okay. I do have some questions on mental health in Defence.
Sure.
If others have got stuff with this stuff, I guess we'll just carry on and I'll wait.
No, you can ask. We don't have outcomes like estimates.
Okay, so I can talk about mental health care?

Senator, while the officials come to the table—earlier this morning we were talking about the audit of ADF estate with respect to cameras in soap dispensers, and I owed you a comeback as to when that audit will be complete. The directive I signed was for completion by close of business tomorrow and a full report to me early next week. I'm happy to share that the three services have completed and that they verbally advised me during the break that those audits are complete. No additional devices have been located.
Thank you. That's very nice to know. I'm sure that that will make many out there feel more comfortable in that uniform. Thank you for doing that.
It is pleasing to be able to report that the Leeuwin incident is an aberration.

Yes. I have a feeling those girls would have went off their chops anyway and gone out and had a look at their own toilets, to be honest with you. But thank you so much for clarifying that. That's great, and I'm glad it's just a one-off incident at this point in time. It's good news.

What changes has Defence made to their delivery of mental health care? Have you made changes in the last 12 months?

Changes specifically, I would say, have not necessarily occurred. What has occurred, though, is that we have seen an uplift in the number of mental health professionals that we have looking after our members, across a range of professional categories—psychologists, psychiatrists, mental health nurses and the like. The other aspect is that in things like the All-hours Support Line, for instance, we've seen an uplift; I know historically there'd been long wait times, call dropouts et cetera. The All-hours Support Line is the health line specifically for people calling in with mental health needs and includes options for family to call in if they're concerned about a member. So, working with our provider, we've seen an uplift of that in both personnel contracted to staff that line and in a reduction in wait times and dropouts. I guess one of the changes, and I don't know if it was within 12 months or before, would be our training for our mental health professionals. It's part of the royal commission recommendation about improving education for Defence personnel generally. The aspects of that, which colleagues could talk to, are not just about educating members and command in suicide prevention training but having our health personnel have a change in that training and an uplift to that. They would be a summary of the high-level changes.
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: Can I just add that, in recent times, we've introduced the mental health and wellbeing strategy, which goes from 2025 through to 2030. It's got a whole series of uplift in capability, training and support for members. We are working through the implementation of the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide's report, which is a whole set of things particularly focused on suicide prevention, including training courses. There's been the introduction of access to more than 25 different educational programs that have an impact on mental health and wellbeing, and we've also got a Defence lived experience framework which supports elements—
Yes, I'm aware of that.
So there's a whole set of things in terms of strategies and packages to train that we're implementing, as well as—
I understand that, Ms Quinn. That's fine; I've got that. There's no 24-hour hotline there, though?
The hotline availability is either with the Defence member and family support line—that I know you're aware of—or the direct healthcare line, which are 24 hours.
Oh, they are 24 hours?
Yes. The all-hours support line is available to triage people who call in.
Who's triaging them?
Health professionals.

That, Senator, is the one I said we've seen an uplift in—the All-hours Support Line. It's specifically for mental health concerns and not just for the member; their family can call in. Our outsourced service provider provides that. Their mental health nurses provide the service and depending on, obviously, the issue at hand, there is a range of outcomes. They can range from providing advice to referral to tertiary care.
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: Yes, they're all slightly different. It's basically like an octopus; they're coming in and then you'll fish them out to where they need to be.
That's correct.
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: With the garrison health contract in place, can you just clarify who—the ADF, the prime contractor or the subcontractor—is ultimately responsible for the mental health treatment facilities? Who's in charge of the staff in there?

If we're talking about garrison health care, the mental health care that we have is on base and off base; that's how we tend to classify it. On base, the mental health facilities we have are part of the garrison health estate. As Commander Joint Health, I'm responsible for the facility, but our colleagues are responsible for the infrastructure.
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: Let me rephrase my question. If there's a civilian, say, a psychologist, who do they report to if they believe their workplace may be being run by the hierarchy of Defence? Who do they go to? Do they go to Bupa? What happens with those civilian qualified professionals? I think there's a bit of coming unstuck here. I'm just trying to work out what's going on.

I understand the question. It is, as you're pointing out, a multidisciplinary and multi-employed workforce, so there is complexity. Within any health centre, there's a commanding officer and a health centre manager. There are also various roles that are a combination of uniformed, APS and civilian, from a leadership point of view. Locally, within the health centre, there are local arrangements, with the commanding officer of the centre being ultimately responsible for that centre and the joint health unit. From a performance point of view, however, the contracted psychologists or contracted health practitioners are also employed through Bupa, as the prime contractor. Their performance is managed there, and they also have that avenue to report as well.
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: So how many complaints have been made to Bupa?
I'd have to take that on notice.
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: Do we discuss this with Bupa at all, between Defence and Bupa?

Yes. The other part of the answer to that question is that there are layers of governance, including garrison management committees, where senior executives at different levels—for me the one most near is the garrison management committee, which met just yesterday or the day before. Senior executives from Bupa and Garrison meet around a range of things, where those sorts of issues around complaints or performance would be discussed.
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: How many complaints have there been in the last year? If I had civilians in there, GPs in there or psychologists in there and if they have a military member that they've got to report to, obviously that's a problem for them. Then, they've got to go to Bupa. What's Bupa doing about it?
It depends on the complaint.
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: If it's a poor performing person in uniform, what is Bupa doing about it, and how many complaints do they have?

If the performance is around a uniform member, that would be the uniform leadership's responsibility. The civilian psychologist could report within the chain of command in the health centre. But, if it's a uniform member's performance, that is the commanding officer's responsibility. If it's a contracted health practitioners performance, that will be Bupa's responsibility. But our teams work together at all levels given that they are multi—
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: If you're working together, has Bupa mentioned anything about complaints coming through to them?
I can't answer yes or no; I'd have to take that on notice. My team would have the answer to that.
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: I'll just note that there's also an anonymous complaints mechanism in Defence that covers all aspects of concerns. If someone has a complaint, there is a mechanism by which they could take it to a new independent complaints resolution area—
Okay. When did that start?

That commenced in January this year. It was a recommendation previously of the ombudsman and the royal commission to ensure that we had an avenue for complaints, including anonymous complaints and also complaints outside of the chain of command. That's been operational since January this year.
How many anonymous complaints have you received?
I think it's 92, but that's just in terms of general complaints. I'm not talking about medical complaints.

We've had 308 complaints overall, and 95 were made anonymously. They cover a whole range of issues. They can go to this service and they will be triaged and will be dealt with through, whether it's an APS member, an ADF member, a military police matter or a—
How many of these have been resolved, out of all those complaints?
I don't have that right here, but I'm happy to take it on notice. It would depend on all the different components. I'm happy to take it on notice.
When it comes to our psychologists, does the officer or the manager of those places in charge of those psychologists need to have actual qualifications in mental health themselves?

Certainly, in any psychology team, there would be a designated leader who has qualifications in mental health. The commanding officer of the joint health unit or the health centre manager do not necessarily have qualifications in mental health. If they are a health practitioner, they will have had, certainly, some of the safe side training I was just talking about, as all of our health practitioners do, but they won't necessarily have specific mental health training.
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: Why is that? I'm hearing you've got some nurses that are in charge too of these civilians, and they haven't got mental health training themselves.
They do or don't?
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: They don't.

No, because it's a multidisciplinary team. In all health teams, whether they be in Defence or elsewhere, leadership is often due to which health professional can fill that role and then done on merit, in the same way that even jobs as my own will have different professional training, but we lead a diverse and multiprofessional team, and you have access to the specialist input required to be able to understand what the needs of those teams are.
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: But, if you're a nurse in charge of psychologists, would you not require that nurse, when they got in, to go and have different training to make sure that they're up on what they're dealing with—which is, for psychologists, to have mental health training beside them?
There'll be two aspects to the leadership. One is the leadership of that person in performance, and the other is the technical aspects, which is the subject matter expertise. So any leader—
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: I'm sorry, but, when you're dealing with mental health and you haven't got any mental health courses you've done yourself, how does that give you expertise to be telling psychologists what to do and how to deal with things? I can understand that and understand some of these guys have been in the war zone and whatever, but what I'm asking specifically is: why don't they have mental health training with them, and why haven't they already started if they're in those positions?

The commanding officer or the leader would not be telling a psychologist what to do from a professional point of view. What they are doing is running that health centre and the command or the joint health unit. They wouldn't be specifically providing advice to a psychologist as to how to manage a patient, for instance.
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: I'm not asking for advice. I'm asking whether or not they have qualifications in that mental health area, because that really bothers me. How are they supposed to connect with the psychologist in there? And yet you've put them in charge. That's very worrying.
All I can say is that that's standard practice in multidisciplinary teams.
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: Well, maybe the standard practice needs to change. I just don't understand that at all. In each unit, when it comes to those psychologists who are dealing with people in uniform, do they each have a consultation room, or are they all out? I'm telling you that a psychologist needs their own room to deal with their own patients. Having a nice big room where we can all sit and be polite, nobody is going to get their thoughts around. Tell me what's going on there, because I'm hearing that's not happening.

My expectation would be that, any time a psychologist sees a patient, they are in a dedicated room on their own. If that's not happening, I'd be very interested to hear, but that's certainly my expectation, and that would be the health standard that we set. That doesn't mean the psychologist will have that room all day, and certainly if they're doing administrative work it may be that there are shared workspaces, but, when consultations occur, they should absolutely be occurring in a dedicated room, one on one.
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: So, other than that, they're thrown in a room, have to take phone calls from there and do their paperwork from there without actually having a dedicated room each. I'm just a bit concerned about that. It's just that they're private matters, and if you're putting them all together in a bunch—so, when you've got someone coming in, you can go into a room. Other than that, you've all got to sit out here?

Well, generally what would happen is that—and this would happen with doctors as well if they're seeing patients and doing consults—they would have a session. It's not just in and out. They would probably do half a day, and then somebody else may come in and do a half a day clinical session as well. There are other spaces for administration where it is still private, people are working at their desk in private cubicles and they can do their work that way.
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: Can the committee have a list of all the psychologists you have, where they are and how many hours they're working, whether full-time or part time.
Yes.
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: If a clinical psychologist resigns, what is the process in place to manage the transition for their patients to a new psychologist? Do we do a handover, or is it just: 'You're gone. Next one in'?

No, there would absolutely be a handover. Whether it's for resignation or for whatever reason a psychologist moves on, clearly, contemporaneous notes are, first and foremost, the most important thing. The health record is what most clinicians rely on, and, then, where possible, depending on the circumstances, there would also be that clinical handover of patients, particularly the complex patients. Often, if it's a complex patient, you'll have a team involved in the care of that patient, so, even if the psychologist is changing out, either the medical officer, the mental health nurse or the psychiatrist would be involved, as well as other social workers and wellbeing. For complex patients, that's a little easier to manage. For individuals, the health record is the most important handover and, if possible, a practical handover would occur.
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: So there are no disruptions during the handover phase. What does the revolving door look like with the psychologists? Are we having a revolving door? What does it look like, in your world, from where you're sitting? Because that bothers me as well. It's no good for anybody's mental health if we we're not trying to keep those psychologists, because it's a trust thing, obviously. If you are churning through them, for whatever reason, I'd like you to get to the reason and try and fix that because it will be a lot more beneficial, I would suspect. Is there a problem between yourselves and Bupa or anything?

No, I'm not aware of churn, but without the data in front of me, I wouldn't like to say there isn't any, so we could take that on notice to understand if there is a turnover and whether that's more than above average.
witness_position: RAN, Surgeon General and Commander, Joint Health

text: Does anybody else have any questions for the health professionals here?
It's fine. We'll rotate the call and come back to you.
Yes, that's fine. You can rotate the call. Thank you.
Senator Shoebridge.

We were talking previously about the United States defence force and its program to have nuclear-armed sea-launched cruise missiles on its Virginia class submarine fleet. Do you remember that discussion?
I believe it's nuclear-capable sea-launched missiles.
I beg your pardon?
That means that they could be equipped with conventional warheads as well, of course.

Yes, okay. Section 1633 of the national defense authorization act for the United States in 2026 requires the defence secretary to ensure that there are a limited number of sea launched cruise missiles with nuclear warheads to enable limited operational deployment of them with the Virginia class fleet no later than September 2032. That's now written into law in the US Congress. Has the US Navy or the US defence department—or war department, as they like to call it—advised the Australian government what the impact of having nuclear armed cruise missiles on the Virginia fleet, consistent with the law passed by congress, would have on AUKUS?

As we mentioned earlier today, SRF-West will be consistent with Australia's international obligations. This was reiterated by the governments of the United States, the UK and Australia on Tuesday, including by Secretary Hegseth. The statement released on Tuesday said:

AUKUS activities associated with SRF-West will be conducted consistent with the AUKUS partners' respective international obligations, including those under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, and Australia's obligations under the South Pacific Nuclear Free Zone Treaty (Treaty of Rarotonga).

While the SLCM-N program is under development, as we've discussed, it is a matter for the US government, and we have engaged with them about the program and with this committee about the program. We can say that the government has made clear that the pursuit of AUKUS will be consistent with all Australia's nonproliferation obligations, including the Treaty of Rarotonga.

Has the US sat down with the Australian Defence Force or the defence department and explained the impact of this congressional law requiring the US Navy to have nuclear-armed cruise missiles on its Virginia fleet by 2032. Have they discussed what the impact will be on the deployment of US nuclear submarines to HMAS Stirling?
It's routine business for the Australian defence department and the US defense department to talk about future programs.
I'm asking about this.

We have engaged on this program; I can confirm that. It is part of our routine engagement on a range of programs. This is six years away and still developmental. The objective is to ensure a certain number of US SSNs will be capable for this program. It may ultimately end up being the platform on which this capability is established. There are a range of different US submarine platforms. My point is that it's still in development.
What do you mean, there are a range of different US submarine platforms?
There's the Virginia class—
Apart from the Virginia class, what other US submarine platform is the US Navy considering putting sea-launched cruise missiles on with nuclear weapons? If there is one, tell me what it is.

The US Navy operates significantly larger submarines that have greater capacity for missile storage and, indeed, could well be more suitable platforms for this program. Our Chief of Navy and our CDF, who is an expert submariner, can also answer these questions.

If you understand that the US is considering putting these sea-launched cruise missiles with nuclear weapons on a platform other than the Virginia class submarine, please tell me what platforms you understand the US Navy is doing it for and then point me to the evidence that says that.

I just want to check the characterisation. As we've said, this program is in development; it's six years away. We understand that they'll be looking at their full suite of capabilities in order to deploy these weapons in six years, subject to their development. It's all very hypothetical. In terms of the suite of submarines that they have in the United States Navy, we will hand to the experts.

This is a law passed by Congress to require the US Navy to have a number of sea-launched cruise missiles with nuclear weapons on them, and the law expressly says 'for the Virginia class submarines'. If you have evidence that there's some parallel project for other US submarines to put on them sea-launched cruise missiles with nuclear warheads, please tell me what these submarines are and show me the evidence.
Are you familiar with the Ohio class guided missile nuclear submarine? It carries 154 Tomahawk missiles.

Yes. Are you saying that the law passed by Congress that required these sea-launched cruise missiles to be put on the Virginia class submarine, with all the detailed design that requires for launch authority, for personnel specific to this class of submarine—that they've got a parallel project with the Ohio class? Is that your understanding?

That's not what I'm saying. I'm not going to speak for the United States Navy. What I will say is that the launch system that launches a Tomahawk missile is the same launch system on a Virginia class as it is on a SSGN, although the SSGN has more capacity—so it would be reasonable to conclude that that would be a similar option. At the end of the day, all three nations stated on Tuesday, according to the statement that Mr Jeffrey referred to, that our obligations under the Treaty of Rarotonga will be honoured. To your point, not all Virginia submarines are required to be fitted as such; it will be a minimum requirement. This will take years. At this stage I think we can honour the words of our ally, and I do not anticipate that this is going to be an issue in the near term.

I never said 'all'; I said 'a limited number'. That's the congressional requirement from September 2032. The requirement to have them fully deployed across a subclass of Virginia class submarines doesn't kick in until 2034, under that congressional law. Are we of one mind about that?
Yes.

That means, if the US Navy acts consistent with the law passed by Congress, there will be a limited number of Virginia class submarines with nuclear-armed sea-launched cruise missiles by September 2032. That's the law, and that's the plan, isn't it?
And, by extension, there'll be many others that won't.

Correct. Have we got an agreement from the US, or have we made a clear demand of the US, to say that they are not permitted to bring nuclear-armed Virginia class submarines to HMAS Stirling? Has that clear line been put to the United States in the same way that New Zealand has done?
We have a clear commitment from the US government to honour our obligations under the Treaty of Rarotonga. That is the agreement.

We know how this government interprets that agreement—that is, provided the nuclear weapon isn't permanently stationed either in the air base or in the port, provided it's just rotating through, you don't believe that's a breach of the Treaty of Rarotonga. That's the interpretation of the Treaty of Rarotonga, and it's been repeatedly reiterated by Senator Wong and others. That's your position, isn't it?
The Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade administers and owns that treaty. Questions on interpretation should go to the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade.

Admiral Hammond, you mentioned the Treaty of Rarotonga. You said this is consistent with the Treaty of Rarotonga. You must have some understanding of what that means. What is it? Is it, as I said, that, provided that it's not permanently stationed there, that it's just rotating through, that's not a breach of the treaty?
I'm bound by a whole bunch of laws and treaties which I will point to as being limitations or constraints on ADF operations, but I'm not going to interpret them for you. That's not my responsibility.

You do things like operate ports and operate air bases. You must know how the Treaty of Rarotonga impacts on your operation of air bases. You must have heard at least a dozen times the Foreign minister and the defence minister both state that their view of compliance with the Treaty of Rarotonga is that it permits the rotation of nuclear-armed US platforms through Australia, provided they're not stationed there. Are you saying you've never heard the defence minister or the Foreign minister say that?
Senator, the—
Admiral. My question was directed to the admiral, in direct response to his answer.
The secretary can answer the question too.
The chief of Defence is here.
Thank you, senators. Secretary.
We were just pointing—

I'm going to take a point of order. My question was whether or not the chief of Defence had heard this being said by the defence minister or the Foreign minister. With all due respect to the secretary, unless she's sitting inside the chief of Defence's head, she cannot answer that question. I put the question again to the chief of Defence.
As I stated in my opening statement, we treat all witnesses with respect. I think we're all keen to hear from the secretary, and I'm sure the chief of the ADF may also want to add.
The secretary cannot provide an answer to what's in the chief of Defence's head.
Well, if you know what they're going to say, why are you asking questions? Let's just let them answer, and then you'll have an opportunity to respond.
Please tell me if the chief of Defence has heard the defence minister or the Foreign minister make that statement repeatedly.
Do you really have to be a smart alec? You've actually done quite well this week.
No, I just would like the question—it's not being a smart alec; this is about nuclear weapons and the presence of nuclear weapons and basic policy.
I knew by Thursday the smart-alec behaviour would be coming out. Just ask your question.
Oh, you are such a—
Come on.
You are such a you.
Come on, colleagues.
Point proven.
You are always you, Minister.
Secretary, do you want to add something?
I always forget you're the smartest man in the room. I keep forgetting that.
And I never forget you are you.
I think the secretary was going to add something—
I only wish I was as smart as you.
and then we'll see if the Chief would like to add something. Secretary.

I was simply pointing out that we clearly are responsible for the interpretation of treaties that the Department of Defence administers. The department of foreign affairs administers the Treaty of Rarotonga. Interpretations of detail would be best put to them. It is clear in terms of the statements that the Treaty of Rarotonga, as published, and as already mentioned in this, is around the stationing of weapons. While, with the greatest respect, the CDF and I have a very close working relationship, I cannot interpret his mind on all matters. But, to be very clear, the ministers' comments stand as the ministers state them, and it's not for the Public Service to reinterpret ministers' statements.

Admiral, I'm not asking you to reinterpret. I've asked you if you've heard statements, repeatedly said, from both the defence minister and the Foreign minister that the Treaty of Rarotonga prohibits the stationing of nuclear weapons in Australian facilities but does not prohibit the rotation of them through Australian facilities. Have you ever heard that said by the defence minister or the Foreign minister?
I've heard you assert that. I've heard you assert those statements have been made. I don't recall being in the room when they have been made.
And, Senator, I have not heard those statements. I have certainly heard about visits, which are different from rotations.

Alright. Have you heard, Chief of Defence, either the defence minister or the Foreign minister say the Treaty of Rarotonga does not prohibit the visiting of US platforms that have nuclear weapons on them?
Senator, can I just offer a quick clarification?
Yes. Perhaps you know what's in the Chief of Defence's head.

Ministers have said that the treaty does not prohibit the visit of nuclear-capable assets. So that is not a confirmation that they are nuclear armed. And I'll take you back to the Australian government's position that we respect the United States policy of neither confirming nor denying—
We will obviously have to come back to this with multiple printouts of the previous occasions.
and that the United States respects our international and domestic treaty obligations.

The word salad that this department applies to try and avoid recognising the basic truth that you permit the US to bring nuclear weapons into this country to make this country a target—the word salad that you apply to try and avoid that obvious truth—has been so apparent for the last 15 minutes of engagement. The sort of doormat approach: we don't ask, we don't test, they can bring their weapons in when they want, that's fine. It just proves how little independence this department has from the US, doesn't it? Don't ask, don't tell.
We don't hold policy authority over that, and they are not the assertions that we've made. And I think everybody else—there are quite a few people smiling at that assertion.
Alright. Last question. I've got to rotate the call, Senator.
I beg your pardon. I missed the last part of your answer. What did you say?

I said they are not the assertions that we are making in this room. We are not the policy authority on those things you're describing. There are some people smiling in this room at those assertions that you're making.
Are they?
I can see them.
Well, that's because they also have the same policy position about being a doormat to the US.
Alright, Senator.
That's why they're smiling.
Alright.
You're all of one mind on it.
Why not support Ukraine then?
Yes, how's Ukraine going? How are those Russian submarines going?
You all have the doormat approach. This is the doormat approach over here—
Here we go. Exhibit A, everyone!
and it's also over there!
Look at how pro-Australia you are!
It's the US doormat approach. You're all of one mind—
Good to see you're on our side, mate.
That's why you're smiling!
You're certainly unique when it comes to not supporting Ukraine.
Hear, hear.
You are very unique in many respects.
Hear, hear.
You are unique in some ways.
Where is your doormat to the US?
Do you want to talk about doormats? How is Vladimir Putin going?
Hear, hear.
You, Minister, are continuing to be you.
Mate, I'm not the one saying Russia should get whatever they want when it comes to Ukraine.
Nor am I, and you suggesting that, if you want this to degrade into you lying, which you're doing now—
Oh, here we go!
Me degrade?
How could this degrade any more?
which I perfectly understand. I am used to you and other ministers lying about the position, but we can continue.
He should withdraw that, Chair.

I know. You should withdraw, actually. You're making characterisations and inferences of the Minister. I actually think you should withdraw that. I think it goes to the character of the individual, being the Minister, who you were just—
I withdraw it to the extent it goes to the character of the Minister.
I think you withdraw and without any conditions.
Oh whatever, I withdraw.
I've got to rotate the call. You've had some time, so I will need to move the call around.
We'll come back to this.

We certainly will. On the topic of Ukraine, I know we've spoken at length in this committee previously about Australia's support for Ukraine. How has Defence been continuing to support the people of Ukraine since we last had you here in estimates?

In 2022 Russia conducted an unprovoked and illegal invasion of Ukraine. This invasion was a profound abrogation of the Russian Federation's responsibilities as a permanent member of the UN Security Council. As you know, by being a member of that council, you are among the architects and the stewards of international law, the foundation stone of which is the territorial integrity of states. It was also a profound breach of its commitments under the 1994 Budapest Memorandum, which, as you know—
It's good to see Senator Shoebridge is now leaving while we're talking about our support for Ukraine, but, anyway.
Unbelievable!
Unbelievable.

There is much discussion in this committee about nuclear nonproliferation and how that works in international law. The Budapest Memorandum was the memorandum under which Ukraine agreed to cede its nuclear arsenal, the third largest in the world at that time, to the Russian Federation in exchange for Russian commitments to Ukraine's territorial integrity and current borders and for Russia to refrain from the use of force against Ukraine and to refrain from economic coercion that would subordinate Ukraine's sovereignty to Russia's interests.

The decision to invade Ukraine in 2022 represents, I think, the most serious abrogation of modern nuclear diplomacy that we have seen. It is one of the reasons why the invasion of Ukraine is so dangerous. It illustrates the mendacity at the heart of Russian disinformation on Ukraine. It also underlines why it is so important that countries like Australia support Ukraine to end this war on its own terms and to ensure that the manner in which the war concludes does so in a way that convinces states that the Russian invasion was a huge miscalculation and sets back its interests by many years. We do not want the invasion of Ukraine to become a template for other states because ultimately the invasion is less about Russian insecurity and more about how Russia might use force to change not only international borders but how the international system works. The nuclear element is so crucial because the lesson states might learn from this is that you never see your nuclear weapons if you have them, or that you might need them if you don't have them. That's why the Budapest Memorandum is so central.

The Australian government has been a robust supporter of Ukraine. The total dollar value is approximately $1.9 billion, getting close to $2 billion. That support is divided into two different key tranches. It is materiel and financial support for the defence of Ukraine, as conducted by its armed forces, and ADF commitments under Operation Kudu, which is how we work with our international partners to help train and develop the Ukrainian armed forces. Also, in this year the government announced an additional $60 million in support of Ukraine. That includes $45 million of Australian Defence Force equipment, $10 million for Ukraine's Energy Support Fund and $5 million in humanitarian assistance, including for the International Committee of the Red Cross and other humanitarian initiatives.

Australia will also join the United Kingdom led Maritime Capability Coalition for Ukraine to support the development of Ukraine's navy. As you know, Chair and colleagues, the Russian Black Sea fleet has been largely kept to its bases or sunk. Ukraine doesn't actually have a navy, because it has worked so effectively with new autonomous systems, and we want to work with them to help develop that capability.

Also, on 19 June 2026, the government announced an additional hundred million dollar contribution over the next 12 months to NATO's Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List. It contributes to a fund that Ukraine can use to acquire capabilities internationally, from the United States and other partners, in the aid of its own defence. Of that contribution, $50 million goes to the NATO Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List initiative and there's a $43 million package for ADF materiel and a $2 million contribution to the Drone Capability Coalition. It also includes sanctions on 45 more vessels linked to Russia's shadow fleet, which, as you know, is a key way that Russia avoids sanctions in relation to its energy exports.

Finally, I will add that activities under Operation Kudu include training for forces of Ukraine's personnel. In late May 2026, Defence pivoted Operation Kudu training support from the United Kingdom's Operation Interflex, and this consisted of a rotational force of approximately 90 ADF personnel based in the United Kingdom who trained more than 3,600 out of 56,000 Ukrainians. It's now being transitioned to a Norwegian led operation, Operation Legio, and we will continue to support that activity along with a range of other nations.

Since 2024, Australian Defence Force personnel have participated in the support assistance group, which is Ukraine working with NATO on developing operational partnerships not just on training but also on logistics and theatre support. That's the list of what the Australian government has authorised in support of Ukraine and that we continue to do on the defence side while our foreign ministry colleagues focus very heavily on working with our partners on peace negotiations.

Thank you for that, Mr Jeffrey. I think that's a really good summary about where we've got to since we last had you in estimates. I know the Ambassador of Ukraine here in Canberra is very appreciative, as is his government. President Zelenskyy and many other diaspora, I think, are very thankful for the Australian government's support. In fact, I should add it's bipartisan support, really, between the government and the opposition towards the people of Ukraine. In terms of our military support, were there any other aspects that we are making a contribution to in its self-defence against Russia's invasion? I'm not sure if there is anything else that you needed to add other than what you've just singled out to me.

No, other than the fact that, of course, there's been some discussion around a coalition of the willing—of like-minded states being willing to enter into an agreement where a ceasefire would be underwritten by a foreign coalition that would be able to reinforce Ukraine's defence and act as a backstop. Those negotiations and discussions continue but ultimately hinge on a durable ceasefire being established between Russia and Ukraine.
What would a policy of ceasing military aid to Ukraine do in terms of benefiting Russia? What are the practical implications there?

I think that Ukraine is committing a large proportion, the lion's share, of its GDP to defend its territory and its people. It has achieved enormous amounts in terms of the development of its battlefield capability, particularly in terms of its ability to grow its autonomous systems, but it would not be able to sustain its current level of combat operations or its defence along its borders and the front line as it currently exists without robust international assistance. Its European partners now are the primary providers of financial and military assistance to support Ukraine's defence. But support from other partners, including from Ukraine's Indo-Pacific partners, remains vitally important, and it would have a serious impact on Ukraine's ability to defend itself if countries began to reduce their assistance.

During the first few weeks in this role, I received a number of requests for conversations either in person or by VTC from counterparts around the world. One of the notable ones was from the Polish chief Wiesław, who was at pains to thank Australia for our contribution to training Ukrainians in Poland and inspired by the fact that a nation on the other side of the planet would make such a contribution to the preservation of a democratic state. Similarly—face-to-face conversations with my German counterpart, Norwegian counterpart, Danish counterpart and the Netherlands only two weeks ago in Japan. They all reiterated their great respect and gratitude for Australia's contribution to supporting them and their neighbourhood in the manner that we have been. So I think that the incredibly positive outpouring of gratitude that I've experienced in my first few months in the job is directly connected to the contributions that we have made to supporting Ukraine over there, and we should not lose sight of that.

Indeed, and I think words do matter in particular in this place. When we've got colleagues on mainly the crossbench, particularly the Greens, referring to Ukraine as the Ukraine, I think that sends a very strong and dangerous message, in particular, to people who are suffering at the moment and who are reliant on countries like Australia to support them. So I think it's important that we've got very good, strong bipartisanship—and obviously the work that the men and women who wear our uniform in the military do every single day.
Sorry, Chair, can I ask one question since you're talking about Ukraine? But if you want to—

I was just going to ask Mr Jeffrey then about the Maritime Capability Coalition for Ukraine. I understand that Australia is part of that. Could you elaborate a bit more on what we are doing with respect to that coalition?

As I mentioned, Ukraine is making great strides in building its maritime capability; however, it doesn't have a formal navy. The UK has set up an initiative and it has asked its partners to contribute to how we work together to support Ukraine's maritime capability, particularly because its access to the Black Sea remains a critical economic lifeline. For Ukraine, in particular, it's its principal source of sea based export. As you know, for an agrarian country like Ukraine, that remains vital, so we will continue to work with the UK and our other partners in support of Ukraine. But I would add, and many people have made this point before, that Ukraine is actually on the technological frontier when it comes to autonomous capability, so we have things to learn from Ukraine too. Indeed, the pace of change and the way in which the battlefield is evolving, as the secretary mentioned earlier today, is extremely intense in these battlefields. For the Australian armed forces to be in a position such that they remain at the frontier, we need to be able to engage closely with our allies and our partners in the area where warfare is changing so quickly.

I think that, proudly, Australia being the largest non-NATO contributor of military assistance hasn't gone unnoticed either. On that, though, there has been a lot of support from the private sector here, in Australia. People have been involved in the defence industry who initially did support Ukraine, and I think they continue to. I'm not asking to go to into great detail. But, as much as you can go into detail in this forum about how much of that collaboration that we've built over the last couple of years over the conflict—what has being able to learn lessons and, sadly, use some of the experience but then be able to continue to support the Ukrainian military meant for our defence industry?

I think that the Australian defence industry is observing, closely, developments in Ukraine, and there are opportunities for co-development and lessons learned between Ukrainian defence industry and our own. As you know, Australia has some significant expertise in autonomous systems and we have a good and strong innovation base and innovative defence industry sector. Ukraine has expressed interest in investing in Australia's industrial base in order to draw on additional sources of supply and industrial capacity.

There are a range of different initiatives at play. These are commercial activities that the government would of course support, and I think that those areas would be ones which are prudent investments for Ukraine and for us as we grow these capabilities over time. As you know, the Integrated Investment Program contains a significant slice that is allocated for the development of autonomous systems, and we would see closer cooperation between Australian defence industry and the Ukrainian counterparts as part of that. I will be travelling shortly to the UK and we will be discussing exactly how we can work with the UK on closer integration of our respective industrial bases, and that of course includes how we would work with our partners like Ukraine.
Senator Lambie, had an additional point on this?
I just have a couple of questions on Mr Streeting in the UK. Has anyone in Defence had an opportunity since the changeover of Starmer to meet with Mr Streeting at all?

Yes. I was with the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Defence in the UK shortly after Minister Streeting took his post, and the Deputy Prime Minister was in fact the first overseas visiting person to attend him.
Okay. I don't really know enough about that, so I'll just cut you off. Have we had any Defence personnel over there to meet him yet?
We have. I have certainly met with him, and we have our senior aide in the UK, who was part of that visit as well.

Has the Chief of the Defence Force been over there yet? I ask this question because this week Mr Streeting has launched a national resilience conversation. He's calling it out, warning that the nation needed to be ready for war with Russia within 1,000 days or by 2030. Have our Defence personnel—not our politicians and that—been able to get over there yet to find out what's going on? I tell you what: Ukraine is struggling. They cannot get help out of the US. Every other Western country is trying to feed them what they possibly can, but they are feeling the impact over there, and I'm just not sure they'll hold for three years. I know this could be a national security type thing, but when can we get Defence, the CTF and them, over to the UK?

We have a significant set of Defence personnel in the UK precisely to connect with the UK military. You don't have to physically attend the UK to have very close working relationships, but I'm happy to hand to the CDF.

I've met with Rich Knighton, the Chief of the Defence Staff of the United Kingdom, on two occasions face-to-face, and we've had several VTCs and connected regularly. We met in Canada at the PACOM Chiefs of Defence Conference, and more recently, two weeks ago, we met in Japan. We've had a number of conversations with the Five Eyes chiefs of defence in the one room, including with Dan Caine. Your concerns about the security outlook in Western Europe vis-a-vis NATO and Russia have been the subject of deep discussion, and I have back-briefed accordingly to the minister, the Deputy Prime Minister.

Thank you so much. That makes me feel better. I have nothing against the Deputy Prime Minister or the Prime Minister; it's just that these are the experts, so I'm making sure they've got their foot right in the door and keeping up with what's going on. I understand. Thank you.
Senator Roberts.

Thank you for appearing again today. Admiral Hammond, on 10 May 2023, Petty Officer Armfield wrote to you seeking help as his 20-year Navy career ended through medical discharge. In that correspondence, he challenged your stay-on-board, people-first commitment in which you stated that, as Chief of Navy, you were responsible for the safety and wellbeing of Navy personnel. You subsequently met Armfield in October 2023. He then provided you with 301 excerpts from a meeting he had with Defence medical and legal representatives, and you acknowledged reading those excerpts. Admiral, having personally received and acknowledged this evidence, what actions did you take to investigate the identified failures, protect Armfield's professional reputation and welfare, and pursue accountability?

I have met with Petty Officer Armfield. We organised for him to be flown to Canberra to meet with me when I was the Chief of Navy in order to hear his concerns and his complaints from him firsthand. I referred those complaints to the Inspector-General of the Australian Defence Force for a full investigation and monitored that throughout. We also flew the warrant officer of the Navy to his location interstate on a couple of occasions to meet with him, and we ensured that there was a support system dedicated to monitoring and supporting him as he navigated that investigative process. I met him again when we were at the Royal Commission into Defence and Veteran Suicide, spoke to him again on the sidelines and enquired about his wellbeing. I have not met with him again recently.

Admiral Hammond, on 13 February 2024, as mentioned earlier, John Armfield contacted you also to identify Colonel Matthew Freeman and challenged the accuracy of his accounts of the support provided to John Armfield. As mentioned earlier on 3 March 2024, you acknowledged receiving and reading the excerpts.

When you name people who are subject to allegations you place their name in the public domain and you subject them to all sorts of repercussions in social media, in their workplace, at home and in society in general. We have a process for investigating complaints that are raised by ADF members, and that is that we refer them to the Inspector-General of the Australian Defence Force. That is to ensure that things are investigated at arm's length from the service chiefs and the CDF, and also to make sure that the rights and protections of respondents are appropriately dealt with until evidence has been assessed. If you'll indulge me, I request you don't name any ADF personnel who are subject to allegations which have not yet been proven.

I should add, though, that we had a case in the past where we do need to tread carefully. We don't want to interfere with any ongoing investigation, and I think there'd be strong advice from clerks over various governments that would back that in. I think, Senator, I'd urge you and anyone else, for that matter—we even had cases yesterday in the Foreign Affairs portfolio that relate to visa matters—that it is better if we can try and have some of these conversations offline, not for anything other than to make sure there is procedural fairness and afford the person that you're probably wanting to help some help rather than air it out in a public forum.

Senator Roberts, if I can reinforce that, Senator Lambie identified earlier today some issues—complaints or allegations—that she wished to raise and undertook to raise them privately with the Chief of the Defence Force so that they can be properly investigated without airing them in a public hearing. I'd ask that you consider the way that Senator Lambie has approached this and think about perhaps doing it in the same way.
I noticed that the chair just said it would be better to be ventilated elsewhere, and you've just offered that same invitation. Is that okay with you, Admiral?

I've been personally engaged in supporting Petty Officer Armfield. I acknowledge that he hasn't necessarily received the outcome that he might have expected, but it has been independently investigated. I'm happy to engage with you offline, one on one, so I can understand what additional concerns or complaints—
Admiral, could I seek your indulgence and see if you're willing to talk to the senator at some point whilst we're here and work out how the two officers can have an exchange of information.

I would extend that invitation to all members of the committee. If you've got concerns about the wellbeing or support of an ADF member, we would all like to hear about it and be given the opportunity to do something about it whilst respecting the rights and wellbeing of all personnel involved.
I'd be delighted to meet with you and discuss this. I don't think it will be happening today because we will be busy until 11, but will your office get in touch with mine?
We'll make arrangements through the appropriate mechanisms, but you know where I live, and I'm not going anywhere anytime soon.
Thank you very much.
I don't know where you live, but we do know where you work!
Could I ask a very short question.

Sorry, Senator Roberts. I was just going to say, just so you know, that the Navy have also worked with us on this same issue for some significant time as well, and they've been very good from their end. I'm not sure whether you've been told that or had an update, but we also have spent significant time on this one person in trying to help them. So I'm not sure how much help we can possibly give.

If there are any dramas or if you're having any issues, Senator Roberts, feel free to also contact my office. I'm sure we can liaise with the admiral, or you can directly. If there are any dramas, feel free to contact my office.
I appreciate the comments of everyone.
I just want to make sure that people understand there are genuine opportunities here to engage on this particular issue.
Yes. That's taken. Can I just ask a very short question.
Yes, go for it. The call is still yours.

My question is on the availability of RAAF Base Tindal for emergency landing of commercial aircraft. Commercial airlines are required to lodge a commercial flight plan which includes the location of emergency landing strips and shows the plane has the fuel to get there. My office has received information that Tindal has advised airlines it should not be used as a designated emergency landing airport at the Top End, requiring all airlines to carry extra fuel to reach Cairns. This makes tickets dearer and planes heavier while increasing the risk for air travellers. What guidance has been given to commercial airlines on this matter?

Senator, good afternoon. I'm not across that particular matter in detail, so let me take that on notice, and I'll come back to you. There are times, for operational reasons or other reasons, when we need to potentially limit access to some of the Air Force bases. Those are done in consultation with industry. NOTAMs and other appropriate notifications are issued. But, with respect to that matter, I'll take that on notice and come back to you.

Correct.
