That's alright. I hope you're not asking for a friend who's trying to land a plane! Are you? I'm glad you got the joke.
Are they still able to fly a plane, Senator Roberts?
That's very clever, I've got to admit.
Hey, it doesn't happen often. Come on. Give me some credit. Senator Paterson.

Thank you, Chair. Don't quit your job. I just have a couple of quick questions, and then I'm going to share the call with my colleagues Senator Blyth and Senator Collins. It's about Mogami again, if the relevant officials could be available. As I understand it—but correct me if I'm wrong—the plan at this stage is for the first three Mogami frigates to be built in Japan and for the fourth Mogami to be built at Henderson.
That is correct.

Obviously, though, that requires Henderson to be ready in order to construct it, and we've heard there's a busy schedule of works to happen in a short period of time to make sure that that's the case. At what point will it become clear, if there is any slippage in Henderson, that that fourth Mogami may not be able to be built at Henderson and it may have to be built in Japan? What's the drop-dead date at which we would know that or need to know that?
We will be doing an assessment in early 2028, and that will be completed by mid-2028, to go to government to determine whether the conditions are right to be able to commence prototyping in 2030.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Major Surface Combatants and Combat Systems

text: Given the lead times required for shipbuilding of this kind, if we decided in mid-2028, based on that advice, that we weren't ready to build ship 4 at Henderson, that would be sufficient time for our partners in Japan to continue that continuous ship build and provide it to us on the scheduled timeframe?

Yes, that's correct. Sheryl and I are engaged with the right officials within Japan, including within MHI, to make sure they understand that. In fact, it was at recent meeting between the Minister for Defence here and the Japanese Minister of Defense that that was reiterated.
So they are on standby and they know that, if there is slippage at Henderson, we may ask and they may be required to do that?

If there is. I might clarify two points there. One is a correction on the record for me. I think I said earlier that the prototyping would start in 2029. Sheryl is correct; it starts in 2030. The second one is that there are two conditions. One is, as you rightly point out, the availability of the Henderson defence precinct for the construction of Mogami. The second condition is the readiness of our strategic shipbuilder Austal.
And, presumably, the progress on landing craft heavy and medium?

Correct, the landing craft heavy program and the landing craft medium program are pilot programs for Austal, so that they can go from where they are today to where we need them to be—building tier 1 warships such as the Mogami.
If there was any slippage in their ability to deliver those platforms, that would have implications for Mogami?

Correct. Sheryl was right again, that the condition check she mentioned involves both of those aspects. We are working on both right now, so we are uplifting Austal's capability as we speak. We are not just reliant on the landing craft heavy and the landing craft medium program; we are also doing a corporate capability uplift with Austal. Then, on the readiness of the yard, that's a schedule that we're working to, to make sure that there are the facilities—the fabrication sheds, construction halls, block building facilities et cetera.
The final date for the decision is mid-2028, but is it possible that it might become evident before then that we're not going to meet those deadlines?
The assessment will be done from the first half of 2028, and then we'll go to government in the second half of 2028.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Major Surface Combatants and Combat Systems

text: But, for example, if we identify issues with the Austal uplift or the landing craft delivery earlier than that, self-evidently there are implications that flow from that for Mogami.

I think the answer's self-evident as well. The answer's yes. But the good news is that we've started that work already, and there are no indications, at this point in time, that we'll be behind on either item.
But it is an ambitious thing for Austal to do. It's no knock on them. They're a great company, but this is something that they've not done before.
Correct, and maybe I can refer to Sheryl here, to talk about the engagement between Austal, Japan and MHI already.
Yes, please. Just quickly, and then I'll share the call with my colleagues.

We've had several meetings, which the Commonwealth has facilitated, to ensure that we get Austal and MHI having initial discussions on their relationship, how they will be contracting and making sure that ADA get the information they need to be able to assess the onshoring, to start doing that preparation work from now through to 2028.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Major Surface Combatants and Combat Systems

text: Thank you. I'm happy to share the call.
Really?
To my colleague!
I thought: 'Aah, the coalition are done. Good!'
Not quite, Chair. Sorry.
Alright, I know you're not done yet; I know. I tried my luck!
I'll be as efficient as possible.
Take your time.
I just wanted to ask some questions around steel supply and the closure of the Whyalla steelworks. I'm not sure—
It depends on what aspect of steel supply. If it's relating to feeding into submarine supply chains, for example, that would be best asked to the Australian Submarine Agency.

It's probably broader than that because, obviously, sheds and all of those things—the infrastructure—will require steel more broadly. Perhaps I can ask, and then we can refer it on if it gets too specific. Has Defence done an assessment on the closure of the Whyalla steelworks and whether that will cause any shortages in the supply chain?

I'm not aware of a specific report. I do know that officials have been working with our officials within the Department of Industry, Science and Resources. I know that more from my previous role than my current role. There have been connections in terms of discussions with both proponents involved in the resolution of the Whyalla situation through the insolvency process. We continuously look at providing information to market on different supply chains we need. I'm not aware of a specific, identified issue relating to the most recent closure of the blast furnace.
Did Defence have any tender or head contractor agreements with the Whyalla steelworks?

I don't believe the defence department did, but many of our industry suppliers may well have, because we have a distributed system. I'm aware of the submarine supply chain more recently, because I've been briefed on that, but there potentially would be aspects where it had gone from Whyalla to other industry partners who produce different types of steel outputs, and then that would go into the supply chain.

Okay. That leads into BlueScope's position. Has Defence assessed what that will mean for BlueScope if it is solely reliant not just on what Defence needs but, obviously, on what your suppliers then need? If they are the primary and only steelmaker in Australia supplying the grade of steel you need, have what international supply chains may look like and what risk that may put the projects under been looked at?

We would've fed in any concerns and assessments in response to questions, with the lead being in the Department of Industry, Science and Resources. They have a taskforce looking at this issue. We certainly are connected and would respond to any requests for information that they would like from us, but the lead is the Department of Industry, Science and Resources.
But so far there hasn't been any impact that you're aware of.

As I understand it, at the moment, there's quite a lot of stock available of the material that came out of the blast furnace, and that will carry the supply chains in Australia forward for a certain period of time. It's towards the end of that that the concern is being raised about structural steel. Structural steel is used in different forms, particularly in big infrastructure such as railways, so it would be a concern for the nation if we didn't have structural steel capability. That's one reason why the government is working diligently to look for opportunities to continue structural steel manufacturing in Australia.

To that point, from what's being reported, Whyalla won't be producing steel for at least four years, and that's if everything goes to plan. Is the Department of Defence aware of international markets from which you can get the structural steel that you need?

Once again, it wouldn't be the department directly. It would be the industrial supply chains that feed into things. We don't tend to be that far down the supply chain, and I'm not familiar with the latest time horizons. I'm not sure that's been settled, because the final proponents of the insolvency haven't been settled. So I think there's some uncertainty about the gap, but, clearly, it's in the national interest—
The furnace can't be restarted, so it will need a new—

That's right. But there are alternative technologies that can produce the same outcome, which is structural steel. Our supply chains would be aware of it. We have been working quite hard to make sure that, more broadly, the Australian steel industry has the opportunity to feed into supply chains to do with the submarines, because that's a significant opportunity—and not just the submarine manufacturer in Australia but the submarine manufacturer in the UK and the US under the AUKUS arrangements. So it is important that we try and maximise supply chains where we can.

Yes. So is it fair to say that Defence hasn't necessarily got a single point of accountability? Obviously, there's demand across Osborne, Henderson, HMAS Stirling and the Mogami build. Is Defence looking at that holistically or not?

We would have the ability to track back through the requests from our industrial supply chain—and we do supply chain analysis—but, ultimately, we are working with our industrial partners. It is for them to produce and source through the system. We keep an eye on it, but it's not our responsibility necessarily to dictate particular supply chains, other than through national security or technology transfer issues.

Given some of the constraints that there may be around getting the structural steel required, is there any contingency in the budgets, or has any modelling been done, if international supply chains are going to be relied on?

We have contingency measures in our projects for lots of reasons, and we talked about this a bit earlier. There are lots of things that happen to supply chains that we can't always predict, so there are always contingency arrangements in projects. For significant supply chains we would have a relationship and a discussion with the industrial providers to make sure they had contingency plans in place. So we do cascade through our supply chains to make sure our suppliers are aware of alternatives if they were to face constraints. The Australian market is well aware of the steel situation, and I imagine that people are very much looking for alternative suppliers, and a lot of that information is being fed into the department of industry, which is responsible for the steel industry in Australia.

I understand that they're responsible for that, but obviously if demand is high and you've got less supply then that can increase costs significantly, and not just for Defence. Obviously state and federal governments are doing other infrastructure projects. So it could have quite a significant impact—
It may do.
possibly beyond contingencies. So has anything been—

It could be an impact, but, at the moment, Defence is a relatively small user of structural steel. We use other types of steel more often. Still, we're a relatively small proportion of the domestic market. But clearly, if cost-effective, we would like to support industrial systems in Australia, and that's part of the government's tender policy. So we provide information about demand, and the market provides the supply.
What percentage of demand do you think you will be over the next—say, if we go through to 2024?
I'm happy to take it on notice—
Yes, sure.
It depends a lot on contingencies, but I'm happy to take it on notice and provide that information.

That would be very useful. Thank you. And then I just have a couple of very quick questions in terms of the estates. I want to confirm: the divestiture of Defence assets that's currently occurring has happened as a grouping, so there doesn't seem to be any individual cost-benefit analysis of selling individual sites. Is that correct?

No. In both the work that the original independent audit of the Defence Estate undertook and then the work that Defence did to analyse and make recommendations to government on implementation, we undertook detailed cost-benefit analysis work. That work looked at market valuations for the potential sale site that could be achieved for the sites recommended. I would note that they were undertaken with a view to understanding the heritage and contamination overlays likely. In addition to that, we worked through with government a couple of other really important elements of the costs to operate those sites. That included an overall sense of the cost to sustain sites of that shape and size, the planned future maintenance that we understood and the planned investments that we understood would be necessary for those sites. So when we went back to cabinet consideration we had a good sense of the potential realisation of value that we would be able to achieve and the costs that it would take to make those changes. We know there is a cost to move people. We know there will be some capability replication. We know there will be decontamination work and some history and heritage work. And the other headline point was that we modelled the planned savings to the sustainment budget for the estate into the future. In the headline figures that the Deputy Prime Minister announced in February, they are the benefits that we see, and that is our desire to invest in the future estate for the current and future operating force.

But it wasn't necessarily done. If we take Victoria Barracks in Sydney, moving that into Defence Plaza Sydney—and I think we heard last week it was $231 million or so over 10 years—is it fair to say that there has been no cost-benefit analysis site by site? It's difficult for the taxpayer to figure out whether moving from a wholly taxpayer owned, government owned facility to then having to pay $23 million a year to lease five storeys—
Yes, we have done that analysis site by site—
You have?

Yes. A really important point on Defence Plaza Sydney is that that is a lease in place. We have that lease in place for the long term. We are already paying that cost. But one of the things we knew and the independent Defence Estate Audit identified is that we entered into that lease and started that process pre-COVID. We know now that office occupancy is much lower than we'd planned for. So there's a significant capacity in that site, which is part of the reason that we want to optimise where we already have an investment and an ability to operate in a more secure and more modern way. That cost we understood. That cost won't really change, but we absolutely modelled across broad sustainment, planned future investment and the cost to move to receiving sites.
Can I ask you to table that individually? We were told in the inquiry last week that it wasn't done individually, site by site. That would be very—

I've read the Hansard. Well, I haven't seen the Hansard yet. I read a transcript from last week. I think Mr West's evidence last week was that we don't break down individual sustainment products site by site, but we've modelled the broader sense now. What we have shared previously and certainly in our responses to questions on notice is that that work forms part of a cabinet consideration and that the government's position has been that making public the specific financial information for the individual sites will diminish our commercial advantage in negotiating for full market value, as we proceed with the sales.
Perhaps you can table what you can; that allows for accountability, and I think it's in the public interest for the taxpayers to know what's happening with Defence assets—with their assets.
Thanks. We'll take that on notice.
Can I ask as well: the audit for this was completed in 2023, and then it was announced and released earlier this year. Was there any revalidation of site utilisation done in that three-year period?
Yes, and we continue to do site validation.
Did any site status change between 2023 and 2026?
Not significantly, no.
So every site that was identified and was marked in that order in 2023 is on the list.

I'm sorry; I misunderstood your question. The independent audit recommended divestment of 68 sites. As you'll know, in the government's response to that, the government agreed to the divestment of 67 sites. There were a number of changes that the government agreed to following Defence's validation of that work. They are, in order, the agreement not to divest the Pittwater Dive Annex. That reduces your 68 to 67. Of a number of the other sites, the government agreed to move from a full divestment to a partial divestment. Defence, undertaking a capability analysis, put the position to government that there were significant capability impacts for a full divestment, and therefore the government agreed to a partial divestment of HMAS Penguin. We have agreed to maintain the operating part of the base. There's Warradale Barracks in Adelaide; that is an important part of our planned divestment and movement from Keswick Barracks, in an agreement with the South Australian government. And there are RAAF Laverton and RAAF Point Cook, where they have agreed a partial divestment.
So those were the only significant changes between 2023 and 2026—
In the divestment recommendations, yes.
Have there been any changes in what that cost benefit analysis is, or was that all done in 2023 as well?

The work that Defence undertook before advising government in 2024 revalidated a number of elements of the work of the independent team, and that included a number of re-evaluations of key sites so that we could go back to government with a more contemporary understanding of likely sales outcomes.
That was 2024?
That's right.
But there's been nothing since then?
Just to be clear, as the process progresses, Defence is working through different sites. There's kind of different analysis. The Department of Finance is responsible for divesting the properties.
No, I understand that.

And so, as part of that process, there will be additional consideration of market conditions as part of the sales, as consistent with the overall framework that the Commonwealth has for selling properties. There's a need to update so that you have a really strong evidence base for market value.
Is it possible that market value has dropped?

It is possible it's gone up. It's possible it's the same. It's possible it's gone down. The Australian real estate market is very divergent, and these are different properties and facilities in different locations.
Has that been taken into account?
It will be taken into account as part of—
So only when it's sold or hits the market?

We are working to the government's policy direction with instructions and clear public policy for us to move forward with divestment of 67 sites over time, in order for that money to be released and reinvested, consistent with the National Defence strategy. That is what we're working to. And, as part of that process, we go through a whole series of technical analyses, including capability, workforce consultation and the transition issues in terms of moving sites, and then they get transitioned to Finance, and Finance does the sales process.
This is my last question before I hand the call to Senator Collins. Is Defence putting in any requirements, particularly around the partial divestitures, in terms of who that can be sold to?

All decisions around divestment will be incorporating all the frameworks we have in government, which will include the foreign investment review framework. There are all sorts of regulatory frameworks, and, as part of that process, there's also government involvement on any restrictions. There will be some areas where we need to work, particularly around splitting sites where there are different operations happening on them, because they may currently be on one title, and we need to split them if we need to do them. So there are a lot of considerations of detailed work going into this process.
Thank you.
Senator Collins.
Please, you can remain at the table. Thank you. The Chief of Army as well, please.
If you could ask a question, we could just make sure we've got the right people at the table.
I will be asking a question to the Chief of Army but also Security and Estate Group, thank you very much.
The secretary or chief directs. But ask the question, please.
Who decided to split forces command between Randwick and Defence Plaza Sydney? And what's the rationale behind it?

We have an integrated approach within the department to assess the transition plans for particular sites. There's a detailed working group, and it considers all the aspects of the transition. We work through the available space at different locations, the capability, the timing and the sequence of those sorts of things. It is an integrated assessment, and we have put plans. Plans have been put to me and others, and plans have been put to the government, and there has been subsequent action. We are in consultation with staff about precisely the implementation detail of the transition, and it is absolutely the case that Army was involved in the discussions in terms of where things go. There are lots of elements. There's health in there, as well, and cadets and reserves. It's quite a complicated process. Quite a lot of people are involved in the discussion.
Lieutenant General, were you involved in this discussion? Was it your idea to split Forces Command? Were you given an option to keep Forces Command together?

As the secretary indicated, it's been a series of discussions. I have absolutely been centrally involved in those discussions for the relocation for Forces Command, and the request that I have asked be considered is that Forces Command, for its longer-term solution, is Randwick Barracks. That would require us to be split in the interim between Defence Plaza Sydney and Randwick Barracks until we can get a permanent solution at Randwick.
How long will it be until you get that permanent solution?
That's going to be a function of the planning arrangements and investment decisions, so we don't have a specific date at the moment.
Give us a ballpark here. What are we talking?
I can't give you a ballpark.
What kinds of buildings are Forces Command moving into in Randwick? Are they permanent buildings?

Forces Command, as part of the transition, will be moving into a range of locations, as you already indicated. At Randwick, in the interim, that will consist of a mix of existing buildings. We will also likely use some temporary accommodation while we finalise the end state that Chief of Army talked about, which will allow us to consolidate all of Forces Command at Randwick.
So you've got Forces Command moving into temporary buildings—
Parts of Forces Command. Some are moving into permanent; some are moving into temporary.

Parts of Forces Command are moving into temporary buildings for an unknown period of time, and we're probably talking years here, by the time you've built the necessary infrastructure. As Chief of Army and former commander of Forces Command, do you think the movement of Forces Command into temporary buildings and split across into Defence Plaza Sydney will increase its capability or diminish it?

Our intent is that we maintain our capability throughout the relocation. The buildings aren't what make Forces Command; it's the people, the processes and our practices. I have very professional men and women in the Command, and we will continue to operate from wherever we are located. Is it optimum? No, it's not. It never is. But we will make it work, because that's what we do.
So soldiers and officers will be hot-desking at Defence Plaza Sydney. What's the ratio of that hot-desk arrangement?
Defence follows the Commonwealth office policy of an eight to 10 ratio.
Will soldiers and officers be required to work from home some of the time?

Defence uses flexible work arrangements for all of our staff, APS and ADF. It's certainly my observation around the country, including in Sydney sites, that many of our people make use of that. In Defence Plaza Sydney we're now working through the location that Forces Command will occupy. I walked through every floor last week. In addition to the allocation that we know they will need, there's certainly still additional capacity in Defence Plaza Sydney. There'd be nothing about the move that would necessitate or require a work from home arrangement. As we've implemented the Commonwealth's eight to 10 ratio, particularly post COVID, I have not had one example, around the entirety of the estate—given people's leave, training and personal responsibilities—where people have come to work and haven't been able to find a desk.
I think you might find that once you move everybody into Defence Plaza Sydney—given the Army is committed to being—
Just to be clear, that's not the evidence we have before us in terms of the number of staff moving and the number of available facilities.
Well, why don't you give us the numbers of people moving into Defence Plaza Sydney and the number of terminals available for them to do their work?
There is more than enough capacity for people to move in.
Can you please give us the numbers.
I'm happy to take that on notice.
I would like the numbers. You've just said that you know the numbers, so I'd like the numbers now, please.

I don't know the exact numbers in my head, but I do know the analysis has been done about the vacancy rate and the staff that may or may not be moving. We are going through a consultation period. That consultation period has still got two periods to go. The first one is finishing very soon. Then there'll be another transition plan put to individual staff. Until that's done, there may well be some changes at the margin subject to the feedback, which is consistent with our obligations under employment law for the Public Service. We are also consulting with the ADF. We're not required to, but we are doing so, consistent with the desire to make sure everyone well understands what's happening. We have done the detailed work. We are not aware of any issues. If you've got other evidence, we're happy to take it.

Given the Army has committed to being ready to fight tonight, if we were to have a large operation exercise and Forces Command has been split partly into temporary buildings and partly into an open-plan setting with a ratio of eight to 10, how is that all going to work? If everybody has to come into work, is everybody going to have the terminal that they need to work from? What's going to happen? Do they have the zones they need to work from and Defence passes? Tell me how the zone's going.

I can take the zone question for you because it's a very important part of this planning. When we fitted out Defence Plaza Sydney, the physical fit-out was to a physical security zone 3. That's a secret zone. That's been tremendously valuable for this work. There are a number of zone 4 spaces in the building. So it is absolutely—
Do they fit the number of people that will be in there required to use zone 4?
Yes, they do.
The increased numbers?

Yes. As I said, we're working through this. Most of the work that we undertake in Defence is at the zone 3 level. Russell headquarters is primarily at the zone 3 level. That's how we operate on the secret network. The secret network is our warfighting network. That building is, from a physical security perspective, probably a better quality of security fit-out than I would say Russell headquarters is, because it's a much newer fit-out.

So your evidence to me is that every single personnel that will be relocated to Defence Plaza Sydney will have their own terminal, they'll have access to zone 3 whenever they need it and there'll be enough zone 4 for them too.
Yes.
Plus, can you also reflect on the zone 5 access, please.
My evidence to you is that Defence Plaza Sydney will have adequate terminals, Defence protected network and secret at an eight-to-10 ratio for the move that we're planning.
So they won't have one each themselves? It'll be, 'You have to wait your turn'?
We have very detailed usage data on the secret network. In almost every Defence location, there are plenty of DSN terminals that don't get logged on to every day. So I'm very comfortable—
But we're not in a war.
I'm very comfortable that with the current plan there will be adequate secret terminals installed in Defence Plaza for the staff who are transitioning.
Okay. What about zone 5?

To the secretary's point and why we need to take on notice some of the details, the site transition plans that we're developing for all Defence sites are extremely detailed. They go through all of the elements of people, capability and supporting services. We're in the change-management process right now, which, as the secretary said, might create some adjustments to that plan. There are a couple of components at Victoria Barracks Sydney that are a little bit more challenging for us. Zone 5 is one of those. There are some other capabilities—
What are the challenges around zone 5?
Zone 5 capabilities just take a bit longer to build and accredit.
Will you have a zone 5 at Defence Plaza Sydney?
I think we will have a zone 5 at Randwick.
You think you will, or are you planning to have one?
We're planning to have a zone 5 facility at Randwick.
Okay. What about car parks? How are the personnel going to get to work? Where do they park?

Car parking is certainly an issue our people at Victoria Barracks Sydney have raised in the change process so far. Certainly, one of the benefits of many Defence sites is car parking, but it is by no means a common condition. It's certainly not a condition of service. At many sites, we either don't have car parking or have paid car parking. So we'll talk to staff about their options around that and modes of transport to get to work, and that will be part of the change process.

Have you given any advice, or have you previously given advice at any other base, to serving personnel about arriving to work in uniform? Is there any security advice that you would give to personnel? Perhaps for the chiefs, is there advice that you would give about arriving to work in uniform and on public transport? Is there any kind of security advice you'd give to that?
At various points, our security threat levels have changed. Historically that has been the case. There are no current directions for our people around wearing uniform to work.
So they would be okay to arrive in the middle of the city every day in their uniform?

As I said, as security threat levels change, we have the capacity to make directions. Our current security threat levels and our very close work with ASIO wouldn't give us an indication that that would be currently necessary.

Is there a fallback option? If, for example, we entered a conflict tonight or the threat level changed tonight, what would be the advice to all the personnel going to Defence Plaza Sydney, where there's only a public transport option and they all have to go and fight for a desk and fight for a terminal? What's going to happen? What's the security that you'd have there?
I just want to clarify your characterisation of fighting for a desk and fighting for a terminal.
It's an eight to 10 ratio.
It is an eight to 10 ratio. Clearly, as we move through elements of the security arrangements, we would have mitigation strategies in place.
What would they be?

Some of that would be, if there were an operational need for people to be in certain locations and there were other people with lower need in that location, they would be moved off rather than the operators moving.
So you're saying that, in a conflict, certain personnel will become redundant. Is that what you're trying to say—the forces command?

Defence Plaza Sydney will have people in it, as it does now, that are not forces command. We have plans in place for this. If our threat level changed, if we were in conflict, we would be reprioritising quite a lot of our activity, and through that reprioritisation we would have mitigations in place. We would also have mitigations in place for our personnel serving in Australia and overseas. So in a conflict we would apply the operating procedures and the overlaying architecture that we have now whether people are at Randwick or whether they're at Victoria Barracks Sydney.

Sorry, can I just jump in and ask a clarifying question there. In a conflict scenario, hopefully we have mobilised. We've turned a whole lot of reservists into full timers. We've put in place return-to-service obligations for former serving personnel. You'd have many more people turning up to work at these facilities, not fewer.
It depends on the facility you're talking about. Some areas will have more, some will have fewer. We will have prioritisation arrangements. That is all part of the planning that we would be doing.

But this facility, which Senator Collins is asking questions about, already doesn't have enough desks for the people who are currently employed. If you're mobilising in conflict, it's going to be nowhere near enough space.

We have a thousand locations around the country, with 70 bases. If we were in conflict, all the current locations would shift as well. We would be prioritising the war-fighting capability of both the ADF, clearly, and the Public Service. We would also be drawing on capability, as you say, through reservists but also across other industry and private sectors. We have plans in place to deal with that issue. It is an issue now and it'll be an issue subsequent to the change in location. One of the reasons for doing the disinvestment process is to invest in new bases and new capabilities that will be central to the defence of Australia.
We're building new bases?
We're adding to bases.
Hang on. You just said there were going to be new bases. Where are the new bases going to be?
This is about reinvesting in our northern bases.
But they're existing bases.

I corrected and said existing expansion. The intention is that we will have more people stationed in the north of Australia than we do in the south of Australia. We'll have them in different locations as we move capability around the country. So it's not the case that we've got static locations of people. We're already moving. We've got more people in Western Australia now than we did three years ago.
Alright.
We do need a break.
Can I just finish that off, please. I've still got more to go, but, if I finish that line of questioning, you can come back to me after you share the call. But I've still got stuff to go.
I appreciate that, but we do have a time that we need to get to. I'll give you a few more minutes, and then we'll break for afternoon tea.

I have one question, and then we'll cut for afternoon tea. It's just related to the security question. Ms Perkins, I've seen a quote from you about wanting to protect the identities of your staff. Defence Plaza Sydney is a public building. There will be a public lobby. There'll be cameras. There are who knows which private companies that are on the three-quarters of levels that aren't occupied by the Australian Defence Force. We've got a Singaporean company that owns the building. We've got a Chinese bank that holds the mortgage over it. So who knows where the security footage from that lobby will go or who's loitering in the lobby waiting around pretending they've got a meeting, following who's going in and who's going out. What security measures are you putting in place to protect the identities of our serving personnel that are going in and out of Defence Plaza Sydney?
I'm not at all clear on what quote you may have seen from me.

I can read it out to you if you like. You said:

As senior leaders in Defence—we actively discourage security clearance holders from a social media presence that identifies us and our roles …
That's specifically about being identifiable on social media.

These are real people. Surely, it's more dangerous to be identifiable as a person going in and following your routine. They could be watching where you go for coffee—there are lots of coffee shops around there—what time you arrive, what time you leave.
It's a slightly longer point, but fundamentally digital and online security—
I'm not worried about the online security.
Just let the official answer the question, please.
It's the security cameras and the security of the lobby and entering and exiting the building.
Deputy Chair, I appreciate that, but please let Ms Perkins at least provide an answer before you ask her another one.

I would disaggregate that quote, which very specifically relates to digital and online security and what we know and understand to be particularly the foreign intelligence activity that occurs online. So it's quite a different vector. I can say a couple of things about protective and physical security at Defence Plaza Sydney and just on the broader point, I think, that all of us in government and in national security, of course, live and work in the community. Victoria Barracks Sydney is in a busy shopping strip in Oxford Street. Many of our sites are in commercial office facilities. Many ADF members already work at Defence Plaza Sydney. I saw many of them last week. On the floors that Defence operates, we of course install our own security fit-out that is entirely—

I'm not worried about our floors. I'm worried about the public areas. I'm worried about the lobby. I'm worried about the entry and exit. As you can appreciate, the Defence Force and the bases like Victoria Barracks—yes, sure, it's in the metropolitan centre and, yes, there are cafes on the other side of it, but it is very heavily protected. It's a base. It's an operational base. The government has a bill coming through in the next couple of weeks—it's just been through the House—talking about protected zones around these military bases. Are we going to be able to do that for Defence Plaza Sydney? Probably not, because it's smack bang in the middle of the central business district.
Yes, we can. The intent of the new legislation introduced this week and the creation of security zones would be able to be applied to a facility like Defence Plaza Sydney.

How are you going to protect the identities and the movements of the personnel going in and out? You could have foreign espionage. You could have people sitting in the lobby watching to see the movements of who comes in and who goes out. When there's an incident, they'll be watching who arrives and who leaves. How do you prevent that?

I just want to say all defence sites operate under frameworks that deal with these issues, whether it be the Russell precinct, whether it be joint headquarters or whether it be Defence Plaza Sydney. The other aspect here is that, as part of the analysis of where people may move in terms of capability and skills and functions that they perform, that's been part of the thinking about what functionality needs to move to Randwick, what functionality can temporarily go to the plaza and, similarly for other sites around Australia, what the alternatives are. This is all about building a stronger defence force. That is front of mind in making sure that we look after our staff and we provide the facilities that they need and the capital equipment they need, which may be secret networks. We do care about our staff, both the public servants who are significantly affected by these moves and the ADF, because we are an integrated force and this is all about protecting our capability over time. There is a tone running through some of your questions that there's not a concern on behalf of the department for the safety of our forces. I just want to assure the committee that that is not the case. We care as much about the people in Randwick and in Osborne as we do the people in Victoria Barracks.
Except that Victoria Barracks is going to be no more, isn't it?
The serving people will be in alternative locations performing functions that defend a nation.
I will return, though. Thank you.
Sure. We will return. Just for clarity, though, when was the decision taken to lease the Defence Plaza Sydney? I understand from AusTender that the lease commenced in 2023.
Yes, that's correct. The lease commenced in 2023, but it was signed on 13 May 2020.
Who was the minister at the time?
I will have to check who the minister was at the time.

We've canvassed this in other committee inquiry hearings recently, and I think you'll find that our evidence previously has been that there was a project to look at capital city office space that commenced in 2019-ish and was looking to replicate space in Sydney, Melbourne and Canberra. The Canberra element didn't proceed. Defence Plaza Melbourne was reconfirmed. The Defence Plaza Sydney site is a new facility. The approval for those two sites as the ongoing enduring capital city leases were approved by the finance minister in the Morrison government.

Yes, which was Mathias Corman. I assume, then, that the Liberal government at the time would have done due diligence and the department would have done due diligence, particularly around the ownership arrangements, which would have been considered as part of the decision—correct?

Yes, absolutely. We maintain 422 domestic leases; 94 of those are offices around the country, and we undertake a security assessment as part of the due diligence process and the approach to market. We also, then, include in our leases provisions that allow us to exert controls, obviously, or requirements to notify us if there are changes to ownership or control, and then, as I've already described, our own implementation of physical security measures and accreditation of those.

Foreign ownership is very common in the commercial property market. How we then apply and accredit those physical and other security measures is important. I would just add that that security accreditation process in some of the zones that have been mentioned—some of those are undertaken by Defence. Others are undertaken by colleagues in ASIO or in the Australian Signals Directorate. So they are both installed and then accredited to the same standard as any other government facility operating at that level.
As I understand it, with my limited experience at this time in this building, these are evolving matters. Security always changes; advice always changes, and you've just got to move with the times.

We have frameworks that we maintain, and, within that, when the context and circumstances change, we update and review those frameworks. And it does change. Threat levels go up and down—locations, particular targets et cetera.
We're going to break.
Senator Roberts, you have the call.

My first set of questions goes to the recent announcement that the Australian Defence Force would be allowing Papua New Guineans to be recruited into our Australian Defence Force. How many PNG citizens will be recruited into the ADF, and what entry requirements do they have to meet?
I'm happy to start while other officials come to the table. It's part of the Pukpuk Treaty signed between Australia and Papua New Guinea.
When was that signed?

Just earlier this year. We're having a pilot project to start with, with the first entrance being available to apply towards the end of this year, but, in terms of additional detail, my experts can—and there are a whole series of conditions and processes—
That's what I'm interested in.

Good afternoon. As you know and as the secretary just stated, we signed the Pukpuk Treaty with Papua New Guinea. It's our first mutual defence treaty with a foreign country outside of the signing of ANZUS with the United States. As part of this treaty there's a commitment to work together on the interoperability of our forces, and that includes a policy around permitting the recruitment of PNG nationals into the Australian Defence Force. As the secretary said, the Deputy Prime Minister last week announced the first tranche of that recruitment of 50 PNG nationals. For the past year, my team and a Defence personnel team led by General Natasha Fox have been working together on setting up the systems for how we do this in a manner consistent with the treaty obligations on both sides and also the domestic constitutional requirements of both countries. That process is ongoing, and we're going to continue to work at it. General Fox can take you through the exact processes for how we are doing that consistent with our broader ADF recruitment system.

Senator, we are opening applications to join the Australian Defence Force from 16 November. That is the application period for the first cohort of candidates from Papua New Guinea. There are some settings around the first cohort. They will be from three universities in Papua New Guinea and aged between 18 and 25. They will not be participants of the Papua New Guinea STEM Overseas Scholarship Program and will have had no prior service in the Papua New Guinea Defence Force, the constabulary or PNG government security institutions. These parameters have been agreed with our Papua New Guinean colleagues. Once the screening has been undertaken, from November through December, we will then confirm eligibility and screen again for a shortlist of candidates of up to 50 for a pilot course of 16 weeks in Papua New Guinea, which is pre-enlistment. And then—
Excuse me. That course will be run by ADF people?
Yes, and some contracted solutions as well up in Papua New Guinea. From May 2027, we will commence the 16-week residential course.
Where will that be?

In Papua New Guinea—Manus Island. And then, at the end of that course, the selection for the ADF will come from that group of candidates. They will commence in the ADF under a temporary visa arrangement that has been agreed with Home Affairs for them to participate in training and then meet the eligibility requirements for citizenship of Australia. That has been worked in conjunction with our Papua New Guinean colleagues, as the Deputy Prime Minister has said.
Thank you. So they'll have fast-tracked Australian citizenship?

No, they'll have normal citizenship, in terms of the time it takes to be a permanent resident and then to apply for a visa in the 90-day period in terms of becoming an Australian citizen to serve in the ADF.
Let me understand. These people are going to be fully-fledged diggers in the ADF?
Yes, across the three services.
Are they going to be integrated into the services or special units in each service?
They'll be integrated, Senator.
Why do you pick uni students?

Because this is a pilot, in the first instance. We want to make sure we're testing to make sure that our systems work. And this is in conjunction with Papua New Guinea. We've limited it to three universities, because it's up to 50 people for the pilot. So we've made sure we—
So you're using the university to screen?
Yes, to make sure, because it's against the entry requirements to join the ADF. It is not a separate entry requirement system; it's against the ADF standards.
Could you go over again what the duration of training in Australia will be for each of these people.
It'll be the same duration in Australia as—
So when they come here they'll start training?
Yes, they'll do the normal training that the Australian Defence Force undertakes.
Why are we requiring PNG citizens to be recruited into the ADF? Is it part of a mutual agreement?

That's right. It is an ambition of the leaders of both Australia and Papua New Guinea to ensure that our forces can work more closely together as allies. Part of that ability to work more closely together and, indeed, to have interoperable and interchangeable forces is to start with personnel. Both governments have therefore asked us to design and develop a process that will allow this to occur in a manner consistent with the domestic and international obligations and the constitutional obligations of both countries, and that's the process that General Fox has set out. Our timeline here is that we envisage this occurring over the long-term. We want to start slow, we want to get this right and we want to make sure that we provide a pathway for PNG nationals to recruit into the ADF that gives them maximum opportunity to succeed and that this will stand as a core foundation for the two countries' defence systems working together into the future.
Thank you. Is there any requirement for Australia to send people to Papua New Guinea?
There is no requirement under the treaty. Indeed, there's no requirement in the treaty for PNG nationals to join the ADF. It's an opportunity available to PNG nationals should they choose it.

Thank you. My understanding over the last four decades, from talking to proud ADF people, has been that one of the most important things for a member of any of the forces is mateship. What is the culture of Papua New Guinea like with that, and will that be dealt with specifically? Will they make diggers?

We already train with Papua New Guinea, and we have already had our Papua New Guinean colleagues come through some of our institutions and train with us, so we already have a pre-existing relationship—certainly across the Army. Given that they'll be undertaking the full ADF training, they will start on day one with their colleagues and they will forge that mateship through that training.
How long is that training—basic training?
The basic training across the three services is anywhere from nine to 12 weeks, depending on which service, and that basic training cycle is adjusted given different training requirements.

Is that long enough to develop a deep, ingrained mateship? Also, will it be enough to ingrain enough mateship to satisfy the rest of the soldiers—Australian soldiers—that they'll be beside and that they will go into battle with?

That's the initial military training. They'll then go on to initial employment training and spend time training in whatever role they're coming into the ADF with. They will spend more time there before they then go to a unit and deploy on exercises or do further training in different units that they go to. So they will build the normal approach where we bring in Australians from right across Australia who have different backgrounds and they join and become friends for life.

As far as I know, that's a very, very prized quality that few if any other defence forces anywhere in the world have—that sense of mateship, reliance and trust on each other. It's not just the Army; it's the Navy and the Air Force.

Senator, you're absolutely right: it is. We're not a homogeneous society within Australia to begin with. We are multiracial and multiethnic, and we take people from all walks of life into the Australian Defence Force. We deliberately build those bonds through our training and force generation system, in an environment of shared experience and shared commitment to each other. There are multiple immigrant members of the Australian Defence Force. I'm one.

I must interrupt. I'm not concerned about immigrants, particularly those who've come here from a very early age, or adults from, say, Britain's army, because they fit in very well to ours. I understand that. I'm just concerned when you're bringing in adults who may not have the mateship of being an Australian. That's all.

I understand, and I've served with people in the Australian submarine force who have come from elsewhere, including from Papua New Guinea in my very first submarine that I went to serve in. That member is now retired; their son is a member of the Australian Defence Force. I understand the concern you've raised, but I have a lot of confidence in the way we train people and bring them into the system. I also have confidence in the exit pathways that exist too. We are ultimately building a unified force to defend Australia, and there are certain values that are required of that force. So we're not changing the standards and we're not changing the outcome. We're just integrating a different pathway into our community of sailors, soldiers and aviators.
So you have confidence that the ADF's system, in each of the three services, can do that with people from just about anywhere?
You don't succeed as a sailor, soldier or aviator without committing to your mate, and that's not going to change.
What about the loyalty to our country?
That's still a requirement upon entering the Australian Defence Force—to make that oath or affirmation.
So this is not a recruitment or retention issue; this is about obligations with our nearest neighbour.

Our retention achievement over the last few years has been exceptional. Frankly, most private sector leaders are envious of our voluntary separation rate, which sits, on average, at 4½, four or five per cent, and our success in recruiting over the last 18 months in particular but also the last few years has exceeded performance parameters prior to the last decade. This is not a recruiting or retention challenge for the Australian Defence Force. This is an opportunity and a policy position of the Australian government, which we are implementing.
Could you give me, please, on notice, the retention and intake numbers for the last 10 years in a graph form? I always like to see data in context.
Yes, Senator, I can take that on notice.
Thank you.
Any other questions tonight, Senator?
Yes, I've got two more brackets, but I'll just go through one of them if I've got time.
Yes.
Minister, are you aware that Defence Housing Australia has increased rent prices by 5.61 per cent?
There's actually a dedicated session with Defence Housing Australia a little bit later on, so that's probably the best place to ask that sort of question.
Okay. Are you also aware that the cost of water has gone up by 1.5 per cent?
This is in DHA housing?
Yes.
Again, I'd suggest we cover that off when the relevant officials are here later.
So it's a 5.61 per cent increase for rent and a 1.5 per cent increase for water, and the cost of living is going up—plus additional household costs and family costs.
I think those—
Do you believe that a three per cent increase in Defence wages is enough to cover these increases during this cost-of-living crisis?

I'm not, for a moment, accepting the sorts of figures that you've put to me. What I'm saying is that I'd require the relevant officials to be here with me to help answer those questions. If your questions are more about the wages of defence personnel generally, leaving aside the DHA issues, we could probably cover that here—
Yes, that's—
I suspect?
Senator, some of your question pertains to Defence; some of it to the Defence housing authority.
Just the ones for Defence.

One of your questions, I think, was pertaining to rental costs. The Australian Defence Force, for those ADF members that are part of our rental scheme—their rent is subsidised by 50 per cent, but the quantum of that is renewed each year in terms of the relevant economic indicators. I can certainly provide you, on notice, with what those changes have been over the last 12 months.

Thank you. In light of the fact, I'm told, that the Australian Public Service staff received a 3.4 per cent increase from 5 August 2026 on top of other increases—in some roles, their pay increasing by upwards of five per cent—do you think that giving the ADF three per cent is fair?
You're asking for a matter of opinion. The reality is that the housing costs faced by ADF reflect the broader market conditions and—
Excuse me. I'm not talking about housing costs. The minister has correctly said I should discuss that with Defence Housing.
Rental costs, then.
I'm talking about the pay increase, which I'm told is three per cent versus, for the Public Service, 3.4 per cent and in some cases up to five per cent.
There's a bargaining process at the moment for APS arrangements. That has not been completed yet, so it's ongoing.
They haven't received a 3.4 per cent increase from 5 August 2026?
Public servants?
Yes.
I don't believe so.
Sorry, can you just repeat that timing? I missed the timing, Senator.
Australian Public Service staff received a 3.4 per cent increase from 5 August 2026, on top of other increases—in some roles increasing by upwards of five per cent.
No. For the Defence Public Service, I can come back to you with the three pay rises over the last three years, which were aligned to be the same as for the Australian Defence Force.
So we have a concurrence between the APS staff and the ADF.
That's what I'm looking for.
Sometimes there's a difference in timing because the arrangements that are made are slightly separate, but there is a concurrence that's generally maintained between the two parts of Defence.
Could you give me the last five years, please, for APS versus Defence.
Yes, Senator.
We are happy to.
Thank you very much. I'll come back with another set later.
I know Senator Lambie has some follow-on questions on recruitment, and then I'll turn to other senators to see who else has further questions. Senator Lambie.
Yes, I just want to talk about recruitment if I can.
We'll just ask Lieutenant-General Fox to come to the table for you, Senator.

Thank you. In the past, Adecco Australia has failed to meet its recruitment targets by almost 30 per cent. How does Defence measure the performance of Adecco in its delivery under the recruiting contract, and what key performance indicators or performance measures are in the recruitment contract currently held by Adecco?

Adecco Australia achieved 80 per cent inflow of targets for the last financial year. Under the performance indicators in the contract, we measure and pay by headcount achieved, but it's not just volume. It's about the nature of the target that we set for Adecco to recruit to. We know some trades are more difficult to recruit to, as they are across Australia, so we would put a different weighted value on recruiting for those particular trades versus trades that we know we can recruit to more generally. We also look fully at the candidate experience and the velocity or speed at which Adecco can recruit.

How long, on average is it taking them to recruit from the day they hear, 'Yes, I want to join'? What does that look like in today's world? Is that now a lot less in months than it has been previously? I'm still hearing people are waiting for months and they're losing interest. Do we have any stats on where people have put in for admission and it's taken Adecco so long to get this moving that these people have now left?
Yes, Senator.
Okay. What does that look like?
The time from application to letter of offer is what we measure. It does shift monthly and it does shift by role. On average, it is taking 269 days.
And that's before they've even gone to recruit school?
Yes.

Is there any way of getting that down to what it used to be—six or eight weeks? I'm just wondering how many you're actually losing, because I am hearing of a lot of people out there over the years saying, 'It's just taking too long; I'm not doing it anymore,' and I think it's really having a negative impact on the numbers that could be recruited.

Yes. That timeframe actually also includes when some of our candidates choose to go on a holiday and are not able to answer questions or come in for appointments. So that's that velocity piece on average. We do have a number of roles that move faster, and we have a program to uplift performance in recruiting, to go faster and to get to 100 days.
That'd be good.

That's based on technology requirements. We were coming off a very low technology base, and we've spent the first part of the last 12 months building a target compendium, where our military recruiters can have conversations with candidates, who often walk into recruiting and don't know the role. They have an idea, but sometimes they want to join the ADF faster. So we can then provide them advice: 'Well, these roles have targets available and are moving fast.' Or some people actually choose to wait because they would like to become a pilot, and that takes longer. So we give the candidate quite a bit of choice when we're engaging with them about roles, but we now have tech solutions where we can have the conversations. That's the first step. We're also bringing in our new future service delivery model that will enable candidates to move through the pipeline faster. I'm waiting for that secondary technological uplift to occur. They're coming in in blocks, not in a waterfall approach. That is absolutely a focus, and we are focused on getting to a hundred days.

Yes, that'd be great. I understand those significant skills out there take longer, but just for your normal transport driver, military police or whatever else in your regiments, it'd be nice if we could get hold of them, and do that in a hundred days, and keep them and get them in. Who's in charge of the recruitment? How's it working with the Pacific Islanders? Do New Zealanders still come over here and do we just do what we've always done with New Zealand?
No, Senator.
How's it all working with these? In Papua New Guinea and that, who's in charge of those? How does it work?

That sits under my responsibility as well. In July 2024, we widened the eligibility of recruiting to recruit New Zealand permanent residents in Australia. The requirement is that you have to have been in Australia for one year prior and that you've not served in another foreign military in the previous two years. We didn't want to have a situation where people were leaving the New Zealand military and coming straight into our military, because we're actually stronger together. It's a deliberate policy of not poaching from New Zealand in that regard. That was in July 2024. Then that opened up to the remainder of Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States.
Is it the same for them? For political diplomacy, is it just two years?
Yes.
Okay.
They shouldn't have been in a force—
So you're maybe only just starting to get that lot coming through now.
Yes.
Okay.
We've opened up that program to Papua New Guinea as well.
Yes.

Since the whole of the permanent resident recruiting opened, we had five in the first year, all from New Zealand, we had 47 in the second financial year—again, more from New Zealand and the United Kingdom—and this financial year to date we've had people from New Zealand, Canada and the United States come through the program. All up, over the financial years the program has been running, 103 people have come into the ADF from the permanent resident recruiting eligibility criteria that we widened.
Okay. So Defence is holding that, not the contracted people. You're dealing with that, because we haven't got a massive lot coming through. So Defence is actually dealing with those overseas?

That program is for people living in Australia, and Defence Force Recruiting still deal with that. We have around 700 applications in from that permanent resident recruiting program at the moment. There is another program, the Overseas Lateral Entry program, where people who may be in another country seek to join the Australian Defence Force. We bring that through Defence Force Recruiting as well. That's based on a skilled migration visa approach that we have, and that is based on where we might have gaps in critical ranks and critical trades.

Last one. When it comes to Adecco and it doesn't reach its performance indicators, is there remuneration? If they're not reaching their targets, is there a consequence for that? What does that look like?
They are only paid by the headcount that they recruit. There's a fixed fee as part of the contract, but we do only pay them for the number that they recruit.
Thank you.
Senator Shoebridge.

I think General Coyle was asked some questions earlier about the review, but I might put them to you too, Secretary. I know that Senator Paterson asked you some questions about the article that appeared in the Nightly last night and this morning regarding the review of Defence spending, and I don't intend to rehash all of those, but I just might ask: is there any kind of formal review in place in relation to the overprogramming?

We are working through our usual processes that we would do at this time of the year as part of the Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook. As part of that, we do look at what the rates of what's termed natural slippage in programs are and where people are tracking against budgets so that we can adjust the budget, because we're within year. Within year, we're required to reduce overprogramming so that we meet our budget requirement by the end of the financial year. So from the start to the end, we need to make sure that we're actually meeting the overall appropriation for the whole of the Defence budget. Every year there's a process of review as we go through the calendar months. Also, as part of the creation of the Defence Delivery Agency, we are looking at individual projects, and there'll be health check processes. As part of the transfer to the delivery agency, we need to make sure that we're very clear about the financial transfers over to the balance sheet of the new agency. So that's an additional process that we're going through at this point in time. That's not specifically related to overprogramming. As part of budget analysis every year—not so much as part of the mid-year economic and fiscal update—there's a discussion around the levels of overprogramming in subsequent years.
So there's the standard annual review to deal with potential overprogramming—
To manage the budget within year, yes.
Then there's the budget preparations that are happening. Are they the same process, or are they different processes?

We use the information from projects for both purposes. There's continual assessment of projects performance, so we use the same information. They might have slightly different—some is targeted internally to what decisions we make within the department, and some points to government in terms of decisions that governments may need to make.
Is there any urgency or further activity being directed in the department in relation to those processes because it became apparent that you were significantly over budget?

No, there's been transparency; the overprogramming was announced and part of the government's process, so there have not been any surprises or anything like that. We're working through the process as we normally would.

The reporting suggests that this is a particularly thorough budget review, with programs having a close degree of scrutiny because the budget impact of AUKUS is now being felt across the rest of Defence. Is there any truth to that?
That's not a characterisation I would use. I would say that there's been a particular focus this year, partly reflecting the movement to the delivery agency, but also—
We'll come to the health checks in a sec, which I think might be different.

Well, not really. There has been increased scrutiny on projects and projects delivery in the financial arrangements as a result of needing to separate out the balance sheet from one entity into two. That covers all sorts of connections that we need to create and separate. I would say that I bring a particular focus to budget management, given my administrative responsibilities elsewhere. As a new secretary, I've been asking a set of questions of staff across a range of responsibilities, including in budget management.

You said that there was this thing called a health check being done in relation to different programs. Can you explain what's different between the health check to the annual review in relation to potential overprogramming and budget control and the preparation for a budget submission? What's the difference with the health check?

In substance not much, but there's a need potentially in moving—in any one year we may not go all the way through all the projects. There might be a risk based assessment. This year, because we are separating projects and moving not all capability projects but quite a lot across to the delivery agency, we're having a more rigorous process on that than we may normally. We want to make sure that the delivery agency is set up for success and for us to be clear about the transition of projects from one entity to another.

Does that mean you've had a deeper dive into their financial position, their spending and the budget impacts than you would have had in a standard annual review? Is that what the health check has done?

Yes, but also, partly because we've created a delivery group, we've brought three different divisions together, and we've had an interim NAD, national armaments director, in place. As part of looking at the structure of the DDA, there's been additional focus on financial matters between divisions to bring them into a new entity. The reforms that we're going through necessitate us being very clear about the staffing, the projects, the funding and the connections.
Has that produced any significant reviews in terms of the budget situation of any project?
There would be a normal business-as-usual approach to looking at things. There is heightened analysis because of the separation.
That's what I'm asking you about. Has that heightened analysis identified a budget deterioration in any of these projects?

Not specifically coming to mind. There are always project adjustments and elements, and it's always the case at this point. Historically, Defence has started with an overprogrammed budget. It has done for at least the last five years that I've looked at, yet the department has come in close to budget, slightly over or slightly under, for that same period. That has necessitated in each of those years an active management of within-year budgets to be able to meet it. That does entail things moving in consultation with industry partners for lots of reasons to meet the requirements of the PGPA Act and the budget rules.
You said not every capability project is being moved over to the delivery agency.
Some of them will be maintained within the department, particularly around the estate and IT, for example.
Could you provide to the committee a list of the projects that are going over to the delivery agency and those that are remaining inside the balance of the department?
I'm happy to take that on notice.
Is that the only dividing line—estate and IT—holding in the department and the balance going across the delivery agency?

There are also a few that would be managed within the intelligence group. I'm happy to take it on notice. Most of the external equipment—all of CASG's, all of the shipbuilding and all of the weapons—are moving, and the rest are broadly staying in the department.
As a separate question—
I've got someone who can just give a bit more clarity to my previous answer.

In terms of the projects that will move over, they will be projects that have been approved by governments. They'll be post-gate-2 approval. There will be other projects that are in the unapproved program that remain with the department. As the Secretary said, all of these are military capability projects. Any other projects in estate or ICT, as the secretary mentioned, will remain with the department. They won't move.
Gate 2 is second pass?
That's correct.
Is that the new name for second pass?
Yes, broadly. Sorry, I use the term interchangeably. Yes, that's right.
We have changed the specification. In some elements, we've added in some requirements for gate 2 as part of the reforms—increased cost assurance and various other things. You could call it gate 2.0.
Sorry?
Gate 2.0 as opposed to just—
Second pass 2.0.
Yes, either.
Gate 1, gate 2.1 or second pass 2.0.
Yes, and we've got a gate 0 as well.

Thank you. Separately, to the extent that your health checks, which are entirely appropriate, or other budget checks have identified a budget deterioration in those projects as you've handed them over, could I ask you if you'd provide, attached to those projects, what the budget deterioration is and what the impact that will have in terms of the—
I ask you to clarify what you mean by budget deterioration?
If they are over budget.

The projects don't go over budget per se. They're not authorised to go over budget. Mostly, when we're talking about assessing projects, it's that the project's time delivery might move or there might be issues about supply of the capability, but it's not—
I've not seen a project of any scope that hasn't gone over budget, I'll be honest. I'd be asking, first of all, if any of them are over the second pass, gate 2, approved budget.
Just to be clear, the department operates against approved budget envelopes approved by government, so, if there were to be—
The original gate 2/second pass budget.
That's not necessarily something that we're looking at in this process. What we're looking at is where people are up to against the allocated funding.
My question is, on the original second pass gate 2, however described, budget, where the budget now for the item is in excess of.
That's not something we would normally look at. That is an entirely different request.

That's what my question is. For the projects that have been passed across to the delivery agency, if you could, identify those that are above the original gate 2/second pass approved budget, and I have the same request for those that have been held within the department and not transferred across.

Could I just anchor that a little bit for you. The secretary mentioned the health checks. They are ongoing processes, and they are essentially, as you said, due diligence before we pass these projects over to the Defence Delivery Agency on 1 July 2027, so we will be working through those. Like you said, it's a lot of projects. This is a big body of work. They are part of the work that's required before we establish the agency. I just wanted to be clear that we will be working on these on a continuous basis. They are not completed. They will be something that we need to do and continue to do over the next couple of months.

I'm assuming it's a large body of work to transfer a bunch of projects from within the department to the delivery agency. I'm not trying to minimise the amount of work, but the department must have somewhere in its records what the original second pass/gate 2 budget was. You must know now what the budget is. That's what my request is comparing.
We're happy to take it on notice, but I just note that—
What the expenditure is.
it may not meet the timelines of questions on notice and the like given the sequence and timing of which we have to do our work.

There are the obligations under the Senate rules, so I'd ask you to comply with them. In relation to the Nightly story and the details that are contained in the Nightly story, has either the department or the ADF commenced an investigation trying to seek who provided that material? Is there an investigation on foot, either formal or informal, of individuals?
There has been a notification of a potential breach of obligations, and so a notification has gone into our system, and an investigation has commenced, yes.
Did you order that investigation, Secretary?
No. We have a process where, if there's a suspected breach, there's a notification, and then there's an identification of whether there has or hasn't been a breach and then investigation.
So who ordered the notification then?
The notification was made from the vice chief defence forces group.
Admiral Hammond, were you aware that the notification was going out, which is the first step in commencing an investigation?

I was aware that there would be a process because I read the newspaper article, and it quotes Defence staff talking about matters that are matters for internal, so I was aware there was going to be a potential—but the formal start of the process is around the people who hold the information.
Who pressed go on the notification? Who authorised that?
The person who owns the information set.
Who? You said it was in the Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group. Who did it?

I'll ask the Vice Chief of the Defence Force to come and respond to that, but, as the secretary said, it's an automatic process. If there is an allegation that someone inside the department has leaked information, there is a process that's automatically triggered.

We had set up what we call a special information protocol around the process of budget assessment that the secretary has described. That was administered by Head of Force Design Major General Matt Pearse when there was a suspected breach of that security protocol. Then he lodged a form called XP188, for a security violation. That form goes to Security and Estate Group. It is racked and stacked against their priorities, but we understand that it will be prioritised and that there will be an investigation launched from Security and Estate Group.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: Can you tell me more about this special information protocol.
It is simply a mechanism to ensure we understand who is briefed into information so that, if there is a leak, then we can identify who's had access to that information.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group

It was an assessment of our budget.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group

It was supporting exactly the process that the secretary has described.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

We have different components of the department that analyse the budget. We have different lenses. There's the capability lens, there's the delivery agency lens and then there's a financial lens. And was there a special information protocol for this process last year?
We'll just check on the timing. Do you mean at this time last year? There would have been at some point during the last year.
There certainly would have, because we were building the Integrated Investment Program last year. So it would be my expectation. If that is not the case, I'll come back to you, Senator.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

Because we were building the Integrated Investment Program.
witness_organisation: Vice Chief of the Defence Force Group
witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force

text: But was the rationale then—so that was a specific and different thing that was happening. That's why you put a special—I assume 'special' means it's not regular—information protocol in place.

It's routine for us to do this where we seek to control information and understand who has access to the information. So I think we're up to 25 occasions, and we've only been doing this procedure for about two years.

witness_position: CSC, Vice Chief of the Defence Force
