We've only been doing this arrangement since 2024. I'm happy to come back to you. My expectation is we'd be putting the same arrangements on any kind of budget processes, particularly if we're going to—this time, there's the extra element where we're looking at the arrangements for the creation of the delivery agency.
It wasn't clear to me from your answer, Secretary, who was covered by this special information protocol.
All staff involved in elements of the process would have had visibility.
What process, though?

The regular updates that we do for the Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook. In particular, there would be individual people who know individual projects and individual programs which would probably not be covered because they would be asked for specific information. As you aggregate information up to a greater level, the security requirements get tighter. So that is the process that the department has used in the past.
Does the implementation of the special information protocol potentially expose people to any additional penalty, or is it—
No, it does not.
information so you can track people down?

It doesn't. Everybody who works in the Department of Defence has obligations under their employment, which go to the security clearances, official secrets act et cetera. There are occasions where information, certainly when it's aggregated, becomes more sensitive, and, depending on the security obligations, we do seek to control the information.
You said that this concept of a special information protocol was conceived in 2024. Is that right?
It was prior to my time, but I understand it has only been in place for a relatively short period of time.

And it's been used on 25 occasions. Can you identify if it is 25 occasions—if it's more than or fewer than 25—and what they applied to. I'm more than happy for that to be taken on notice, unless you have all 25 of them here to read.

We fall into Defence's three-letter acronym whirlpool. The SIP that's been referred to this afternoon is the sensitive issues protocol. It was developed around 2024. I don't have to hand how many times it has been used. It's used in a range of different ways to manage particularly sensitive matters across the department.
The term that I heard before was 'special information protocol'.
That was a mistake.
That's okay; there are many acronyms.
There are many acronyms. It is known within the department as the SIP, the S-I-P.
But they're the same thing?

They are the same thing, yes. So it is the sensitive issues protocol. It was developed about two years ago. It's used across the department to manage particularly sensitive types of information of a range of kinds—whether capability, operational or policy—where they need to be particularly protected and restricted to a smaller number of people. It involves putting in place a register of all those who have access to that information and controls on that information. Depending on what that particular compartment looks like, those controls might be hard-copy-only distribution of information or restrictions on various emails. As the Vice Chief of the Defence Force has said, this particular SIP—as I said, I'm not sure which number it was—was put around the process that the vice-chief was running this year.
That's been helpful, Mr Reid. Could you take on notice—it may be 25, more or less—the number of projects/activities that have been the subject of a SIP. Is each one a separate SIP? Are they numbered?
They are.
So can you take on notice the numbers of SIPs, the dates of SIPs, if you can, and the subject matter or projects that they applied to—however it's best described.
We'll take that on notice.

That's correct.

text: In September, Iran captured a Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle made and operated by Anduril. We know that Iran has a history of reverse-engineering drones when it captures them, and this will likely happen again now, because the photos seem to show a very intact device. The Dive-LD shares a great deal in common with the Ghost Shark. Have Anduril and/or the US government provided the Australian Defence Force a briefing about the security impacts of the capturing of the Dive-LD by Iran?
The Dive-LD is not the same as Ghost Shark; there are quite a few differences. It is not the same baseline.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Major Surface Combatants and Combat Systems

text: I'm happy to repeat the question. Is it necessary to repeat the question?
In your question you made a characterisation that there were shared or common elements between the Ghost Shark and the device.
I think the exact words were 'shares a lot with the Ghost Shark'. Do you disagree with 'shares a lot with the Ghost Shark'?
I disagree, yes.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Major Surface Combatants and Combat Systems

text: They have a common ancestry and they have common features. I'm not suggesting they're the same, but they have common ancestry and common features. If you could, please answer my question about Anduril and/or the US providing a briefing about the security risks of Iran capturing an intact Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle.

We have not had a briefing from Anduril about that specific capture. However, we are aware that Dive-LD and Ghost Shark, approximately, have been designed for different operational requirements, mission sets and capability outcomes. The two vehicles differ significantly in their size, complexity, autonomy systems, communications, architecture, sensor suites, payload options and security classifications, so they are significantly different.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Major Surface Combatants and Combat Systems

text: Is this because you've had a briefing from Anduril about the differences between the Dive-LD and the Ghost Shark?
We understand the differences, from Anduril Australia, between Dive-LD and Ghost Shark.
witness_position: First Assistant Secretary, Major Surface Combatants and Combat Systems

text: Since the capture of the Dive-LD autonomous, did Anduril Australia provide you any information to give you comfort about the differences or to give you comfort that any commonalities would not place a security risk on the Ghost Shark?

I had a briefing from Mr Goodrich, who is the general manager and CEO of Anduril Australia—not Anduril in the US—in Sydney, when I was up there a couple of weeks ago, in relation to the matter you were talking about. In that specific briefing, which I would characterise as a short brief of five to 10 minutes, he identified that none of the most sensitive elements which were in our Ghost Shark submarine are resident within the Dive-XL capability, which, as Ms Lutz has indicated, is a very significantly different capability. It's half the size of the Ghost Shark, it has a different control system et cetera. In that particular verbal brief, he sought to give me assurances that the sensitive elements of the Ghost Shark were not common to the other vehicle.
Vice Admiral Buckley, thank you for that. You said initially 'none of the most sensitive' and then you said afterwards 'none of the sensitive'. I want to be clear. What did he say to you?
What he said to me was none of the sensitive elements of the Ghost Shark were common to the Dive-XL. That was how he would characterise the briefing.
Did he describe to you the elements that were common?

He described, in the broad, the common types of elements, which are to do with some of the general form of the whole type of the vessel et cetera. If I could describe them, they might use some common fibreglass materials or some common-type structures to operate the chassis, potentially, as opposed to the sensitive control systems and the sensitive payloads, which are different to the Ghost Shark.
Vice Admiral Buckley, I appreciate you telling us about the verbal briefing that went for between five and 10 minutes. When did you say this happened?

It was in the order of two to three weeks ago, when I was up at the Anduril facility for another activity, which was a week or two after—within a week or so of, I should say—the capture of the Dive-XL.

Is it true is that nobody in Defence has sought a formal briefing from Anduril about the potential security risks or the impact on the Ghost Shark of Iran's capture of the Dive-LD autonomous underwater vehicle? Has that not been requested anywhere across Defence?

I'm happy to take that on notice, because there are different elements of connections. We have our Defence scientists connecting to the system, we have our Defence intelligence connecting to the system et cetera. So, rather than take it from the different individuals who are present here, I'm happy to take it on notice and provide you an accurate—
But, to be clear, no-one sitting here has sought a briefing from Anduril apart from the oral briefing given to Vice Admiral Buckley. No-one sitting here has sought one.

I was with Vice Admiral Buckley when we got that brief. Vice Admiral Buckley and I had heard from David Goodrich on the day of the capture as well, and we both had a verbal briefing. The two of us have been briefed on the topic.
What did he say on the day of the capture?
The same information that Vice Admiral Buckley has just espoused.

This is a very serious matter. The Ghost Shark is a very expensive project. There is a common ancestry. I would have thought standard practice would be to get a formal briefing to see whatever risk is associated, and I do find it pretty extraordinary that it appears there's been one phone call and one five- to 10-minute oral briefing.
No, Senator, you misheard. We both got the same verbal briefing together at Anduril facilities, and we both got the same message and the same phone call from David Goodrich.
That's one phone call. Or did you each get parallel phone calls?
He sent a message to both of us on the occasion of the event.
Was it a phone call or a text?
It was a text message, and I called. I can't confirm if Vice Admiral Buckley also called, but I certainly called.

Text message, phone call, five- to 10-minute oral briefing—it's not materially different to my proposition that I put to you. But, in the face of what I think any fair-minded external observer would think, this would require at a minimum some kind of detailed, considered briefing to ensure that what is likely to be a multibillion-dollar project hasn't had a significant security breach. But you're satisfied with what you've done so far, is that right, Vice Admiral Buckley?

Senator Shoebridge, you've made some characterisations that have not been supported by the evidence provided by witnesses about how common or not the two different capabilities are. We have had assurances from the capability development manager and the industry that's providing the capability to us about their assessment of the risks. We work closely with this partner, and there would be conversations at working level on a regular basis. There's detailed understanding of the capabilities et cetera. There would have been discussions with the organisation, and I've already taken on notice in relation to other aspects of connections between the system. We take seriously any potential breaches of technology and options. You've heard today from the witnesses about the actions they've taken, which is an assurance that there are no sensitive matters at risk. We would, of course, go through our usual processes. I'm happy to take it on notice, but I just want to correct the insinuation that I heard—you might not have been meaning that—that, somehow, we were not taking this seriously. The issue is that we are, commensurate with the risk and the knowledge we have in terms of the capability and the concurrence between the two platforms.
We know there are plans—
Last question before I move the call around, Senator.
As I understand it, there are plans to attach drones and mines to the Ghost Shark.
Different payloads, yes.
Some of those will be lethal, is my understanding. Mines, for example, would be lethal. Is that correct?
Potentially, yes. The intention is for it to have payloads that do different effects, yes.

Given that it's a partly AI platform, given it's operating remotely and given that its payloads are intended, in the future, to be lethal, does the ADF have any formal policy around how to manage AI and autonomous weapons? And I note that, as we were talking about Anduril, Palmer Luckey has made it pretty clear that he's very supportive of fully automated weapons being delivered by Anduril. Does the ADF have a policy about managing AI and autonomous weapons? If so, where do I find it?
We do have a responsible use policy related to AI across the enterprise, including in our capability platforms.
But my specific question is about AI and autonomous weapons.
The responsible use of AI applies to everything we do, including autonomous capabilities.
Yes, there is a responsible use policy that was published earlier in the year which does provide a comprehensive overview of Defence's position.
witness_position: Chief Artificial Intelligence and Information Officer

text: What does it say about AI killing people?
Pardon me?
witness_position: Chief Artificial Intelligence and Information Officer

text: What does it say about AI killing people—AI delivering lethal force?

The responsible use of AI is governed by the policy. The policy is published online. This is required by government for the adoption of artificial intelligence into military systems. As you know, artificial intelligence will transform warfare and is already doing so. The big risk for Australia is that we face ongoing and increasing asymmetric disadvantage by potential adversaries who are increasingly integrating AI into their kill chains. We need to keep pace with that. However, we need to do it in a way that is consistent with Australia's international, domestic and constitutional legal obligations. The purpose of the policy is to ensure that Australia can integrate artificial intelligence into military capability according to the principles set out in the policy. Of those principles, the most important among them must be a human in the loop to ensure that the allocation of force and the targeting of assets is always an act authorised by a human in the targeting system. How we integrate it into the force is the responsibility of our operators and, of course, the CIO.
I've just searched the policy and it doesn't include the words 'target' or 'targeting'.

The policy is to allow for us to integrate AI into our capability such that it is able to more quickly identify targets that are seeking to project force against Australia. Everything to do with military capability ultimately needs to find, fix and affect a target.
But it doesn't at any point—

Before you go there—I know we are deep in conversation here, but I need to rotate the call. I've given you well over 40 minutes. How long have you got left with this line? I need to manage the other senators.
If you'd just allow me two more questions—
Sure.

The policy does not require a human to make a decision about the application of lethal force. The policy says humans will be accountable for the delivery of lethal force, but it seems to be consciously drafted not to require humans to make the decision about the delivery of lethal force. Was that an intentional part of this policy?

No. The policy is determined by the obligations of lawfulness, adherence to values-based principles and proportionate control measures. If you just give me a minute I'll outline the values-based principles. They are:

Accountable 1. Defence personnel must exercise informed judgement and care in the research, design, development, deployment, use and decommissioning of AI technologies, and all outcomes will be attributable to an identifiable Defence official. Bias and Harm mitigation 2. AI technologies must be designed to enable the detection, correction and mitigation of unintended bias and unintentional harm, where it can be reasonably anticipated. Explainable 3. The function and relationship between inputs and outputs of AI technologies must be traceable, and the technologies able to meaningfully accommodate human-machine interactions. Human-centric 4. All AI technologies and their use must be considered in light of their planned, likely and potential impact on humans at all levels of involvement. Reliable and Secure 5. AI technologies must perform reliably against well-defined use cases, with resilience to change or interference, including mitigations and provisions for the risk of failure.

These policy settings align with Australia's international legal obligations and domestic law, and they will ultimately be the basis on which we seek to integrate AI technologies into Defence capability.

Yes, Mr Jeffrey. Then, as I read the policy, it allows and permits AI to make the decision to kill somebody and to apply lethal force provided there's some chain of command or some chain of accountability back to a human. It is consciously and deliberately allowing AI to make the kill decision.
No, Senator. I just wouldn't accept that characterisation, with respect.

Identify the provision in the policy that prohibits AI making the kill decisions, or identify the element in the policy that requires a human to make the kill decision. I'm more than happy for you to take that on notice.

If you refer to point No. 1, under lawfulness, it actually highlights:

Human judgement and accountability is central to lawful, legitimate and responsible use of AI, and designated Defence personnel (Accountable Officers) will always be accountable for its use, decisions and outcomes.
witness_position: Chief Artificial Intelligence and Information Officer

text: Correct. So humans set it up, AI kills somebody, and the humans are accountable for the AI kill. That's what that says.

No. I can just add that AI is essentially another tool in the ADF capability set. Anything in the capability set, particularly anything that's lethal to effect a target, ultimately has to be directed within the ADF command chain. AI can speed up that command chain, it can identify more risks and it can enable us to defend ourselves more effectively, but, ultimately, its application—its use in the context of the application of military force—has to be directed.
I ask you, again on notice, to identify the provision in this policy that requires a human to make the kill decision.

We're very happy to take that on notice. It's a very important issue that you're raising, and it's one that's been well ventilated and discussed in Australia within the defence forces. I'll just make the note that this is something we need to grapple with, because, as we move forward, AI is being integrated into all aspects of our life. We're very happy to take it on notice and set out how it matches with the appropriate language in the policy. You've heard the explanation from witnesses, but we're very happy to take it to the next step and join it together with the published policy.
Senator Roberts, I understand you've got a few questions, and then I'll come to the Deputy Chair.

Senator Roberts, you asked about the pay rises. There is a slight mismatch in pay rises between ADF and APS staff, because ADF staff received their pay determinations in November and APS staff had previously received their determinations in March. For historical reasons related to APS bargaining, they're not lined up. For both increases, in November 2025 and March 2026—the APS following the ADF—3.4 per cent was given. The most recent pay rise has been three per cent for the ADF. There's been no determination yet through the bargaining about what the APS increase would be, but there are arrangements in the framework that, if the APS were to achieve a greater bargained outcome than was given to the ADF, the remuneration for the ADF would be reconsidered. The intention is that both move together.
Could you still—
I'm happy to take the historical information—
give us the graph of the last five years for each?
Yes.
What is the current deployment allowance for ADF people deployed for Operation Aslan in South Sudan?
The deployment allowances vary depending upon operation. I will need to come back to you on notice with the Aslan deployment allowance.
We've been told by a member of the Defence Force that this allowance was reduced from $200 to $140. Could that be true?
We regularly review deployment allowances. They are linked to the classification of the deployment. If the deployment is reclassified, then the allowances are reclassified.

That makes sense. The ADF members are primarily serving in the Juda region, which is the reason they were given for the reduction. Is the Juda region not one of the most dangerous regions in South Sudan?
One of my colleagues is best to answer this, in terms of the classification of the nature of the operation.
But it might be best if we take on notice what has happened and why it has changed, if it has changed.
Could you also take on notice why the assessment for this took place.
Yes.
Going to a similar issue, what is the classification of service for ADF members in Europe serving near the Ukraine-Russia conflict?
Again, we're very familiar with this issue, but we are best to give you the different allowance structures as they pertain to the classification of the particular operation.
Okay, and could you give me what allowances the ADF members are entitled to under that classification?
Yes.
And how much that equals in a day?
We can do that. There are a number of allowances in addition to the operational allowances, so I think context is important too, which we'll provide.
And could you tell me how it stacks up against other deployments of a similar nature across the world and Australia?
We may need to narrow that question. Comparisons to other militaries—was that the question?
No, to other operations.
Australian operations, yes.
Yes, we can.

My office has received notice that missiles have been intercepted near the ADF members base. It was close enough that it shook their tents heavily and woke the base up. Would that not change the classification of service? And what does the review process look like for a reclassification?

We're happy to take that on notice. We have a detailed process where we look at the operational context for different operations. You're very welcome to put some of these specific questions on notice so that we can get your intent. It's complicated and it shifts over time, so, if you are interested in particular timeframes—like current timeframes—it's going to be easier for us to deliver that information to you.
Thank you. Would you be able to commit to a review if there's an anomaly?

All these allowances, the classifications, the security classifications and the stance of the operation are reviewed regularly through operation intelligence procedures, and then it flows through into the allowance structure. So they are regularly reviewed. If there are particular concerns you're receiving, we are happy to receive those for us to consider as part of those regular reviews.

Okay. I will go back to Sudan—I'm sorry, I'm jumping around. We've received knowledge that the ADF members have to pay rent for their accommodation on the base in Sudan and, due to having no messing facilities, are required to purchase their own food. Would that be correct?
I think we need to look at that issue. I'm not aware of that. We will follow up on that.
Can you contact my office?
Yes, we can.

Thank you. Being separated from their families for such a long time can be very hard on ADF members, especially in a high-risk area. Are ADF members serving on Operation Aslan entitled to a separation allowance?
The secretary noted there is quite a complexity with who gets what allowance in terms of the situation but also the timing. Again, we can look particularly at that question.

With the elections in South Sudan taking place on 22 December 2026, there will be an increase in political unrest in the area. We've also seen the recent drone strike in the Abyei region, which killed more than 150 people. Will there be a reassessment of deployment and consideration of a reverse of the reduction in the South Sudan allowance?

We do monitor the situation where our troops are stationed on a regular basis and we do take into account all the latest intelligence as part of our assessment. So that would automatically be occurring.
And we can discuss that. Thank you very much.
Senator Collins.

I will start by tabling, please, a contract that I've just printed off the website. Secretary, it is a contract that you confirmed for me during the last estimates—you might remember that you came back after morning tea. It is regarding the lease of Defence Plaza Sydney. It will come to you shortly and we can maybe pick that up again. I want to clarify a few things. Apologies, Admiral, for not calling through you before. Could I please have the Chief of Army back again; I would like to talk about the morale of the Army.
Of course.
Lieutenant General, what do you anticipate to be the impact on morale of the sale of Victoria Barracks Sydney?

I can't speak for every individual in the Australian Army on how they feel about the sale of any of the sites that are in question, including Victoria Barracks Sydney. What I can tell you is that we're a professional fighting force. Our men and women are proud to serve, and wherever we place them, we make sure they are fitted appropriately to be able to deliver on capability and readiness. We look after their welfare and their families', and that is first and foremost in everything that we do.

I appreciated hearing from the Admiral this morning about the commanders' intent, and that part of that is about strengthening 'the resilience and wellbeing of our people and their families to ensure that they are supported, respected and protected throughout their service and beyond'. Can you reflect on morale being part of the doctrine for the Army?

Morale is a critical capability for our people, and it's on every leader from the Chief of Army down to make sure that our men and women have a positive lived experience in their workplace and that they're supported and enabled through everything that they do, so that, whatever role or function they chose to join the Australian Defence Force to do, we provide that environment for them to thrive and to succeed. Morale absolutely underpins every aspect of what we do.
Would you regard Victoria Barracks Sydney to be a spiritual home of the Army?

There is a very rich history of Victoria Barracks Sydney in the history of the Australian Army and, indeed, Australia's history more fulsomely. As you alluded to earlier, I have lived and worked on that barracks, like many others, and there is absolutely a connection to the barracks.
Have you had any serving personnel give feedback on how they're feeling about the loss of Victoria Barracks?

When a decision is made by government for us to relocate, we enact that direction. That is what we're doing at the moment. It's not relevant how we feel about it. A decision has been made and we are moving forward.

I understand. The Defence Force don't have a voice in this, and I understand that. I have had hundreds if not thousands of people reach out to me, and there is grief, there is anger, there is frustration and there is a palpable sense of loss already, and Victoria Barracks hasn't even been sold yet. I can only imagine the feedback that the department is getting and that the government is getting. Given that morale is a defence capability, what do you anticipate the Defence Force is going to do if morale takes a big hit?

Can I give a reminder that the whole purpose of the Defence state review and the transition in the Defence estate is to be consistent with the national defence strategy, which is about building the force that we need to defend Australia. That means moving from bases in the south of Australia to expand our capabilities in the north. This is about building a defence force that's able to meet the needs of the future. That involves changing locations and changing roles. We've heard, through estimates procedures, about how parts of some roles in the ADF at an operational level are shifting with the addition of technology et cetera. There was discussion about the defence legislation; we're removing the need to compensate for bullocks because we're going to automate all those systems—
With all due respect, I'm asking about morale here and I was asking the Chief of Army. I'm just going to quote a little bit from Australian military power about—
But it's also very important that we're giving—

With all due respect, Secretary, I wasn't asking you; I was asking somebody from the service, because they understand morale. I'm going to quote this:

Morale is an essential component of combat power. It feeds the spirit and the will to fight … Breaking the adversary's morale is a clear goal of war.

I'm asking the Chief of Army what they anticipate they will do to address the hit to morale from the loss of Victoria Barracks Sydney.

If I could just finish my intervention, I am happy for the Chief of Army to then continue. There are different elements of morale. It's also about building the capability, the equipment and the locations from which to fight—so there are different elements of morale. The intent of the government is to use the additional funds from elements to provide the capability to fight for and to defend Australia. The additional capability that's achieved will be supportive of morale. There are lots of different elements that go into the complicated and important element of the defence forces.

The truth for us will be what is next after we divest off Victoria Barracks into our permanent location in the future—that it enables us to continue to be operational, capable and ready as Forces Command. There are other locations that are on the barracks that are divesting for their equities as well. How we do that and support our people through that transition is how we will maintain the morale and welfare of our people. The proof is in the pudding, and we are working as a department to ensure that the divestment and relocation is done appropriately so that we can maintain our capability and our readiness as we do that, and support our people and their families.
I appreciate the support you're giving to your people. I'd now like to ask some questions about the Defence Security and Estate Group.

While we're waiting for the officials to come to the table, I acknowledge your advocacy for our people. I also highlight that this is not a new experience in some respects. At the turn of the century, the spiritual home of the submarine force, HMAS Platypus, was divested. In the past, the Middle Head facilities have been divested. There is an element of change that we are used to. We decommission ships in the Royal Australian Navy quite regularly. Our people feel a connection to the infrastructure, the platforms and the equipment, and it's right to acknowledge that. I also highlight that we are and we remain a professional warfighting force. Whilst this is a consideration, it does not define us.
Thank you. Ms Perkins, you have allocated Forces Command to villages in Defence Plaza Sydney; is that correct?

Yes. In the design and fit-out of that building—I'm not sure if they're called villages or neighbourhoods. Across the floors, in the design of the building, there is, as I described earlier, quite strong physical security from where you exit from a lift onto a floor. When you enter into a village, as you described, within the security perimeter, there are internal staircases. That allows us to lock down parts of that tenancy to particular work groups, but it allows them to move freely across a number of floors without going outside the security perimeter. We use that term I've used—I've heard 'village'. It just refers to the way we've broken down the levels of the building, so you won't necessarily move from 14 to 22.
These are war fighters we're talking about. They're not Smurfs. Why 'villages'?

'Neighbourhoods', 'villages'—different people use different components. You've heard Ms Perkins talk about a characterisation of a module. I understand Victoria Barracks Sydney is a training force. We have worked through the capability and the functionality required for what's currently there, and we have determined the appropriate place to go, in consultation with the areas that look after that capability. I would say that characterisation of our defence forces and our public servants as fictional characters is potentially not treating them with the respect they deserve.
I don't think calling these areas 'villages' is treating them with respect.

We have a few villages on the estate. Woomera village is my favourite village. The tenants of the building—we had some of the Forces Command team visit last Thursday; I hope they're very comfortable. In the way they operate in the space, they're free to call it whatever feels best and most appropriate to them. It is just a property term. It in no way denotes disrespect for the work of any of the people in the building.
Do the Defence Plaza Sydney lease conditions require the Department of Defence to obtain approval from the landlord to undertake works?
I'd have to take that on notice. We have quite a degree of flexibility in the terms of the lease.
Perhaps Mr West might be able to answer that one. You've overseen the infrastructural upgrades.

As I indicated in my testimony last week, we don't at this stage anticipate undertaking works. We anticipate using the flexible workspace. It is designed to be within the parameters of its design. We are able to move walls without what I would call construction. We're able to move desks. As far as I'm aware at the moment, we're not anticipating what I'd call constructional work—so I don't believe so. But we will take on notice whether we would be required to, if we needed to do that sort of work.
You've done about $83 million worth of works in there previously. Did you have to get that approved? No. And what about having a zone 5 area in there? Will you have to get that approved?

No. I will just clarify—and thank you; that makes your question a bit clearer—the terms of the lease arrangement. I just want to correct something Senator Blyth asked about in the previous set of questions. The overall contract value is for the totality of the lease, not annually; that's an important distinction to make. In the terms of that lease arrangement, it is both the 10-year lease and extensions, and the fit-out. In the way I described security elements and the broader fit-out, Defence is responsible, in the terms of the lease, for that. Within that, we have, as Mr West described, the ability to add extra cabling for more ICT and so on and so forth. It would be if you wanted to do quite significant structural work, as described.
Secretary, on the contract I tabled before, can you just confirm for me that that's for the lease at Defence Plaza Sydney? If it's not, what is it?
I am not an expert in the way and do not have the history, but I believe the numbers line up.
Without going back to the team and sourcing the original documents, I believe this is from a previous answer that the property team provided. I'm happy to check again.
I'm just a little confused, because you said that the lease was signed in 2020, yet this is saying the—

No. In the discussion with the chair, we were talking about the approvals to proceed with the lease. We've discussed this with you before, Senator. Once the approvals from government are undertaken, then there's often a period of negotiation. I believe we've confirmed in the past that the execution of the lease—and that would have involved a period of negotiation around the terms, the fit-out and so forth—was in early February.
Who was the minister that signed the lease in February 2023?
The signature of the lease would have happened within Defence. They're delegated authorities that flow from the Minister for Finance.
Who was the minister responsible for that, though?
I know we've had this conversation also before.
We have, yes.

This was just following a federal election, but this was a decision held over, approved in the previous government. I'm going to take on notice who in my organisation signed the lease, but it would most likely have been my assistant—

That's okay. I don't need to know the person. I just want to know the minister overseeing it. I've checked February 2023; it was Defence Minister Marles. I just wanted to clear that up. Just back to Defence Plaza Sydney, our soldiers have to pass a BFA every year. What's the gym like? How much capacity does the gym have at Defence Plaza Sydney?
The gym is about half the floor plate of a floor of the building, the 14th floor.
How many people can you fit in the gym at a time?
It would seem to have reasonable capacity for an office gym. It's part of the work we're doing with Army on the transition plan.
How many people are going to be in the defence plaza at the not-full capacity? Are we talking hundreds? Are there going to be hundreds of people at the defence plaza?
The defence plaza has currently 1,146 work points.
How many people do you think you could fit in the gym?
I could take that on notice, but I use a lot of Defence gyms around the estate. I would estimate that it's about twice the size of the Campbell Park gym. It's a good gym.
I don't know what—
Alright, let's not worry about the gyms.
Chair, with all due respect—
How long have you got left? I'm mindful that Senator Shoebridge has a few more questions.

Half the floor is going to fit about 10 people at a time. When you've got serving personnel that need to do exercise every single day, I'm just trying to understand how you're going to cater for that. Passing your BFA every year is a requirement.

We've taken on notice the capacity constraints of the gym. There will be operational requirements about how many people can operate it safely. We're happy to take that on notice. Of course, we would be factoring that into the elements that we need to provide the services. Just to be clear, not all of the 500 or so people are moving to the defence plaza. Some are going to Randwick instead. So we're talking hundreds of people, not thousands of people.
And you'll be coming back with the numbers of people that you'll expect to have in there on a daily basis? Thank you. That was a question asked previously. How many change rooms are there?
I'd have to take that on notice.

Thank you very much. I would appreciate that. Just back to the question of security cameras, we never really got an answer on that one. What measures are in place to ensure that the security footage from cameras in the rest of the building—particularly in the lobby and if there is a car park for a select few people underneath or out on the street as you enter the building—doesn't go to people, companies, private companies or governments that we don't want to have that footage?

I can only repeat comments I've made earlier that for every facility that we operate—and we operate many leased facilities—we undertake a security risk assessment and then we match the security treatments to the assessed threat. We wouldn't treat Defence Plaza Sydney any different to any other facility unless there were a change in that threat setting. We have many office facilities in many locations, and our people do move freely throughout the community.
Not all of them have Forces Command in them. What is the security assessment of Defence Plaza Sydney and the footage that could be captured through cameras in the lobby?

As I've mentioned earlier, the current tenancy of Defence Plaza Sydney includes a great many different elements of the Defence organisation. The incoming Forces Command colleagues don't materially change the overall threat assessment.
I'm asking what happens with the security footage.
Why don't we take that on notice?
Who owns it?
I'd have to take that on notice.

So you don't know? You're the deputy secretary of the Security and Estate Group and you don't know where the security footage goes, who owns it, what happens to it, what the limitations are around it or what the constraints are around it? What measures are you going to put in place to protect our people?

Senator, we've said we will take that on notice. I just note that's a very specific, very technical question. It would be known within the department, and we're happy to take it on notice. But, as Ms Perkins has said, the current assessment is that the addition of the particular people who will particularly be moving doesn't change the overall threat assessment at this point. Obviously, we keep that under review. Part of the assessment about who goes where as a result of the change would have gone to the functions and capability and risks of the activities that they're undertaking. That is part of the operational concerns that we undertook as we did the integrated assessment about the transition planning.

Alright. A question on policy, then: what measures have you put in place to protect the security footage that is taken in that lobby? I'm not asking who owns it; I'm not asking where it's going. I'm asking: what have you done? You've made an assessment of it. Is your assessment that you don't need to do anything?
We've made an assessment that there's no material change to the risk vectors as a result of a few hundred people moving from one location to another—
I'm not saying 'moving'; I'm saying 'going in and out on a daily basis'.

and transitioning in and out as well. So we're happy to take on notice to provide you the approach that we take, which has been articulated at a high level in these estimates and previous committee discussions. We take the approach to protecting our staff—APS, ADF and contractors—seriously. We do risk assessments across all 1,000 locations that people operate out of. We then put in place mitigation strategies. It is the case that there are ongoing assessments about technology. We can all be photographed and tracked in ways that we weren't able to be before. That is a concern across the whole estate, and it's part of—we talked earlier about the Leeuwin incident. So it's something that we have front of mind when we talk about the security of our staff. It's no different in terms of entering and exiting existing locations or new locations. We do an assessment on the basis of the facilities and the functions that are occurring within.

Okay. That was all sort of broad policy. What is your security assessment specifically of Defence Plaza Sydney and the security that they have, the security cameras that they have and the infrastructure that they have? What security are you going to have at the front? This is just so I can get this question right and get the answer right; I want to be really specific about this. You mentioned that you make assessments on the security vectors. What is your assessment of Defence Plaza Sydney and the interaction with the public—people we don't know—going in and out of the building alongside our Defence personnel?

For Defence Plaza Sydney, and for every Defence site that we operate, the process is essentially the same. So I won't speak specifically to Defence Plaza Sydney—we've already taken that on notice—but I'm happy to describe it.
Just your security assessment of it, just specifically. What's the assessment?

If I can describe how, it will help us frame how we can come back to you on this. We undertake annually a Defence security threat assessment. We do that in very close consultation with ASIO. That sets out—and CDF referred to some of them this morning—the core security threats and risks as they accrue to Defence across a number of vectors: foreign intelligence collection, counterterrorism, insiders, maverick individuals and so forth. We then require, at every base or facility level, the local base leadership—our senior ADF officer and the base support team—to undertake a risk assessment for that site and then to use both the existing physical and other security controls in place and any additional issues that they identify as important to that site so that they can work with us to apply them locally. There is a requirement for every site to do that annually. Where they can enact those controls, or additional controls if required, locally, they do that. If they require more support, they escalate that through a formal process.

Ms Perkins, we're about to break for tonight. I'm going to have to stop you there. I was very specific about my question. It's about your assessment of Victoria Barracks. You've just used words there about security controls, so I'm going to reframe the question for you. What security controls have you put in place for the camera infrastructure that is in the lobby of Defence Plaza Sydney?
We've taken that on notice, I think, but—
No. Security controls—what do you do? How do you stop it from being used, sold or watched by people that you don't know?

We're happy to take it on notice, but there's a series of assumptions that I'm hearing in relation to your question, which is presuming that there's an additional vector for security cameras in this particular location. I am not sure whether that is true or not, so we are happy to take it on notice. There are video cameras in lots of different locations et cetera. That vector of concern is not just in this location and would exist, now, against the existing functions. We've taken it on notice; happy to provide it. I just want to be clear that I'm not necessarily agreeing that there is an increased risk from the movement of a few hundred people into a facility that fits over a thousand, but we're very happy to take it on notice.
You were Treasury; you weren't Department of Finance, previously, but there was a shift, before, to change the camera infrastructure, wasn't there?

There has been a tightening of security across a lot of different vectors, including video cameras, drones and lots of different things. That comes under a whole different set of security procurements, including purchasing IT equipment and phones et cetera. We are aware of all of those security requirements.
A few years ago there was a change of the security cameras, because we couldn't control where those images were going. That was the national security risk—

No. That's not correct. A number of years ago, under the direction of the Deputy Prime Minister, we undertook an audit of all Defence sites of the country of origin of manufacture of CCTV cameras. They are closed circuits and, by definition, weren't internet connected, but it was part of a broader approach around controlling the supply chain. We worked through, and, where we had Chinese-manufactured CCTV cameras, we removed and replaced them across the Defence estate.
What I'm asking is have you checked Defence Plaza Sydney for those sorts of—
We've taken this on notice in a couple of different ways.
So you haven't. You would be able to say whether you have or you haven't.

I want to check that that was part of the work that we did. I just want to be really sure—it was a number of years ago, that activity—whether a distinction was made between the owned or leased estate. In my view, it should have been the leased estate. But I need to check, and we will take that and come back to you on that.
As the deputy secretary of the security and estate group, you do not know whether you've checked that element of security at Defence Plaza Sydney?
When we did that work, I would pore over the list every week. It's been a number of years since we did that work. I would like to just refresh and make sure we get the correct answer for you.
Thank you very much.
I understand, Senator Shoebridge, that you've got seven minutes.
Yes. Maybe even less.
Let's hope so, then we'll be able to release the department.

The first question is for the Chief of Army. Chief of Army, this is about a very sensitive matter. I note, with deep tragedy, about Corporal Brendan Hannam and his death earlier. My question is about training fatalities. In the last five years, are you aware how many training fatalities there have been in the ADF, and how many of them have been from rollover incidents?
Yes, I am. If you just give me a moment, I'll grab the relevant sheet.

While you do that, for the benefit of everyone who's watching, the committee has agreed to release officers of the Department of Veterans' Affairs, the Repatriation Commission, the Veteran Family Commission, the Repatriation Medical Authority and the Australian War Memorial. We're going to hold a spillover at a future time given that we are not going to get to them by 10 o'clock this evening.

Can I start, please, by acknowledging the loss of Corporal Brendan Hannam and acknowledge the deep impact that's been felt not only across his family and his mates but across the wider Army and community, also acknowledge the five soldiers who were wounded as a result of the Supacat rollover.

In terms of vehicle accidents and vehicle safety, we have one of the largest and most diverse vehicle fleets. We have approximately 15,820 vehicles in the Australian Army across a broad range of platforms. In the last five years, we recorded 2,536 vehicle incidents, with 57 of them meeting the threshold for 'notifiable incidents'. As a result of that, there were four incidents where we had fatalities.
How many of those were rollover incidents? I know I said five years, but could we go back to 1 July 2021. That would include the incidents in, I think, August of 2021.

That's right. In terms of delineation of 'rollover', I'll have to do more work and come back to you on that. But the delineation that I will provide is the difference between a layover and a rollover. A layover is where a vehicle will tip onto its side, whereas a rollover is where it's had multiple rolls across the vehicle.

By all means articulate where they're layovers and where they're rollovers. Could I also ask you, if you're doing that review—and I'm not asking you to time limit this; I'm just asking it in relation to the Supacat high-mobility vehicle—are you aware of previous incidents where there have been layovers in relation to the Supacat?
Yes, I am, and I can provide that information now.
Yes, please.

There have been four reported incidents involving variants of the Supacat vehicle in Australia. The first was in 2014. It was a Nary variant of the vehicle which was involved in a rollover. It occurred in Special Operations Command in a testing activity in 2014. There was no reported injury or fatality with that rollover. The second one occurred on 29 June 2020. It was an HMT Extenda. So it was similar to the one that resulted in a fatality in Mount Bundey. It was involved in a layover during a training serial at Holsworthy. The third one occurred on 28 July this year. It was an Extenda vehicle that was towing an M777 howitzer. The vehicle didn't lay over or roll over. It was actually the M777 that actually had a mechanism fail with the vehicle that was attached. It jack-knifed under the towing, which was caused by the towing element, but the Supacat itself did not roll and the suspension remained in place. Then the fourth one you're aware of on 5 October was a rollover.
Thanks. My final question is about dead whales on Garden Island and HMAS Stirling. Are dead whales in your bailiwick, Admiral Hammond?
Can you provide more context?
There have been multiple reports of dead whales washing up on Garden Island on the side of HMAS Stirling, including in July and August of this year. Are you aware of that occurring?
I can confirm that in or around July a dead whale was in Careening Bay, adjacent to HMAS Stirling.
I've received reports of two dead whales in or about HMAS Stirling and other injured whales. Are you saying you only have reports of one dead whale?
That's correct.
Could I ask you to take on notice if there are other reports of dead whales?
Absolutely, yes.

Under EPBC regulations, when a whale dies or breaches, there's a requirement to notify the Department of Climate Change, Energy, Environment and Water. Do you know if that happened in relation to HMAS Stirling?

Let me just confirm. I was informed of the event as it occurred and as the removal was enacted. We work very closely with DCCEEW on all the elements of our environmental management of HMAS Stirling. Let me just confirm the sequence of events there and include that in the answer to the question on notice.

As I understand it, EPBC Act policy statements require that, where there is the death of a cetacean, which includes a whale, there is required to be a 'power down and stop work' procedure. Do you know if that happened in relation to—

Just to be clear, my understanding of the incident is that we don't believe the whale died at the site but rather that it floated in as part of the southern migration. But, as I said, we work very closely with DCCEEW on a number of really stringent environmental controls for the works we're doing at Stirling, so we will include that in our answer for you.
Can you include whether or not the policy was complied with. I'm not certain whether the policy requires it only when the death has occurred on the site or when the dead whale appears on the site.
We will confirm that for you.
And you say you're not aware of a second whale dying near HMAS Stirling? I'm advised that happened in or around late August.
I'm not aware.
But you'll make inquiries about that?
Absolutely.
And answer on notice?
Yes.
Thank you.
On that note, thank you, everyone. The department is now released. Thank you very much for your time today.
I would like to welcome Vice Admiral Jonathan Mead AO, RAN, who's the Director-General of the Australian Submarine Agency. Hello, Vice Admiral. How are you?
I'm very good. Chair. It's great to be back here again.
Excellent. I love that. It is good to see you again.
Thank you very much.
Surprisingly!
Yes.
Good evening to all your officers here as well. Do you have an opening statement, by any chance?
I do, but, noticing that you have a number of other agencies to go through, I may just do a very abbreviated summary of that just to set the context.
Do you have one already prepared that you might be able to circulate with the committee?
Correct.
Okay. Let's do that. We'll table that version, but, if there's a high level that you'd like to talk to, I'd appreciate that.

Thank you for allowing me to make an opening statement. We're clearly pleased to be before you at this quite significant point in the delivery of the AUKUS optimal pathway. As you know, this week we welcomed USS Colorado to HMAS Stirling for our fourth submarine maintenance period. At the same time this week, the three ministers made the announcement that USS Colorado would be the first US Virginia class submarine that would operate as part of the SRF-West rotating forces in just over 12 months time. With each maintenance period, Australian personnel are building the skills, experience and confidence needed to support this rotational presence, while critical infrastructure upgrades at Stirling continue to prepare the base for 2027. Today, nearly 110 Australians, many of them trained at Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard, are applying those skills across Australia's submarine enterprise and collectively supporting the maintenance of USS Colorado, demonstrating the growing maturity of Australia's sovereign submarine workforce. The next chapter is SRF-West, and we are ready for it. We are already seeing that tangible transition take place. SRF-West is not just on track; it is a fact. Five years on, the strategic rationale remains compelling for AUKUS, and the results are becoming increasingly tangible through growth in our workforce, infrastructure, industry and capability.

In closing, I would like to make the point that those things that hurt us also instruct. For that reason, the Australian Submarine Agency acknowledges and respects the challenges we face. We welcome the instructions that these challenges bring with them. Our continuing test is to identify them early, confront them honestly and act on them decisively. That mindset guides the Australian Submarine Agency. Like our AUKUS partners, we have adopted a mindset to be self-aware, self-critical, self-correcting and self-sustaining. As we strengthen the Australian enterprise alongside our AUKUS partners, absolute competence, relentless attention to detail and unyielding intellectual honesty remain fundamental to how we approach this mission.

Thank you, Chair. I welcome the committee's questions.
Thanks, Vice Admiral. Now, Senator Blyth, do you have some questions you want to kick off with?
I am happy for Senator Shoebridge to have the call if he's here. If not, I can take five minutes. I'm in your hands, Chair.
Generally, I go to the opposition first, but I'm happy to go to Senator Shoebridge. Senator Shoebridge.
Good to see you, Vice Admiral Mead.
Thank you very much, Senator—good to see you.
I keep thinking, 'This'll be your last estimates,' but then you—
I didn't think it would be, but we had tears in our eyes last time, when we were departing—
Yes, it was quite emotional last time, and now you're back again!
Yes, I know!
You're drawing this out.
He's teasing with you, Senator!
Is there a timeframe in terms of your replacement, and what's been the discussion with you?
I remain the director-general. The government is looking for a replacement. Until that time, I remain the Director-General of the Australian Submarine Agency.
Has the government given you a timeframe to allow you to organise your life?

Not really, and I think they're doing the right thing. They want to select the right person. I'm proud to be in this position. It's a privileged position to be in—to be part of the ASA, to lead the most complex and demanding endeavour any government has undertaken. So I'll remain here at government's pleasure.
Minister, can you provide any timeframe for the replacement of Vice Admiral Mead, and what's the process to replace Vice Admiral Mead?
I'm not in a position to provide a timeframe. As Vice Admiral Mead has indicated, there is a process underway, and I'm sure that will be completed in due course.
What is the process?
I'll see if I have any information on that. Feel free to pose another question while I review my notes.

Thanks, Minister. Vice Admiral Mead, the USS Colorado is now at HMAS Stirling, and it's undertaking a submarine maintenance period. Previously, the US held any waste created during maintenance and took it back to the US. Is that right?
That's correct.
What's the intention for the waste produced—in this case, any radioactive waste produced—during the maintenance for USS Colorado?
USS Colorado will retain the waste and take it back with them.
At what stage is the ASA's development of a domestic waste storage facility for nuclear waste? Where are you up to?
I might hand that over to Mr Tim Hodgson, who's the lead for that.

We're going through the process, at the moment, of setting up the processes and equipment to do that. We will be simulating these types of activities as part of our process of getting our licences in place. Once we have satisfied ourselves that we are ready and we have satisfied the regulator, we will then be issued our licence to be able to do that, and we're confident in being able to do that to meet our timetable against the SRF-West timelines.
What is the timetable?
The timeline is to meet the SRF-West requirement of later next year.
The second half of next year, the third quarter, the fourth quarter next year—
Quarter 4, 2027.
And the intent is to store the radioactive material onsite at HMAS Stirling? Or do you have another facility where you're storing it?
It'll be temporarily stored there until we move it to either another interim storage or its final disposal site.
But the licence you're intending to get and have operative by the fourth quarter of next year—where is it intended to store the radioactive material under that licence?
It'll be temporarily stored in HMAS Stirling.
At that stage, you're not—I understand the timetable is you won't have completed the site analysis, let alone the licensing, for a permanent storage facility. Is that right?
We won't have decided the final location for the long-term storage of low-level waste at that point.
Have you identified sites for it?
No.
Have you scoped out potential sites?
No.
So, when you say a temporary storage at HMAS Stirling, what's the timeline, if you haven't even begun scoping out sites for a permanent site?
We're working with our colleagues in ARWA to refine our approach to coming up with a longer term solution to that.
You're working with your colleagues where, sorry, Mr Hodgson?
The Australian Radioactive Waste Agency.
What is the role of the Australian Radioactive Waste Agency in terms of identifying a site?
They're providing us with advice.
Who's the minister responsible for the Australian Radioactive Waste Agency?

Minister King is the lead for that. Of course, there is a significant amount of low-level radioactive waste produced by a range of institutions in Australia. We've spoken about this before. There are universities, hospitals, mining sites and the nuclear facility at Lucas Heights. I think it was, clearly, a very sensible decision to be made that we should join up with ARWA and go through the process of working together for low-level-waste disposal sites.
To go back to Rotational Force-West, there was an $8 billion budget associated with the upgrades at HMAS Stirling announced in 2023. Is that still the budget?
Correct. That is still the budget.
That was, as I understood it, intended to be expended up to 2027 in order to have SRF operational. Is that still the intent?

No. There were a series of what were called priority works that needed to be conducted in order to satisfy the criteria that the US and UK had given us in order to be what we call SRF-West ready. The $8 billion expands upon the priority works and gets us to what we've already spoken about—being sovereign ready. Those are additional facilities that will allow us to be in a position to take ownership of US Virginia class submarines. I have my chief operating officer and chief financial officer here who can tell you the exact amount of money that's been spent.
Yes, I'd appreciate that.
The priority works have an approved budget of $2.5 billion. Of that, accumulative estimated expenditure to 30 June was about $805 million.
To June.
Cumulative till the end of June.
Last financial year.
And the preceding years that the work started in.
I understand that. The cumulative spend up to the end of last financial year was $805 million. Do you have an estimate of what the budget is up to now?
It's $708 million for 2026-27. That's the annual budget. The overall budget—
No, I get it. By the end of this financial year, it'd be about $1.5 billion.
Yes.

Given that it was $2.5 billion to get it ready for SRF-West to commence, how do we explain the gap between the $1.5 billion that will be expended by the middle of next year and the $2.5 billion in the priority budget?

The capabilities that are required to support Submarine Rotational Force-West will be in place by quarter 4 of 2027. The remaining facilities that come online will come over a period that precedes that date and handovers.
Is it anticipated by quarter 4 of 2027 that $2.5 billion of priority works will be expended?
No. It will extend beyond that.
When will you consider Submarine Rotational Force-West to be in operation?
We are aiming for quarter 4 of 2027 to be at what we're calling the initial operating state.
What does the initial operating state involve, Vice Admiral Mead?

That involves us being in a position to safely and securely support rotating US Virginia class submarines operating from HMAS Stirling. It will mean that we'll have a trained workforce that will be able to conduct short maintenance periods on board those submarines, just like what we are doing at the moment. It will allow the defence regulator to be in place. It will allow an Australian supply chain to be able to provide the support for the submarine: obviously, logistics support, housing for US personnel and a range of other activities which are going on at Stirling at the moment.
Does the $2.5 billion include the housing budget, or is that separately through Defence Housing?
No, that is correct. It includes the housing for the initial tranche of people.
How much of the $2.5 billion is for housing?
Sorry, the housing is separate to the $2.5 billion. That's only work on HMAS Stirling. DHA has provided the capital for—
Alright, so it's as I understood.
It's separate, yes.
Defence Housing, okay. Can I ask, then, about HMAS Henderson. How much has been spent out of the ASA budget on HMAS Henderson, if any?
Nothing. That's not in the Defence budget.
That's entirely out of Defence?
Defence, yes.
That's my understanding.
Just a clarification, it's not a HMAS—it's not a commissioned military establishment.

Henderson sustainment facility or whatever it's called. I might move on to another matter. Admiral Mead, in August of this year, the US government accounts office—which is effectively their audit office, as you know—published a report, Navy readiness: actions needed to address costly attack submarine maintenance challenges. Have you familiarised yourself with that report?
Not exactly, no.
Has anyone in ASA familiarised themselves with that report?
We'd probably need more information.

It's the August 2027 report, entitled Navy readiness: actions needed to address costly attack submarine maintenance challenges, published by the US government accounts office. I can't give you any more information than that.
I'm aware of that report.
Have you read the report?
I've read parts of the report.

The report found that the US Navy has lost more than 15,000 operational days, which is the equivalent of 41 years, over the past decade from its Virginia class fleet due to maintenance delays and idle time on active attack submarines. The report indicated that addressing those maintenance delays is going to have a significant impact on its ability to meet the workforce to provide for the construction of new submarines. Has anyone in the ASA had discussion about those workforce stressors and the impact of those lost 15,000 operational days on the US Virginia fleet?

We've had numerous discussions with the US Navy and US naval reactors on the US submarine industrial base over the previous months, in particular with their senior leadership, and, more importantly, the investments that have been made recently to increase the production of Virginia class submarines.

You've all been very generous with me. I think I said August 2027, and you're quite right, that it wasn't August 2027. It was August 2026. If you had read the August 2027 one, Ms James, you'd have done a sterling job!

By way of example, the Virginia class submarine build rate is up by 10 per cent this year. The forecast is that it will increase by another 10 per cent next year. The enterprise hours are on pace for a 30 per cent improvement by the end of 2026. Importantly, they have commissioned two Virginia class submarines this year—2026—USS Massachusetts and USS Idaho, and they are already deployed overseas. And they are on track to commission two further Virginia class submarines, Arkansas and Utah, in quarter 1 and quarter 2, 2027.

We've spoken about this on many occasions—that that $17 billion which they invested in 2024 would take some time to wash through the system, and we're seeing that happen now. There are tangible outcomes that the US are making. On 6 October, the President made the announcement that there would be a new Anduril facility of $6 billion in Maryland to manufacture critical components of the Virginia class submarines; on 12 October, the US Navy established an additional submarine component repair facility in Ohio; and, on 23 October, there's the commencement of the construction of a new submarine-manufacturing facility in Mississippi. All of these investments will help support Australia's future acquisition of Virginia class submarines.

Admiral Mead, the new facility in Mississippi—can you tell the committee what the scale of that facility is and compare it to the current two production facilities, because it's my understanding it is in no way comparable. But perhaps you can shed some light upon the Mississippi facility. It is not even close to comparable.

What the US Navy is doing now, what the Pentagon is doing, is establishing a range of outsourcing arrangements around the US so the work is not all being done at the shipyard itself, where there are blockages. What they're doing is establishing outsourcing arrangements in smaller facilities specialising in some areas. The one in Mississippi is focusing on the propulsor. Some other areas are focusing on other parts of the supply chain. The aim of this is to allow the shipyard to focus on what it actually needs to do in parallel with a range of other facilities that are being built or being repurposed in order to increase the production rate.

Admiral Mead, it was confirmed in the middle of this year by a senior Pentagon official that the production rates for Virginia class submarines were still at 1.2 a year. Admittedly, that's an increase from 1.1. Is that the 10 per cent increase you were referring to?

No, I do not believe so. I think the 10 per cent is on top of that, and the enterprise hours, as I said, are on pace for a 30 per cent improvement. The tangible outcomes of this are that, over the past three years, we've seen the US now being able to produce two submarines this year and two submarines early next year.

Admiral Mead, the only reason that's happening is that they've been producing about 1.1 or 1.2 a year, and that 0.1 or 0.2 has now accrued so that they've managed to launch two in this year. But it doesn't reflect the capacity to build the equivalent of two ships in a given year. It's simply the effluxion of time, with that incremental part of a ship having been built each year up to this point. It in no way reflects a capacity to produce two ships a year, does it?

What we're seeing is those ships being produced, which increases the force flow of the US Navy, but we're also seeing an actual increase—as I said, a 10 per cent increase in the Virginia class submarine build rate this year. Enterprise hours increased by 30 per cent this year, and they're expecting the same in 2027.
At best, the 10 per cent increase, which only commences at some point this year, would raise the production rate from 1.2 to 1.32.
Yes.

And I have not seen any independent data on that. If you've got independent data that provides that, can you provide it to the committee. Have you got a document or some evidence from the United States?

I do have evidence from the United States from the direct reporting portfolio manager submarines, who answers directly to the Deputy Secretary of War. It was a new position established approximately 18 months ago to review, revitalise and reinvigorate the US submarine industrial base.
Is there a name and a title attached to this person to make it easier?
Admiral Robert Gaucher.
Are you saying that Admiral Gaucher advised you that the US Virginia class submarine production rate has increased to 1.32 per year?
He said that the build rate is increasing 10 per cent this year and that the enterprise hours are on pace for a 30 per cent improvement by the end of 2026.
Increasing 10 per cent this year means, over the course of this—is it this calendar year or—
Calendar year.
Did he say to you that over 2026 it will be increasing 10 per cent?
Yes, by the end of 2026.
Admiral Mead, the requirement to meet the US's needs and the additional three for AUKUS means that the US has had to be producing 2.33 Virginia class submarines a year since 2022-23.
That's not entirely correct.
How is it wrong?

So 2.33 is not a figure that the US uses. The president has not used the figure of 2.33. Secretary Hegseth has not used the figure of 2.33. The Chief of Naval Operations has not used the figure of 2.33. The director of naval reactors has not used the figure of 2.33.

The Congressional Research Service, who's had a look at the US Navy's intended production schedule and intended service fleet numbers for the Virginia class submarines, has independently and repeatedly verified the 2.33 figure being to meet the projected and budgeted numbers of Virginia class submarines for the United States Navy as set out in their long-term planning, as well as to provide the surplus three Virginia class submarines for Australia. They have set the figure at 2.33.
They have.
Do you disagree with it?

No, I don't disagree with the analysis that the Congressional Research Centre has done. What I'm saying is that it is a figure that the US Department of War is not using to determine the requirement for the transfer of the Virginias to Australia.

Given it is based upon the combined authors' multiple decades of experience, given it's based upon the identified published projections that have been adopted by the US Navy and given it's based upon the known production rates in the two shipyards that produce Virginia class submarines, it is the single authoritative figure in terms of the requirements for the United States to meet its discretionary obligations under the AUKUS agreement. Are you able to point to a different figure?

I think we're talking at cross paths here. I understand what the Congressional Research Service does. It produces publications and has come up with a theoretical figure. What I'm saying to you, Senator, is that that is not a figure used by officials or politicians in the US system. I have never been told by the US that we need to get to a figure of 2.33.

I think going forward that's probably true. Having not met that figure—in fact, having been only meeting half of that figure from 2023, 2024, 2025 and 2026—that actually means now, going forward, to meet the projected requirements for the US Navy as well as the AUKUS requirements, the figure would no longer be 2.33. The figure would be closer to three a year on the same maths—wouldn't it?—because there has been a significant shortfall for the last four years.

What I can tell you is that I'm working with the US on a daily basis at a very senior level. We've had the president, who's said, 'It's full steam ahead.' The US is committed to transferring Virginia class submarines in the 2030s once we are sovereign ready.

I've heard this. You see, Admiral Mead, the difficulty that you have and that the Australian Submarine Agency has is that each year the production rates for the Virginia class submarine don't even come close to meeting the US's own domestic needs, which is a minimum of two per year. Each year, the gap grows, and, even on your more positive assumption that there's been a 10 per cent increase this year, that only brings it to 1.32. Even assuming you get another 10 per cent—and the gap grows again this year—increase next year, you'll get up to about 1.45. The gap will grow next year. If you get another 10 per cent the year after, the gap will grow again, and the difficulty is compounded by the evidence in the Navy readiness report from the government accounts office, which is their audit report, because you'll not only have the shortfall in production of new Virginia class submarines but the US Navy will also, because of the way they're cannibalising their existing fleet and with their maintenance shortfalls, have even fewer boats in the water. That's this combined problem that you're facing, isn't it? It's not all of your making, but it's the problem you're facing

The real issue here is looking at what the US needs. What are they looking for here? What was in the NDAA, essentially, is that they want boats in the water. There are two ways to get boats in the water. One is production. We've just spoken about that at length, and I'm talking about increased production rates of 10 per cent per year. The second aspect is maintenance, and it's aspects like SRF-West where we will be generating significant availability days for the US Navy and for US Virginia class submarines because of the maintenance we are doing in a separate facility—separate to Pearl Harbor and separate to Guam—which will then allow those workforces to focus on other submarines. You join the production with the sustainment, and you end up with boats in the water.

Admiral Mead, the most recent report from just August of this year—not August of next year, I accept—from the US government accounts office says that this problem of maintenance is getting worse for the Virginia class fleet and that it's now a non-virtuous circle. It means that the boats that are in the water that are able to be maintained and stay in the water are doing longer hours and longer tours, and are working harder. They are being worked at a harder rate and requiring more maintenance. They're coming offline more, and this non-virtuous cycle in the maintenance thing in the US Virginia fleet is meaning there is less and less availability for the United States for the Virginia class fleet. If you add that problem to the repeated historical and, on all projections, future shortfall in production capacity, the ability of the United States to have any kind of surplus or capacity to provide Virginia class submarines to Australia in the early to mid-2030s is close to zero because of that combined impact.

I'm looking at it from a different angle here. I'm looking at increased production of 10 per cent a year. I'm looking at, in 2027, SRF-West facilities up and running. That will provide the US Navy Virginia class submarines with an alternative additional shipyard to do maintenance. That assists the US Navy in getting more boats in the water.

If you read the August 2026 report, that would make a marginal difference. The maintenance thing is a lack of skilled workers and a critical lack of key parts, and the lack of key parts for the maintenance means they are sabotaging—pulling apart—one Virginia class submarine that's been waiting in maintenance in order to put the parts on another one. Opening SRF with a marginal maintenance capacity is not going to come close to dealing with the maintenance problems.

I disagree there, Senator. We just spoke about this at the very beginning. What is the requirement of SRF-West? It is to have a skilled workforce. We will have 500 ASC trained workers there by 2030. We already have approximately 300 trained ASC workers that will be ready to conduct maintenance on US Virginia class submarines. We are investing heavily in approximately 140 companies in Australia to be able to feed into the US supply chain. All of that will take pressure off the maintenance of Virginia class submarines in the other shipyards in the submarine industrial base. SRF-West is an additive to getting boats in the water.

Admiral Mead, I'm not arguing that it's not an additive. My point is that it's incredibly marginal given the fundamental industrial workplace and production shortfalls that are evidenced in that August 2026 report. You might disagree with me, but I'm putting that proposition to you. Do you agree with that?
No.

Alright. Admiral Mead, I asked you questions previously about whether it was the ASA's understanding that the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024 put the President of the United States in personal control of money Australia contributes to the US industrial base for the purpose of AUKUS.
