I did go back and review your answer, but I had trouble comprehending exactly why you appeared to disagree with that. So I might just read to you directly from that act, which sets up the account into which Australia's AUKUS contributions are paid. It says:

(1) In general.--There is established in the Treasury of the United States a special account to be known as the "Submarine Security Activities Account". (2) Credit to account.--Contributions of money accepted by the President under subsection (a) shall be credited to the Submarine Security Activities Account.

That's the provision. Do you accept that the President has control over the moneys going into that Treasury account from Australia under AUKUS?
Can I hand over to Ms Mikaela James, who will be able to provide a response.
Yes, by all means.
Senator, that account, as you noted, was set up through the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2024, and that is where our contributions are being paid into.
And those contributions are subject to presidential acceptance and presidential control because they're an account in the executive, aren't they?
I would have to take that on notice.

Alright. I think it's fairly unambiguous that the President is in charge of the executive and an account in the US Treasury is therefore subject to presidential control, but by all means take that on notice. A further reply that was given to my question on notice—it's portfolio question reference No. 139, and the question was asked on 16 June 2026—stated in part:

Australia has appropriate mechanisms in place to ensure we have transparency over and assurance about US expenditure of our contribution …

What are those mechanisms?

Those mechanisms are part of our negotiations with the US over the contribution, and we have in place those mechanisms to ensure that we understand where our funding is going and that appropriate reporting is in place.
I'm sorry, Ms James, but just repeating that there are mechanisms and that those mechanisms have been negotiated doesn't explain the mechanisms. What are the mechanisms?
The US provides us visibility of the expenditure.
So they tell you where they're spending it?
Yes.

But the answer said:

Australia has appropriate mechanisms in place to ensure we have transparency over and assurance about US expenditure of our contribution …

You've simply mentioned transparency. Does Australia have any say over where the money will be spent?
I may have to take that on notice as well. We have mechanisms in place to provide us visibility of where the funding is going and assurance around how that money is being spent.
What's the difference between transparency over where it's going and assurance over how it's spent? What are you intending? What's the distinction there?

Through the negotiations of the industrial uplift, we obviously negotiated with the US that that money would be spent on AUKUS related activities. That's set out in the NDAA. Those industrial uplift activities that Ms James refers to are then reported through to us. So, if there were activities on that that were not part of the agreed industrial uplift base, then that would be subject to further discussions between us and the United States through the mechanisms in the arrangements set out.

As I understand it, the appropriate mechanisms are reporting. The US reports upon where the money is expended, and that's the mechanism. Can you explain how that reporting happens. Is it quarterly? Is it monthly? Is it ad hoc? Who provides the reports?
The reporting happens with the organisation that we work with, AUKUS I&A—
We're struggling with the acronym.
We'll take it on notice.
Why don't you describe the entity to me. Is it a US Navy entity, or is it a separate government agency? What is the entity that you're engaging with?

They're set up inside the Department of War, inside the Pentagon, and they are AUKUS Integration and Acquisition—I think that is what it stands for. Essentially, they provide us with a regular report as to where those funds are being spent.
To the extent that those reports have been provided to you, could you please provide them to the committee.
Yes, we'll take that on notice.
It's important to say that we have Australians embedded in that organisation, the AUKUS I&A.
As at 30 June, I understand US$2.2 billion had been provided to the US under this AUKUS arrangement and, I assume, to that submarine security activities account. Is that right?
That's correct.
Do we know what that equated to in Australian dollars?
That is equivalent to A$3.377 billion.
I assume the amounts didn't all happen at once. That's taking into account the currency fluctuations as the payments happened. Is that right?
That takes into account the spot rate at the time the payment was made.
Have any payments been made since 30 June 2026?
No.
Are any payments expected to be made this financial year?

Currently, there are no planned payments in the current 2026-27 financial year. However, I will reiterate the previous evidence that the exact timing of those payments are at the mutual agreement of both Australia and the US.
Can you remind me again what the total envelope that's been agreed for Australia to provide to the US is?
Three billion US dollars.
Is there a deadline? Is there an end period over which that has to be provided?
There is a further US$800 million adjusted for inflation that is scheduled to be transferred within 10 years from 2026.
That's the $3 billion plus the $800 million. Is that right?
No.
That is the total, so US$2.2 billion has been paid; a remaining US$800 million is to be paid.
That's US dollars to be paid?
Correct.
Is any of that money going to the new Virginia builds, the VPM builds that have the potential to be nuclear armed? Is any of the money going to the Virginia VPM?
They're going into the Virginia class submarine industrial base. Workforce, a range of upgrades to the infrastructure—that's where we want the money to go to increase the production.

I know that we've had a discussion previously, but given these same shipyards are also building the Columbia class ICBM fleet, how much of the Australian support is also going to building the Columbia class? Do you have an analysis of the proportionality in the shipyards?
We've been given confirmation from the director of naval reactors that none of that is being directed to Columbia.

I find that some somewhat hard to understand in practice, given the same shipyards, the same workforce, the same dry docks and the same cutting sheds are being used for the Columbia class as are being used for the Virginia class. How could it possibly be the case that the Australian contributions—
It's not exactly the same work.
are not going towards the Columbia class ICBMs?
Supply chain would be different. Workforce would be very specialised. The Virginia workforce would be specialised on the Virginias; the Columbia workforce would be specialised on the Columbias.
They are the same shipyards. They use the same dry docks.
Yes, but you were drawing an analogy that—

They use the same sheets. It was the same workers to do the Columbia. They don't say, 'Okay, everybody leave who's been building the Columbias because we're now going to do something on Virginias.' It's the same workforce. It's the same infrastructure. How could it possibly be that you get an assurance that our contributions are not going towards the Columbia? It just defies common sense, doesn't it?
No. It doesn't defy common sense.

Senator, in the US, the US government is not able to accept financial contributions from foreign partners unless they are provided for providing a defence service or article or there is an authority established to accept funds for a specific purpose. As you've pointed out, the NDAA in 2024 authorises the president to accept Australian financial contributions to the US submarine industrial base via the Submarine Security Activities Account. That account is explicitly established to accept contributions from Australia for non-nuclear aspects of submarine security activities. The NDAA does not provide the authority to accept contributions for nuclear weapons programs or for the contributions to be used to fund the US nuclear weapons program.

No, but that does not prevent it from being used to fund the workforce that creates the Columbia class submarine. Given that the Virginia class submarines will have Virginia payload modules in them—the ones that are being built now, which are going to have sea launched cruise missiles that are nuclear armed—that also creates a difficulty if your assertion is true. If the money can't be used to build Columbia class submarines because they are nuclear armed, then the money can't be used to build Virginia class submarines with the Virginia payload model because they will also be nuclear armed with sea launched cruise missiles, which have a nuclear warhead.
We won't be receiving the Virginia payload module. We will be receiving the block IV Virginia class submarines.
Yes, but what's being built now is the VPM.
Ms James made it very explicit what the NDAA prohibited, and that was nuclear activities.

Vice Admiral Mead, the issue here isn't the second-hand submarines we're getting that have been built before, because that's Block IV. The issue is our financial contributions going towards what's being built now—I assume that's what they're going towards—and what's being built now is Block V with the Virginia Payload Module, which from 2032 will include nuclear-armed sea-launched cruise missiles. If what Ms James said was true, that our contributions couldn't go towards the Columbia class because they will be nuclear armed, it does seem to put a difficulty in front of you towards contributing to the Virginia Payload Module Block V, given they will also be nuclear armed. I might ask you to take this on notice, given the time: does that create a difficulty under either US or Australian law?
I said we won't be receiving the Block V, but I will take the question on notice.
Thank you.
Senator Payman.
Good evening. From 2027 under the Submarine Rotational Force-West program, Australia will host US and UK nuclear powered submarines on rotation. Is that correct?
That's correct.

I understand that as part of this operation there will be maintenance of those submarines generating low-level radioactive maintenance waste, which is planned to be stored at the Controlled Industrial Facility at HMAS Stirling; is that correct?
That's correct.
Is the Controlled Industrial Facility completed?
Let me pass that over to Mr Tim Hodgson.

No, the facility is not yet completed. It is a staged process. We have largely finished in preparation for SRF-West next year. Initially we will take low-level waste, and our ability then will build to have more improved labs and other capabilities over a period to reach full operating capability for when we become sovereign ready. It's an ongoing process, by which time we'll have the entire facility. We shall be sufficient to take low-level waste. There are things we've described before, such as rags, filters and tools. We'll be able to clean tools and return them as necessary—that type of routine maintenance activity.
Is there a rough date or idea of when this is going to reach completion? The construction is going to be complete by next year—is that what you mentioned?
As I said, it's a staged process. I'll hand over to Mr Josh Watkin for the detailed dates in the construction schedule.

As Mr Hodgson said, we have capabilities and facilities sufficient for the initial, expected low-level waste. That's in place at HMAS Stirling at the moment with the appropriate licences being finalised in readiness for Q4 next year. As those rotational forces continue, the capacity required will continue to grow. We are in the process of finalising procurement for a head contractor to develop and construct the enduring Controlled Industrial Facility. The site preparation and site-clearing activities have progressed. They are almost complete. We expect that the contract for the head contractor of the Controlled Industrial Facility will be awarded in the coming months and will be complete in the next 24-ish months, sufficiently in time to finalise testing, commissioning and being ready in all respects with the additional labs well before we require that capability and capacity in future rotational forces.
Do we know what the total cost of the construction or expected cost upon completion is? This is including all the costs of preparing the assessment documents, investigations, licensing—all of that.

I'll take that question on notice. The Controlled Industrial Facility is being designed, developed and delivered in conjunction with our delivery partners at Security and Estate Group. I'll take that on notice to provide a response.
Is there any financial arrangement with the US or UK government to recoup costs for the construction of the facility to store their radioactive waste?
No, that is not the plan. That was never agreed to.
Is there any other waste that is expected to be stored here, other than the maintenance waste from US and UK nuclear-powered submarines?

No. The only waste that will be there will be waste from routine maintenance activities, initially from US and UK submarines, to enable us to build our capability to handle this type of article. Obviously, in the longer term, it will be Australian generated waste that will be predominantly in there.
But, initially, it's for the UK and US.
For the UK and US, and it is only the low-level waste we're talking about—only those items I've already described.

Yes. Under a scenario where Australia, for whatever multitude of reasons, does not end up with its own nuclear powered submarines, Australians would have spent however much—when Mr Watkin lets us know—on a radioactive waste storage facility, which is also known as the Controlled Industrial Facility, which could be exclusively for the US and UK visiting nuclear-powered submarines; correct?
That's a hypothesis that it's difficult to answer at this stage, because we are planning against our own need, not against such a hypothesis.
I understand that, but we can still answer hypotheses. In those sorts of situations, it would be difficult for us to spend so much money to house the US and UK nuclear submarines.
All I can really talk about is our plans, and our plans don't recognise that as an occurrence. I apologise.
Thank you. That's all from me, Chair.
Are there any other senators with questions to the ASA?
I have one.
Senator McLachlan, welcome.

Admiral Mead, I asked you a question around workforce management. You're creating a very specialist workforce. I inquired around the worry that you train them and they leave, and your response then was that they're enthusiastic and have good morale. Do you have anything to enlighten us further? Has the risk of people leaving increased and, if so, how are you mitigating that? Have you, by necessity, changed your leadership or management approach?

I can talk about the Australian officers and sailors who are being trained in the US on Virginia class submarines, either in the specialised nuclear reactor courses or in other broader aspects of the Virginia class submarine. We have 200 people that have either been trained or are in the training system. We have about 60 to 70 sailors and officers at sea right now on US Virginia class submarines. The attrition rate is extremely low. I interview all the officers that go across to the US and I ask them the question: why are you transferring? Many of these people come straight in off the street. They have done basic training at our training establishments. I say, 'Why do you want to enter the nuclear powered program?' Their answers are varied but will always have the same singular answer amongst their other reasons, and that is the sense of purpose and the sense of duty in being part of a deterrent capability that will defend Australia. They are also very enthused about operating and being part of some of the most advanced and complex engineering machinery in the world.

It's a very similar answer I get when I go to the US. As I said, the attrition rate from all those people doing probably some of the hardest courses in the world and working extremely long hours to attain their qualifications is less than one per cent. We're having a magnificent success story with this, and we're also seeing this with the industrial workforce that are going across to Pearl Harbour that are being trained. We currently have about 250 ASC workers over at Pearl. About 25 or 30 have graduated and are back in Australia. We have a very low separation rate there as well. They are really excited right now, because they're working on USS Colorado, but they're really looking forward to 2027.
Are there any reservations about the allowances or remuneration that we need to reflect on going forward to maintain the workforce for your needs, both strategic and in the interim?

Defence has gone to the Defence Force Remuneration Tribunal to recognise a nuclear specialisation. My understanding is that has been successful and there are allowances that the Australian Submarine Corporation are paying their people that are over at Pearl Harbour undergoing training. That's in a way to act as a retention benefit but also to compensate them on the skill sets and the work that they have invested for the benefit of this country and their fellow countrypeople.
No further questions, Chair.
On that note, good to see you, Vice Admiral. Whether we see you next time is in question, I guess, but all the best.
Thank you very much, Chair.
I hope to see you next time but, for your sake, maybe not!
I wish the committee all the best.
Thank you. Have a lovely break and Christmas, and all the best for the future too. Thanks to all your officers as well. It was good to see you all.
Thank you very much. I wish you all an enjoyable Christmas, and I hope you all get a good break over that time period.
Let's hope so.

agency: Australian Naval Nuclear Power Safety Regulator
text:
Good evening, Chair and senators, and thank you for the opportunity to make a brief opening statement. The Australian Naval Nuclear Power Safety Regulator, ANNPSR, is independent, specialised and dedicated to the task of upholding nuclear safety for naval nuclear propulsion activities in Australia. Nuclear safety is at the centre of all of our decision-making, and, as a statutory body, ANNPSR is accountable to the parliament and, ultimately, the Australian public.

In four days time, it will be one year since ANNPSR commenced, and we've made significant progress in developing our regulatory framework, conducting licensing activities and building our technical capabilities. We've also been out engaging on our role regulating for Australia with our regulated community; our peer AUKUS nuclear powered submarine regulators; defence industry; state and local governments; community leaders, including First Nations representatives; and the Australian public. We've been actively speaking with people about nuclear safety and our part in delivering Australia's nuclear powered submarine capability, because that's what we expect of any licence applicant as well. Our regulations require that licensed applicants must undertake meaningful consultation with relevant stakeholders, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples and the broader community. This regulatory requirement enables Australians to engage and support our shared interests in keeping nuclear safety at the centre of the development of Australia's nuclear powered submarine program.

Alongside our engagement activities, ANNPSR have been getting on with the job of regulating, and our interests now spanned three key locations. Firstly, in South Australia, on 12 June this year ANNPSR issued its first licence to Australian Naval Infrastructure for the Osborne nuclear-powered-submarine construction yard, authorising them to start preparing the site for the naval nuclear propulsion facilities that will build SSN AUKUS. This licence decision is an important milestone for ANNPSR in applying our new regulations to a significant regulatory assessment. Importantly, since June we've also been back to South Australia to conduct inspections and ensure that ANI is meeting the conditions of its licence.

Secondly, at HMAS Stirling in Western Australia—since I last spoke to this committee we've been actively working with the Australian Submarine Agency to consolidate the licences they were issued by the Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency, ARPANSA, to prepare and construct the low-level radiological waste facility at HMAS Stirling. We now have a single licence to ensure continuity for nuclear safety. The scope of licence activities remains consistent with what was authorised by ARPANSA.

Finally, also in Western Australia, at the Henderson defence precinct, following the government's announcement of the precinct's footprint in August this year, we're engaging with Defence, the ASA and other stakeholders to support a shared understanding of the regulatory requirements and expectations that will need to be met to build the facilities for Australia's nuclear powered submarine sustainment over the coming decade. Being clear at the start is important so we get nuclear safety right for the long term.

To conclude, as we approach the anniversary of our first full year of regulating, I'm pleased with the progress that ANNPSR has continued to make in establishing itself as Australia's independent naval nuclear power safety regulator. Thank you, Chair, and I welcome questions.

I'd now like to welcome Abigail Bradshaw, Director-General, Australian Signals Directorate, and officers of the agency. Good evening. It's good to see you. Do you have an opening statement, by any chance, tonight?
No, Chair.
Senator Collins, do you have some questions for ASD?

Yes, I do. On 21 September, the ABC Four Corners program called 'Asleep at the wheel' exposed the cybersecurity risk to Australian motorists and to our security more generally in relation to connected vehicles. With vehicle camera technology, access to content held on drivers' phones and over-the-air data transfers, connected cars, as we've seen through that show, are sophisticated surveillance devices on wheels. The program featured a segment where the journalist was driving a new Chinese XPENG G6 EV, and a person who was identified as an insider within XPENG was able to remotely connect to the car and view every single system within the vehicle, including speed travelled, turning of the steering wheel and even the position of the seat. The insider could see exactly where the car was. The reporter said this was not a hack; it was a system feature held by the manufacturer. I'm just wondering, and perhaps the minister could help with this, what regulatory provisions do we have in Australia to protect vehicle owners from being secretly surveilled remotely by vehicle manufacturers or by a surveillance state?
Thanks for the question, Senator. Just by way of introduction, ASD is not a regulator or compliance entity.
I understand.

Our statutory responsibility relates to giving advice and assistance about cybersecurity under section 7 of the Intelligence Services Act. We have acquitted that function in relation to electric vehicles via a number of public advisories. They include the Introduction to connected vehicles, first published in June 2025; the Internet of things devices, initially published in September 2020 and then consolidated into the Personal cyber security handbook in 2026; Choosing secure and verifiable technologies in May 2024; and a variety of other related advisories. In relation to the Four Corners program you're referring to and the interaction of ASD's advisory and assistance function, I heard colleagues from the Department of Infrastructure giving evidence on this topic earlier this week, and my evidence will be consistent with that. That is that ASD has engaged with those colleagues, as the relevant regulator, to give advice on cybersecurity, and those matters inform, I think, the present position of the regulating department, which is to introduce a UN standard which would address some of the features that you've referred to that were picked up in that reporting. I'll just ask Ms Crowe to talk about the relevant standard.

The relevant standard is the United Nations Regulations No. 155 and No. 156, related to cybersecurity, and also over-the-air updates relevant to the Four Corners program. There are two risks that are consistent with the advice that ASD has stated publicly already in our advisory from June last year. Those are the unauthorised recording risk as well as remote access to vehicle functions. In our advisory, we set out advice for individuals concerning both of those risks. We talk about the primary risk being that connected vehicles collect extensive amounts of data due to their connected nature—with the infotainment systems as well as other features in the vehicle—and there are settings that you can undertake to minimise the amount of data that is sent back to the manufacturer as well as how you should secure the connected services related to your vehicle such as the applications that can remotely lock or unlock cars or change settings in the vehicle remotely.

Minister Watt, you might be able to help with this. It's good to have advice, and such a huge part of it is the education piece. But are there any protections or regulations in place for consumers, for drivers of connected cars? What do we have?
As Ms Bradshaw mentioned, the infrastructure and transport department plays that regulatory role.
Yes, I didn't actually hear. I wanted to go back to that.

I'm aware that they are currently doing some further work in this space. I must admit I'm not aware of what the current regulations are, but I'm sure there'd be information you can get from that department.
Does ASD receive any reports about any kind of hacking or—what do we call it?—system override, that sort of thing?
I don't recall receiving any such reports. I'll just check with Ms Crowe.
No, that's right. We have not received reports of that in Australia.

But of course we are aware of the public reporting, and we have engaged with peak bodies that relate to the motor vehicles industry. In fact, we engaged with those bodies as we were drafting the Introduction to connected vehicles last year.
You engaged with the car manufacturers?
Yes.
So you're aware of the different systems and—
We are aware of the different systems and the very different views amongst the different manufacturers.
What sort of different views?
Well, there is not one cohesive view on issues such as data management. It would depend on the vendor.

I'm not going to speak to intelligence assessments in this forum, but that's obviously why we are under the jurisdiction of the PJCIS. Our public advisory is on the basis of our technical understanding of Internet of Things systems.
So you've engaged with every different manufacturer of an EV or connected car?
No. We have engaged with—Ms Crowe might remind me of the name.
The Australian Automotive Association.
Which one was that?
The Australian Automotive Association, AAA.
So it's not an actual manufacturer but a—
It is a peak body.
Was that to understand the different models that were coming through? I thought you were trying to understand the different systems.

That was for the purpose of ensuring that the public advisory which we put out, which we publish on cyber.gov.au, did in fact pick up those issues, not just that we were seeing from a technical perspective but engaging with the peak to understand it from the motor vehicle association perspective.

I was confused by that. You weren't understanding the different systems and their capabilities to get this data and information or control from afar; you were engaging with the peak body. What were the different views about? Can you just go into that a little bit more just so I can understand?

Well, there are different views amongst vendors, for example, about data retention. They have their own views about where data should be held. For example, quite often if you buy a connected vehicle, for servicing purposes, you might be tethered to the manufacturer. There are views about whether there should be more freedom in relation to movement amongst the market.
In what sorts of places could data be held? You said that they would have different views about where the data could be held—the data retention.

Well, it depends on where the vendor is and what the arrangements are for the connected vehicle. A vehicle which is being updated via the internet, for example, might have connectivity to a vehicle and might be being updated from offshore.
We don't have any protections in place to keep that data onshore. How much of that data, in your assessment, would be going offshore?
I'm sorry. I wouldn't have a view of that.
We don't make any electric vehicles here in Australia, do we, so all the manufacturers would be offshore. Were there any car manufacturers that were keeping the data onshore?
I'm sorry. I think that's really a question for the relevant department that is setting standards for vehicles.
But you had the conversations with the AAA and you were discussing the views on retention.
Yes.

In those discussions, did anybody indicate that they would rather keep it onshore? You talked about where you're going to keep it and obviously it's all going offshore, so let's just talk through that discussion.
Sorry. What I said was we talked with the AAA in order to get an informed view from a peak body that was actually associated with, in this case, the vehicle sector.
So it's the consumers, not the manufacturers?

Correct. Well, no; it's actually both. We did not in the course of those interactions seek advice on statistics on the manufacturer or how much data was here. That really would be beyond the scope, I think, of ASD's function, and our focus is really on the connectivity rather than the operation of the vehicle.
The scope of the discussion was about the connectivity. What was the scope of the discussion about?

The scope of the discussion was initiated on our end because we knew that, despite the fact that we had a whole bunch of information public facing on Internet of Things devices and the cybersecurity measures that we recommend in relation to using those devices, there was a need to now address questions that were being raised around connected vehicles as a newer entry into the market, so we engaged with the peak body—as we quite often do when we're writing advice for a sector—in order to ensure that our advice was going to meet the market need in terms of a general Australian public who would want advice on cybersecurity for connected vehicles.
Did you meet with the federal chamber that represents the manufacturers?
I did not.

It's very difficult, at the stage that it's at, to be able to protect consumers because it looks like we don't really have progress in that. You understand the security risks of these connected vehicles, so have you given any advice to the government about what they can do to better protect consumers here in Australia?

We have given advice consistent with the advice that's contained in our public advisory, including those measures that mitigate or address those risks. We have given advice, as I mentioned and as Ms Crowe mentioned, to the regulator of the relevant sector, and that is the department of infrastructure.
Just to be clear, the advice that you give on connected cars is all publicly available?
That's right. It's on cyber.gov.au.
On 22 June the ASD stopped publishing routine tender notices. Is that correct?
That is correct. I'll get the chief operating officer to explain the context.

That would be correct for the financial year going forward—for this current financial year onwards. It was about us reviewing a range of information that we had in the public domain. It began with the review of our annual report, and from the committee there was advice to look at how we had different reporting arrangements. From that, we then did a thorough review about other information. Consistent with the other national intelligence agencies, including ASIO, we commenced a process to not report against AusTender.
Can you just give a, I guess—I'm sorry; it's so late at night. Can you give a more concise answer as to why there's no public visibility on that anymore?

Senator, I'll help the chief operating officer. In the course of producing our last annual report, it was highlighted to us that we were including information that was in addition to and in excess of information which was being released by other intelligence agencies. In the context of the present threat environment—in particular, foreign interference—we looked at the sort of material that was being released in those AusTender details. It included, for example, information and specifics around the quanta and type of software or ICT products which we were using. In the context of our function of the current foreign interference environment of the fact that we are overseen by the PJCIS—and that information is available to the PJCIS—and to be consistent with the rest of the intelligence agencies we transitioned to align with their reporting processes from this new financial year.
I understand. Surely not everything is sensitive, though, because you would have things like cleaning contracts. Procurement is one thing, but things like services—

That's right. The standard we apply—the chief operating officer will help me out, as he did the detailed work here—was to align with the disclosures made by the other intelligence agencies. We've aligned ourselves, for example, with those disclosures that are made by ASIO.
Does that mean that you will still publish some tenders?

In looking at what the other national intelligence agencies did—and we had traditionally exempted a range of different contracts; we had never always fully published all of our contracts—the approach that they were taking was to not publish the full range of contracts, because, even to the point of the cleaning contract, there would be information there that, to Ms Bradshaw's comment about the foreign interference, would suggest an avenue of information.
Why didn't you do this from the beginning? If the other agencies have been doing this for so long, why now?

It's a great question. I asked myself that. It hadn't occurred to me that there was a differentiation. ASD didn't become an independent statutory agency until 2018, and, because it was born, if you like, out of the Department of Defence, at the time that it was part of the Department of Defence and didn't have a separate identity, there was a different risk profile with the detailed disclosure, because they were buried in inside of a much larger department. It wasn't looked at at the point at which ASD transitioned out and became a statutory agency. It was the review of the annual report that brought the matter to our attention.
Who reviewed it? Who brought it to your attention?
This committee's review of our annual report in 2025.
Oh, we did! Now we want to know all about it!
Those annual reports that we do are fantastic and lead to some wonderful reforms. I'm mindful Senator Pocock might need to go to another committee.

Thank you very much, Senator Collins. Thank you for your time this evening. I'm interested to ask about the PHP, the hypertext preprocessor issues. What date did you first learn about the PHP2Shell vulnerability?

We had advice earlier. Around mid-October we were advised by OpenAI that their security research had identified a vulnerability on PHP and that a patch to address that vulnerability was being worked on. The normal process in the case of a vulnerability which does not have a patch and there is no evidence of that vulnerability being exploited either in Australia or globally, which was the case with PHP, is to wait until a patch is available. The alternative, which is to advise people that there's a vulnerability, runs the risk of the availability of that vulnerability being discovered by people who would use it for malicious purposes, so, following that process, we were working up to a planned disclosure process when the patch became available. Unfortunately, a third party disclosed the vulnerability early, which is actually inconsistent with well-understood traffic-light procedures.
My understanding was they released it six hours early, so it wasn't a huge change in the timeline.
I'm not sure that six hours is right. Do you recall?
What's your understanding of when OpenAI were going to tell the world?
They were planning to release that publicly on 22 October. We found out about the unintended disclosure on the 21st—24 hours, thereabouts, beforehand. It was supposed to be released.
Not a huge difference. What date in mid-October did OpenAI tell you that there was an issue?
On 12 October.
Did OpenAI tell you when they were first aware of the vulnerability?
I don't know the answer to that question.
Maybe take it on notice, then.

I will take that on notice. What I will say is that, as a consequence of the OpenAI incident, we have worked with OpenAI on instant reporting protocols to improve the reporting that occurred in the case of the websites that were impacted. One of the principles under the revised and agreed incident reporting protocols is for early notification. In this case, this was early notification in the sense that it was notification of a vulnerability prior to the availability of a patch, in the course of a patch being worked up.

From what I can see, OpenAI first found out about this along with the Calif researcher, Ryan Austin, on the 11th. They took a month to let the Australian government know. Do you think that, in the wake of—
Sorry, I don't have access to that information. I'm not sure.
Just going on what's on the internet.
Can you help us out with the name of the report where that's stated?

It's probably been reported in a bunch of news sites. That's why I asked when OpenAI first knew because you'd think, in the wake of hacking Medicare, that they'd probably take less time than a month to let ASD know, but I understand you probably can't comment if you don't know when they actually found out. But, maybe on notice, can you comment on when OpenAI told you they first found this vulnerability and your comments on their timeliness in letting you know. You said you're working with OpenAI more closely now. Do you have access to Daybreak?
Yes.

When did you receive that access? Maybe, while you're looking for that: in response to a question on notice about which government agencies have access to Daybreak, OpenAI said that it was prioritising access to 'affected entities', but they also listed the Vic department of government services as having been given access. Were they hacked as well?
It was the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare and National Notifiable Disease Surveillance System, and the Victorian department of health was one of the websites.
Sure, but they said they'd given access to the Vic department of government services. Do you know why they've given them access?

I don't know why they've given them access. Having spoken to OpenAI, whilst it is right that I have read their public apology on 29 September and, in that public statement, they indicated that they would provide assistance to impacted entities, I am also aware that they've suggested that they would make Daybreak or other assistance available more broadly.
I see that two New South Wales men are facing charges for accessing restricted government data. Why is OpenAI not facing the same legal consequences?
Sorry, Senator; that really is a matter for the Attorney-General's Department or the Australian Federal Police.

Okay, I'll put it to them, then. Do you have any intelligence that suggests that the hack that occurred around the world at the same time as the Medicare hack was part of a deliberate strategy from OpenAI to identify cybersecurity weaknesses?
I don't.

Have you asked them about that? I mean, they say that they didn't intend this, and the bots were just looking for information, but do you have intelligence looking at whether or not they actually deliberately did this?
I've read OpenAI's open apology of the 29th.
Who's trusting Sam Altman? I'm interested in beyond that. Do you have any—

I think that's actually a question that you should put to OpenAI. I can take their statement—both the public statement and their advice to us—on face value. Their statement to us is consistent with the statement which was made on 29 September. That statement indicates that they were testing a model not publicly available without sufficient guardrails and human oversight, and that the model was being tested to answer questions in relation to medical research. That is their public statement about what has happened here.

I will add, on the phase that we are going through at the moment in relation to AI and these models, that the present cadre of frontier models happen to be very good at coding and reasoning. So the fact of finding vulnerabilities of itself is the purpose, actually, of the models. I would be in violent agreement with you if what you are proposing is that there ought to be stricter controls and greater human oversight of the development and testing of those models.

It just seems a bit suss that you've got a company that finds all these vulnerabilities and says: 'Oh, we didn't mean it, but here's a solution. Have this solution to protect yourselves from us.' I think there's a healthy degree of scepticism amongst the public. Finally, in that same response to a question on notice from OpenAI, they said that access to Daybreak can be facilitated through a third party. Do you know who these third parties are?

It may be a variety of hyperscalers or others. I just want to answer your question. We got access to Daybreak on 11 August. Can I just explain that Daybreak is in fact more complex than it sounds. It is a model which is not available publicly, and therefore there are various versions that don't have safeguards which are available publicly. I can tell you from experience it is a difficult thing; you don't simply just turn on Daybreak or these frontier models. There are a variety of security protocols that you need to go through in order to harness the models securely and, in fact, to set rules around data retention and other conditions of use to the benefit of both the user as well as the provider. So the process of utilising Daybreak is not a is not a simple one.
How long will the $10 million in credits last?
That depends entirely on the usage by the entity and the way the tokens operate; generally, the more complex the prompt, the more tokens will be used.
How many tokens have ASD used so far since 11 August?
That sort of information about the rate at which ASD consumes frontier capabilities is really more a matter for the PJCIS, I'm afraid.
So the public won't know how long the $10 million will last us?
That is actually a matter—the $10 million is provided to the entities, not to ASD. It's a credit for them.
Sure, but if people won't tell us how many tokens they're using, then it's very hard to know how long it's going to last us.

That is really a matter for the entities that enter into an agreement to have the Daybreak access. That, of its own, is a matter for each one of those entities. I just can't tell you what ASD uses, but ours is not part—

Can you explain—crossbenchers aren't allowed on PJCIS. It is only for the major parties. What would you be giving away if you told us how many tokens you're using on Daybreak? I think most Australians would expect you're using as many as you need or as many as possible.
Because the rate of consumption of tokens would give an indication of ASD's capability to use tokens for intelligence purposes.
So if it's low, people might think, 'Oh dear, you can't do it.' Fair enough. Thank you very much. I appreciate your time.
Any other questions, colleagues?
I have a couple of follow-up ones on that topic.
Sure.
It would be ASD's role to advise ministers on that particular hack. Is that correct? Are you giving advice on that?
Are you talking about the OpenAI incident?
Yes.
Yes.
Are you aware of when the Prime Minister first became aware of the incident?
I'm not sure that I do know exactly when he became aware of the incident.
You didn't break the news to him?
No.
Did the government inform you about it?
Did the government advise us when they advised the Prime Minister?
Yes.

No, we were not aware—we were aware generally that because of the significance and context of the matter that it would be a matter that would be briefed up to the Prime Minister, particularly in the context of him being at the UN.
So when they advised the Prime Minister, the government came to you and then you briefed the Prime Minister on what it all meant.
No, we did not. ASD did not brief the Prime Minister.
You didn't provide any advice on it at all?
Not to the Prime Minister. We most certainly did to ministers.
Which ministers were they?
I have spoken with Minister Burke and Minister Gallagher. Ms Crowe has spoken with the Deputy Prime Minister.
That's right.
Other ministers?
Minister Gallagher and Minister Burke.
Yes.
Why not the Prime Minister?

Because there were others who were reporting that advice to him from us. We don't necessarily brief him personally on every issue but ensure that officers that do brief him have it. I also think he was involved in international travel.
The Deputy Prime Minister at the time was the Acting Prime Minister.
Sorry, I beg your pardon. That's correct.
So he was off to New York, and two weeks after the notification, he revealed the incident. Why did it take so long to notify the public of it? Are you aware of that?

I think as the Deputy Prime Minister Marles and Minister Gallagher said publicly during their statement, the incident was reported via an email to Services Australia as a vulnerability disclosure on 10 September. On 15 September, Services Australia shared that email advice with ASD. ASD immediately reached out to OpenAI to get more content. At that stage, given the nature of the advice from OpenAI, which was a vulnerability disclosure, it was being treated as exactly that. As we've discussed this evening with Senator Pocock, it is certainly a very normal process for ASD to deal with a vulnerability disclosure, and it is, in fact, part and parcel of the mainstream work of OpenAI and others to work with researchers to discover vulnerabilities.

The novel aspects of this incident were not disclosed until the morning of Sunday the 20th. Those are features such as the fact that the vulnerability was discovered during model testing; that it was what we would describe as a misaligned model—that is, a model doing things that it was not intended to do; that it was an agent involved; that the model was not publicly available; that the model, or the agent, had undertaken unauthorised access; and that the model had operated without safeguards. All of those aspects did not become clear and were not communicated at a senior level by OpenAI until Sunday the 20th, at which stage we had organised a technical engagement, because there is a process of verification which is required. Technical verification requires logs, to assure ourselves that the technical advice contained in the email is practically true. On Sunday the 20th, that was the point at which this matter was elevated. I spoke with ministers on the Sunday morning, and then a process of briefing began quickly after that. Then, as I mentioned and as the DPM and Minister Gallagher mentioned, we had the technical exchange on the 22nd.

It wasn't with the Prime Minister until all that time. You did all that testing in between. It had gone from Services Australia to you. You engaged with OpenAI. That took 12 days, and then you informed the Prime Minister and the DPM, who was Acting Prime Minister here. Is that correct?

We got the initial advice around 5.30 on the evening of the 15th. We immediately, an hour after receiving that advice, reached out to OpenAI—an hour later. As I said to you, we did not get confirmation of the novel aspects of what had actually occurred from a senior level out of OpenAI until Sunday the 20th. That's five days—actually, it's four if you discount the hour—and then two days—

That's right. I'm just trying to work out when it got across to the Prime Minister. We want to understand when the Prime Minister was first made aware of it. Do you know when he was first made aware of it?
I'm sorry, I do not.
Were you informed the Prime Minister would reveal the OpenAI incident from New York on the 26th?
I should just clarify also that, as Ms Crowe's mentioned, the Deputy Prime Minister was the Acting Prime Minister.
Yes, that's right.
Can you confirm that briefing time for the Deputy Prime Minister as the Acting Prime Minister?
I briefed him on—
That's okay. I would prefer to know more about the revelation of the incident in New York—whether you were aware that it was going to be revealed there in New York.
No.
No.
Did the PM&C or PMO request any information from ASD for that press conference?
ASD routinely briefed ministers' offices ahead of that, but we were not involved in determining the nature of when or how that statement would occur.
You mentioned before the word 'novel'. Is the attack methodology itself novel?

Absolutely, yes. As the Deputy Prime Minister said during the press conference with Minister Gallagher, in and of itself, the incident and the consequences of the unauthorised access are not the serious aspect of this, nor is the vulnerability, frankly, in what is a public-facing website that is designed to store aggregated statistical information. The novel aspects of this are that it was during model testing and that it was a misaligned model—that is, it is an agent that is working in a way that is not intended by the operators of that model. The risk of misalignment and the fact that that occurred on Australian infrastructure is the first time that that has occurred in Australia that we know of and, probably to my knowledge, the second destination in the world.
Could an individual have gained the same unauthorised access to the Medicare information without the use of AI?

I'm not sure about the answer to that. I think it would actually depend on how long an individual persisted with that sort of attack. I mean, we are talking here about a very powerful model in a testing mode, and we know that those models are capable of detecting vulnerability in code that are not actually able to be found, or not without enormous effort, by a human.
How can you be sure that no other attacks have happened on Australian networks before?
Well, I can't be.
One final question on the tenders: was the decision to stop publishing tenders a decision of government or was that a decision of ASD?
It was my advice.
Your advice to government?
Yes.
Thank you very much.
I don't believe there are any other questions. On that note—
I didn't do an opening statement but, if you don't mind—
Yes, please do.

We did release this week the annual threat report. We did talk in that threat report about a really dynamic time in terms of the cyber context. From an ASD perspective, we are, as set out in that report, responding to a significant uptick in cyberattacks, some of which are associated with AI and the capacity to identify vulnerabilities, which, paradoxically, is also the same sort of technology that's going to change our prospects. Our incident workload has doubled. Twelve months ago, we were managing about 40 incidents at a time. As of today, we are managing over 100. Critical vulnerabilities are accelerating. We're tracking 261 critical vulnerabilities in the last seven days. Published vulnerabilities this time last year were 4,274. Today they are 15,719. In that context, I want to thank the officers of ASD who protect our digital networks and also CISOs all over Australia who are defending those digital networks. As people go off to Christmas this year and have their video calls with loved ones or stream Die Hard or Love Actually, whichever genre you're into, or you're downloading your recipes—
Or watching the Australians play cricket—I don't know.

Yes, streaming Australians playing cricket, buying tickets for a holiday, doing your shopping online, the defenders of those digital networks will be hard at work making sure that that happens. For the ASD officers and for CISOs in industry that work with us, I want to thank them.

Indeed, yes. I'll give you a bit of a shout-out this week in the media about that report. Well done. It's scary stuff, but I think it's fair to say there were five essential actions that people and businesses need to take note of. It is worth reading it. What was the website again?
It is cyber.gov.au.
Please log on and download what you can.
Thank you for the for the call-out.
On that note, thank you very much. Now we're going to move on to Defence Housing Australia. We've agreed to release the Defence and Veterans' Service Commission. Sorry about that. Have a good night.
Hello, Mr Jaggers.
Good evening.
I'm glad you're still smiling. Do you have an opening statement?
Chair, with your indulgence, I wouldn't mind making a very short statement of condolence.
Given the time, we're happy table it and have it circulated to the committee, unless there's something that you really needed to verbalise from it.
No, that's okay. I don't have it in written form, but we can provide it to the committee after.
Thank you. If you can get your office to forward a copy, an electronic version, I'd much appreciate that. Senator Collins, did you have a question or two?

My question is about the Defence estate and the divestiture. Have you been engaged by the Department of Defence, the Department of Finance or the Security and Estate Group in the Department of Defence in relation to any of the land that they will be selling?

We have had some discussions with the Department of Defence and the Department of Finance in relation to the audit process or the estate sale process. We've had some engagement with the Department of Finance since they have taken carriage of the matter in relation to a number of sites of interest.
Which sites are of interest?

We've had some preliminary discussions with them. The Department of Finance is running a process in relation to the sale of those sites, so I don't think it would be appropriate for us to be signalling those publicly. We may be involved in procurement processes down the track.
I understand. Have you had any discussions about remediation of sites and whose responsibility that would be?

I don't believe we've been discussing remediation of individual sites. We've probably had some general discussions with the Department of Finance, because DHA has been involved in the remediation and preparation of sites for housing.
Did you say DDA?

DHA has been involved in the remediation of a range of ex-Defence sites in the past, so we've had some discussions with Department of Finance about those processes but as more of an informal exchange of information as an agency that may be able to help with some knowledge in that space.
How has it worked previously? If you've bought Defence land that needed remediation, who's done the remediating?
We have bought sites or had sites provided to DHA in the past where DHA has managed the remediation of those locations.
Even the ones that you buy, you pay for, you have to bear the cost of the remediation?

I imagine it's a general principle that the state of the site is factored into the transfer arrangements. There have certainly been instances in the past where DHA has been given access to land without having to purchase it and examples where there have been some acquisition costs, as well.
Derwent Barracks has been handed over to the Department of Finance. Have you been talking about that with the Department of Finance?
I think our conversations have been mostly of a general nature about the process.
The evidence given to us last week by Mr West at a Defence estate hearing was that he'd been in discussions with you about Randwick Barracks. Is that correct?

There are a number of sites where DHA has a current interest, either looking after houses on those locations or where there had been a proposal previously put that DHA may assist with some development onsite. I think Randwick Barracks is one of those locations, so we would expect some ongoing discussion with Defence about that site.
What's the current need? How many houses does DHA need to build or buy at the moment?
I'll ask Mr West—our Mr West, not Mr West from Defence—to provide some detail.
Sorry. I'll make sure I differentiate.
We currently have a portfolio that we look after of around 17,800 homes, and we have projections to grow that over the next three or four years. Mr West can provide the forecast.

Yes, that's right. We've got just under 18,000 properties at the moment. We have an annual process with Defence that determines what the future requirements look like. We're in the throes of doing the most recent one at the moment, so we haven't formally responded to them on that, but the expectation is that, over the next four years, we'll grow the portfolio by around 1,500 properties—1,200 or 1,500. But that number, obviously, is subject to an annual process so may change in subsequent annual processes as well.
That's 1,500 houses over four years. Is that particularly around bases like Osborne, or is that right across the country?
It is concentrated in a number of regions, yes. It's not universal. There are a number of regions where there is a higher requirement. Adelaide—Osborne—is one of those regions where we see growth.
Do you have the space for it out there? Do you have the land that you need, or is it going to be difficult?

If I take a step back for a moment, most of our portfolio—about two-thirds of our portfolio—is leased property, not properties that we own. Going forward, we expect a similar proportion, if not slightly more, to continue to be leased. So it's not a matter of whether or not we've got the land available or the ability to build in the region; it's whether or not we can provide them through a combination of acquisition and/or leasing and constructing ourselves in locations where we do have land. That kind of varies, as Mr Jaggers said before. We have a range of sites that we have previously obtained from Defence where we will build, but there are only a limited number across the country.
Alright. Thank you very much. Thank you, Chair.
You're welcome. My pleasure.
I did wait for you.
Good on you. Mr Jaggers, thank you to you and your team. Have a good night.
Now we're going to have before us the Director of Military Prosecutions, Air Commodore Sara Gul. We're a bit pressed for time, with the 12 minutes we have left. Welcome, Air Commodore Gul.
Thank you very much.
Sorry you had to wait a bit long tonight. Do you have an opening statement at all?
I don't.
Fantastic. Senator Collins, you've got some questions for Air Commodore Gul?

I do. We've had recent legislative change, and I want to understand it a bit better. What was the problem we were trying to fix there? The explanation of the legislation was that the government was trying to align the defence minister's powers with the Attorney-General's powers, but are there any examples of where that was needed previously or might be needed in the future? What's the problem that was really trying to be fixed there?

Ultimately, that's not a matter for me, and that's because I'm the subject of potential directions rather than the person conceiving of why those directions might be needed. If some context is helpful, I was appointed on 10 August this year, so I'm just over two months into the role. As I understand it, the discretion to commence or to discontinue prosecutions under section 87 of the Defence Force Discipline Act will remain at my discretion. But, as to the intention of the legislature in introducing that section, ultimately that's not a question for me.

But it does say in the legislation that the minister will have the power to direct in relation to prosecutions. They're the words in the legislation if I remember them correctly, and it was pretty specific in the way that it said that the DMP must comply with the direction. But you've just given evidence that you'll have discretion in that. So how does that work, if it's in the legislation?

In terms of the changes to the act recently, and the ministerial guidelines, that was more about the efficient operation of the Director of Military Prosecutions. There is an annual report from the director. It's a ministerial appointment, so it is designed for that ministerial oversight. But the independence of the prosecutor—on what they choose to prosecute and not—is as the DMP has said.

Okay. But I do remember it very specifically, because I went around and around in circles with the minister's office as well on this and that. Yes, you're absolutely right, Lieutenant General; the first half of it was about the guidelines and the policy. That's right, and that's pretty straightforward. I don't think anybody would disagree with that. But the second part was about being able to direct on prosecutions, which was the bit that stood out to me. There was no wriggle room in that in terms of the discretion in the way that the language was set out. I know you've only been in the role for two months and, clearly, you haven't been directed to prosecute anybody yet or stop prosecutions. I'm just trying to understand why that particular clause was put into the Defence Act. What problem was it trying to fix there?
It was for parliamentary oversight.
So closing the distance between the military justice system and the parliament.
And it's similar to what the CDPP has, as well, so it was bringing that, in a comparator sense.
Yes, but the CDPP oversees the civil justice system.
Yes.

The military justice system is, by design, separate—always has been, which is why we have the Director of Military Prosecutions. But now we've got an executive member that has power over the Director of Military Prosecutions. So—
Not for the purpose of the prosecution. That lies within the power of the Defence Act under the DMP.
But there is that clause in that particular part—schedule 5, part 10—where the minister can direct the DMP to begin or stop a prosecution. It's what is in there.
I'll take that on notice.
That would be great. Thank you very much. Maybe, while you're here, we could go to the broadening of the definition of investigation officers. Would that be in your remit?
It's not in my remit, Senator. Investigations sit more broadly with Defence. Effectively, I don't own investigations; I consider briefs once they've come to me from investigators.

Okay. Another change in that particular bill was that the DMP could represent in a federal court. Has the DMP needed to before and not been able to do that? What sorts of cases would that be in relation to? What's the necessity for that change?

As I understand it, and I'll just bring up the section, the DMP has always been empowered to appear in, effectively, appellate-style proceedings. That's either appeal proceedings in the DFDAT, the Defence Force Discipline Appeal Tribunal, or the Federal Court. Federal Court matters generally come up when, for example, a person is seeking judicial review or they're seeking a statement of what the law is and how it applies. As I perceive it, the DMP has had the ability to appear in that jurisdiction previously. Realistically speaking, it's something that's rarely utilised or rarely needed.
Has the government forecast any directions to you yet?
There's going to be a consultation process.
On what?
On the directions.
What sorts of directions?

This goes back to your original question, which is the power that the minister has to issue directions. The section is 188GAA of the DFDA. As part of that there'll be a consultation process as to what they contain and how they apply.
So it's not actually written into the legislation yet—you guys are still yet to design what the powers actually look like?
Again, it's not for me to design, but I expect that I'll be consulted in respect of them.
What do you foresee the powers, the directions, to look like? What do you think they're going to be?

It wouldn't be appropriate for me to speculate, but, as I understand it, the intention of the legislature is not to subvert my authority; it's to set down guidelines in respect of procedural matter probity, record keeping and the like. Section 87 of the DFDA means that I stay independent and that the discretion to prosecute or not will stay with me.

But that consultation process hasn't happened yet, so it's clearly not set out in the legislation as it stands, that independence. I guess it's up to the negotiating power between the DMP and the DPM.

I wouldn't describe it as a relationship of negotiating power. They're directions that are to be issued to me and that will go through the ordinary process of consultation, as I understand it, when it comes to setting down legislative instruments, which is what these directions will be.
Sorry—the directions will be what? Legislative instruments?

Yes, as I understand it. That was the amendment, as I understand you saw it on the last occasion, so that parliament can disallow that instrument if a decision is made or a direction is made that doesn't meet the satisfaction of parliament.

That's right. Before we get there, though, before the direction comes to you, the direction has to come through parliament, and the parliament or Senate can disallow it. But, first, you're going through a consultation process on what the directions look like, so can you give us a sense of the scope of directions?
Not yet.
Senator, my understanding is they're still being drafted and they're not ready for consultation.
What about the guidelines?
Perhaps I've misperceived your question. That's what I thought we were talking about: the guidelines.
Senator, they're the same thing.
The amendment—

In the actual legislation there were two parts to that particular section. One was about policy and guidelines, and the other part was directly in relation to prosecutions. I guess we'll just have to wait and see how those consultations pan out.
